SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION
Interview with Sam Wooding
by Chris Albertson
Washington, D. C.
April 22 - May 8, 1975

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5395
rfm
P R O C E E D I N G S
Okay, this is Chris Albertson interviewing Sam Wooding, April 22, 1975
I think we should start with, Sam, where you were born and when you were born.

Well, Chris, I was born in Philadelphia. June 17, 1895. Well, at that time, most of the black people lived in South Philadelphia, so where we have -- my father was lucky enough to have his own home, it was rather small. But all three of, our four children, were born at 1119 Rodman St., where we grew up until the place had become in such a condition that we couldn't live there because my mother had -- and father had a daughter, and the place had been going rather bad. So he decided to move to another place.
What sort of business was he in?

Well, my father was what we called in those days, a butler. He worked for a very fine family, in fact one of the first families of Philadelphia, the Biddles. He worked at a place on 1420 Walnut St., and there he had to do most all -- he was the butler and the steward and everything else, because he had to do all the buying, he had to wait the tables, and he did all, in fact he was the handyman in the family.
Mm-huh. And, was he into music at all?
How did that come about?

No, I'll tell you. If he was in music, he kept it quiet. I never knew that. And I'll tell you why. How he -- he was a lover of his own people. So, when we heard- I must have been about six or seven years old, when he heard there was a colored show coming to town, he immediately got his wife, my mother, and the four children together and took us to the theater. But, at that time, we were not in Philadelphia, because every summer he worked in Atlantic City at the Brighton Hotel. And by working at the Brighton Hotel, sometimes he had a day off. So, he was a waiter there -- so he said to my mother that he would like for us all to see this show.

Before that, I was supposed to be a dentist, in their mind. My one brother was supposed to be a doctor. My older brother was supposed to be a preacher, and my sister was supposed to be a nurse. But, only two of these things happened. That is, my brother turned into be Cornelius Wooding he turned into be one of the finest doctors in Philadelphia. And I turned out to be a hambone musician in Atlantic City.
(laugh)

Now, well, where I got my inspiration was, when we went to this theater, we saw Williams and Walker. Williams Bert Williams was a great comedian, George Walker was a dancer, and George's wife was also a dancer and a singer.
But the thing that puzzled me mostly, was the man in the

pit. There was a fellow named James Vaughan, I think his name was. Well, he was conductor of this orchestra. Now, so I can tell you, that's what I wanted to do. And I worked a long -- it took me forty years to get to that place, where I conducted something. But I eventually got there.

Now, it was really a treat for me, at my age, to have seen Bert Williams do his slide, his funny slides, and tell his jokes. And George Walker, who was the greatest of the strutters. He could strut better than anybody. In fact, the strut, I think the black people took from the horses. Not the race horses, the show horses. And I think the way they'd raise their legs and throw it, just like you see a race horse, a show horse, not a race horse. But, Ada Walker was a very clever singer.

Well, these things impressed me. And then, there was another man in that show called Will Marion Cook. Will Marion Cook had a group, and they did the different songs, I think was one was Exaltation, and then all of these fellows'd meet and another song, that's stayed with me a long time, because the words are, 'Brother, should smote on the right cheek, turn the other one around.' And, you know, 'there's not going to be any rain if you hear the dog barking', and things like that.

Well, these things all excited me. After that, I wasn't much good for education. So, we come back to Philadelphia and I wasn't doing so well in public school. In fact, I went to the public school and the first day I was there, I got into a

fight. A guy hit me with an orange peel, and we went to fight, and Old Man Jacobs of Jen Kins Quince and Pine [streets] told me after lunch, that that evening he was going to take care of me. So, I told my mother, and she said, "You're not going back there any more for him to take care of you. I'm going to put you in the Catholic School." At that time, it was a Catholic school, at 12th and Lombard. And this school was more missionary in those days. All the Catholic schools for blacks were missionaries mostly.

And so, I went to this school clean up until I was six years old and I turned out fairly good there, because for two years I didn't miss a Mass, and -- but they couldn't convert me, for some reason. In fact, I've been struggling to try to be converted up 'til now, and so far I haven't been successful. So, anyhow, as things went on, I began to take to thinking of Bert Williams and George Walker, and Vaughan, I began to think about them so much that I wasn't doing much in school.

My mother had an organ. She used to sing sometimes, "Jesus, lover of all my soul", and I can hear some of these women singing now the way she was just singing. Anyhow, she'd sit down there and play for you with two fingers, "Jesus, lover of all my soul", and belt it out.
But when we'd get on the organ, I had a teacher, but this fellow would do a whole lot of sleeping. And as he was
asleep, I'd go in to try to play one of these ragtime things. Course we didn't know anything about swing and bop and those things then. It was only the ragtime, see.
Is that what the music was when you heard Walker and Williams? That was ragtime music then?

Yes, there was only ragtime music and carnival music, that's all they used in those days. See, because we hadn't got up to the place, And, you see, the blacks were the first ones to use four-four. And have any ragtime at all.

The white Americans had come from Europe. They only knew of two types of time. And that was the waltz, like the Strauss waltzes, and the one-step. So, you see they didn't know anything about what we were doing. And that's why we called it 'ragtime', because, most of us -- it was such a thing that -- it wasn't thought much of. Because my parents, they certainly didn't want me to play a ragtime, because they said, "Only bums play ragtime." And I didn't know that I was going to be a bum later.
(laugh)

But they only said -- and there was only one thing that was going to happen to me for playing ragtime -- you'd end up with consumption, tuberculosis, or you'd end up in somebody's penitentiary. So, for being too smart. So they said -- after they found that I was going to play the music, anyhow, they said, maybe

"Well, let's give him a good musical education so that he can play on the church choir," Cause we were all members of Bethel AME Church. That was the church founded by Richard Allen. He was one of the first black bishops in the Methodist Conference, and he had a church down at Sixth and Lombard. Well, we used to go down there every Sunday. And we'd play around there and even go down around his tomb. They've got him buried in there.

But I didn't think much of that, because, on the corner was a saloon. And while these people'd be in there playing, all like that, another crowd was hanging in the saloon, and the man -- the church couldn't move him because, at every rally, he gave the church $50.00 or $100.00, so he went on down there so, right from the beginning I wasn't so for religion anyhow. But I tried to get it, but I got out there and they shouted over me, and stomped and dust and stuff up, but it didn't work.
So --

What I decided to do was, I wanted to play what was called ragtime then, because we didn't know anything else, so I had a friend of ours, and we got together and started playing these little rags, or what we could get together. First thing we started in. And the funny thing, all the music that I could read was in the key, like, F, C, E-flat and B-flat. But we started our rag in F-sharp. And we played F-sharp for quite awhile. You know, F-sharp is -- and C-sharp, then we got
on to C-sharp. I still can't play -- by, improvise in any kind of way, in the other keys. So --
How old were you at this point?
At this here, I was about ten.
Ten. And you were playing the piano or organ?
Oh, we were playing the organ. And when I could get to somebody's house that had a piano, we played the piano.
And what did -- was it a trio, or--
No, TRIO?
Just you and another friend?

Well, this other fellow was trying to play the piano, too. So we had -- we used to go around and if he heard anything, he'd come in and tell me about it. And if I heard anything from somebody -- one of the great guys that was playing around there -- cause there were fellows playing. Like there was a fellow called Jesse Pinkett, and there was a fellow called Jack the Bear. So, they were playing and I'll tell you about another man a little later on -- that year, we went to Atlantic City again, because every summer he went to Atlantic City.

Well, my brothers were much older now, they had started going away to school. Because they had a little difficulty going to the high schools in -- especially in the Catholic high school, at that time in Philadelphia. They weren't at the place where "JACK THE BEAR" WILSON.

they was acceptin' blacks in the high schools. See, they thought, when they finish the elementary school, that was enough for them. That would enable them to read so they wouldn't give their boss no poison, and that was enough. They didn't need to go to high school.

So, there was a school in Raleigh, North Carolina, called SHAW Shore University. But, it was academic, too. So my father got the money together some way, and they went to school. But this year when they come back from school, he had a bright idea. He bought a couple of busses. In Atlantic City they called at the time, what we'd call NICKEL ET TES or now, jitneys, but it was a bus, you know. And their horse and team. So this was, I imagine, about 1905, or 1908, and like in through there. Well, there wasn't any NO automobiles then of any consequence. Only the very rich had automobiles. So most of our people, especially on the back bay in Atlantic City, they had these busses, and they did all their transportation. You carried your -- you'd crawl on a bus and say, "I want to go to Indiana Avenue." And at Indiana Avenue, you'd say, "I want to go up to Virginia Avenue, or Maryland Avenue.", and the fellow got 25¢ or something for taking you up there.
Well, my father, he decided to do that with the people. And here's what happened. So, at night, I used to go ride with my brother when they worked late at night, see. And they'd go

to a place just like -- there was a place called Scott's, and there was a place called the Bay State. And there was a place called Boathouse, and then like these places were running then. And so, the busses would stand up there at these places, and when somebody'd party'd come out, if they were too drunk to walk or something like that, they'd take a bus ride goin' home.

So -- but, in this place, they had a fellow, a man, called Madison Reed. Madison Reed had the show in there. And he had in that show -- his piano player was a man called Eubie Blake. And Eubie Blake -- and he had a singer called Mary Stafford. And I don't know what was the names of some other people, but he did most of it. He was one of the greatest entertainers of that day, this Madison Reed was, see.

So, I used to go to the window, on the outside, and stand on a beer box or something like that and look in the window. And when I looked in the window, I could see Eubie in there playing. And there was a song come out about that time called, "I Wonder Where My Easy Rider's Gone". And then, Madison did a piece called, "Black Prince". And when Eubie used to play these things, and I thought he was the greatest. He was very good. He was very good. He played this -- and that was why I took my ambition as to be a great musician. And I've always honored Eubie, because I know that he was behind it all.
And now, I had my inspiration from Williams and Walker.

Now, this is another dose of it. So you know I'm not going to take up dentistry. So I started in now to be exactly what I am. It took a long time to do that, because I watched Eubie for two years, until then I got a notion I wanted to write a piece. So -- and this was another advancement in my education -- I wrote, I had a little piece and I told my father about it and he told the maid, the maid that worked where he -- at 142 Walnut St. for the Biddles, was a Irish lady that was raised in a convent. So she said, "Your son's eleven years old and he wrote a piece?" Said, "Well, have him come up and hum it for me and I will take it down for him and then he can send it and have it copyrighted."
Well, the little piece was called, "Won't You Be My Little Sweet Household Queen". As corny as it sounds...
(laugh)

That was the name of the piece. Well, I went up there, and she actually took it down and then made a piano copy. Well, with a piano out or anything, now, this was something, really something new in my life, see. I didn't know anybody could do anything without the instrument. See, so when she did this, and I said, "What was that?", and she said it was a solfeggio. Well, I knew just as much then as I knew before, 'cause she could have said, "Spaghetti" it'd have been all the same to me. Solfeggio. Anyhow, so I was very curious to know what

this was all about. And we copyrighted the piece. And my father and this woman laughed about it and they said, 'Well, your son is going to be a Mozart one day.' See. So, I missed Mozart, but I did get to be a W.C. Handy, so.
(laugh)
Do you still remember the piece?
Huh?
Do you still remember the piece?
Yeah, I remember it.
Yeah?
(singing), 'Won't you be my sweet little household queen?' That's the way it ended up, see, as corny as it could be.

Anyhow, now I'm in the sixth grade -- this is a little later. We have a teacher called Miss Jordan. I'll never forget that. I went to 17th and Pine, to the public school now. My mother took me out of the Catholic school, 'cause she said all I was learning was the 'Hail Mary, full of grace', and she said, 'Look, son, I want you to know something about life. And I want you to meet the people that haven't been put in that condition.' So, what I said, I said to her, 'Well I will go, I want you to put me in this public school.' So I went into the public school, and this teacher, Miss Jordan, in the sixth grade. Miss Jordan played a very important part in my life, because, in the class,

she'd line the class up and we'd sit there, and we'd say, now this is a singing period. And she would get her tuning fork, she'd give us the key by singing down, either from C down, or from te, do, te, la, or she'd be singing from do, mi, so, mi, and that'd be the key note. And so, all this was -- and then we'd go through and do it, she'd give us different parts and all like that. She was a very fine musician, also a school teacher.

Well, then we were able to sing songs and the boys would take one note, and we'd sing it in two parts, and sometimes three parts. So, all these things were shaping my life, see. And now, I stayed in school, but each year I was playing a little better.

So when I got to [be] about fourteen years old, I was able to play for the house rent parties. You know, the house rent parties in those days were not for fun. For the people giving the party was to make a living. Because they'd only charge you ten cents. Then a lot of people come into them, and then they had a side issue, they would serve say pigs feet and potato salad, and sometimes they'd have something else, but that was the most thing, was pigs feet and potato salad.

Now, we would get maybe, some time, we'd come in a party of three, because we could play because in those days there wasn't no pianola, there wasn't no radios, there wasn't no television, nothing like that. So, we had to -- the only way they could have any fun like that, where a piano was concerned, it was with, on just
an ordinary piano, that's all most poor people in those days could afford.

So, we'd play at these parties. Well, each time we'd meet other fellows playing at the parties, and we learned how to, what you call, swing. There was a guy -- or, stride. There was a guy there that -- for -- a fellow named Rawson, Ralph Rawson. He came over from New York, and he -- and there was another fellow there we'd call Duke something -- this fellow could take "Onward Christian Soldiers", and really swing it. What we called swing today, but stride, but stride, and I'll tell you about this stride business which a lot of people don't know. We got stride from watching, listening to bands. You see, the bass, when he goes down, it was the bass and the trombones, things like that. When he came up, he was alto horn. Like when you say, "oom-pa, oom-pa, oom-pa, oom-pa,". Now, and then the right hand, well, there was a left hand in the bass clef, and the right hand was always, it took off the trumpets or the clarinets, or one of those things. So, we found out from the older piano players, that this was the way a band would play. We would play the same thing on a piano, that's that stride piano. We'd play all such things like Sousa's marches, and like, the March of the Director. (sings) Da da da da da da da da da da da da da da da da da da da.

That was the alto horn. And the bass would go -- (sings) But, so, and then the right hand was playing the melody. And these things happened so that we got so that we could master those things pretty good. And the next thing, we had time. Because a lot of times, there was no drums with you. And if there was drums, they couldn't afford drums, because the houses and the walls was too thin, and first thing you'd know, somebody else would be complaining about the drums. And so, if you had drums, you wouldn't last much -- long. So, we went on. We passed on.
Before we go on, what about these rent parties. Were they in Philadelphia or Atlantic City?
This was in Philadelphia.
I see.
I was very seldom in Atlantic City in the wintertime, because we was only down there with my father. See, and he worked and when Labor Day, then we all came home.
Well, how much did they charge, then, at these parties?

Ten cents at the party, and then it worked up. High toned parties got a quarter. And then you had to buy your own pigs feet and potato salad. And the people started bringing a little bootleg, and a little blackberry and gin, and things like that, and whisky, in the bottle parlor, so that
a fellow -- you'd pay a quarter for a drink, and like that's where I learned how to drink. And then one day I got ahold of some blackberry and gin, and it tasted kind of good, and I had one too many.
(laugh)

Another time, another a friend of mine, he went overboard. But, one thing, I never did go overboard. But this fellow went overboard, and we took him home, we were all kids and we was afraid to let his people know it, so we stood him up on the steps and we told him to hold on to the doorknob and we rang the bell and run. So, when he come to the door, they find him out there, and that didn't work in my favor because, after all, she, his mother, told him, "See here, I want you to stay away from that old Sammy Wood -- Wooding", she said, "because he ain't no good. If you all hang together you know the first thing --"., And I come home and my mother told me the same thing, "Want you to stay away from Maceo White, because if you hang with him --", but we was learnin' how to play together, we was studyin' together, so and then she told me, "You'd better stay away from him because he ain't goin' to get you in any trouble."
So then we went on through high school.
Also, before we leave the rent parties, what sort of music would you play there? What kind of tunes?

No, we played songs, we'd get songs together. There was a song called, "At That Million Dollar Ball", and I remember some old songs we played, "Fiddler, Fiddle on Your Violin", and we played these songs, and there's some more of them, "When the Midnight Choo-Choo Leaves for Alabam", like that kind of and I can't remember the songs.
Were people dancing to this?

Yes. Well, that's what we played for them. And that's one thing about the stride piano, because it had a strict tempo, you see. Now, the difference between American music and European music -- now you take the French. Their altos hit on the beat, like take the French National De Fil. (sings). Well, now, you see, that doesn't, that was the reason why the white race didn't really get to swing, because you notice, even today, when they applaud, they applaud, when they applaud for you or when they clap, they clap on the beat. We're after the beat, you see. And that was the difference, and that was the reason why we have what we call today, swing, jazz, and they didn't have it. Because it was the way you clap. But we got ours from not having any instruments, so our foot was our bass, and the hands was the alto, and the voice was the center. Because long before they had pianos, you know, we had to make our own singing, like at fish frys and all like that, well we didn't have nothin' but to stomp their feet and clap their
hands and sang, sang the different songs.

Well, now, that's where we get -- when we came over here, well naturally, we came over here with rhythm. 'Cause that's the only thing we had, was rhythm. And then we developed ring shouts, what we called. After the spirituals, we had the secular music, was like ring shouts. Where we all get around and we had a leader and they carried us in the church, even. Like we'd say, like you take the song, "Amazing Grace, How it Sweet Sound", we'd say, this leader would say, "Amazing Grace, how sweet sounds to save a soul like me", and the congregation would all sing, "Amazing Grace", and then he'd sing, "And on we go, beyond the great divide", and they'd sing, "On we go.", you see there's a repetition, you know what I mean. But, he'd lead them and that was our main goal. Because, after all, the Baptists was the, I mean the Methodist was the oldest church, and we had long meter that the Baptists took on later. And they had the, more -- gospel, the gospel wasn't known yet.
So, see, we were doin' gospel all the time, but we wasn't knowin' that -- I mean it hadn't been labeled.

Oh, a lot of our things that we did, like the Blues was just a secular form of the spirituals. Or when -- anything like that. And like blues, "I Hate to See the Evenin' Sun Go Down", that don't belong to nobody. The man that captured it was W.C. Handy, but it didn't belong to Handy.
Right.
It's just the blues. And then when the great singers come along in the age later on, like Bessie Smith, Ethel Waters, and all of them, they sang blues.
When did you first hear -- had you heard blues at this point in Philadelphia?

Oh, yes. Oh, yeah, you heard that with the guitars. The guy would stand on the corner and they'd be selling oysters or something like that. Or there'd be a blind man playing that, you know, we'd filled a pepper pot. And most of the guys were like from Baltimore. That was Eubie Blake's home, Baltimore. And Chick Webb's home was Baltimore. A lot of the musicians and all. But Baltimore was a great center for music, too.. Philadelphia was. Philadelphia piano players. Baltimore give you guitars, and tenor banjoes and banjoes, at the time.

Then, as you go farther south, the poor people were poorer, and they didn't even have those instruments. I've seen guys make as much music as Gene Krupa or Chick Webb with two bones. They'd just take these two bones and rattle them, clack, clack, clack, and could really to do a dance. So, as far as that goes, they been havin' to do that because we didn't have anything else.

And, in sports, our greatest runners, what do they do. You don't find the black people goin' in much for golf or tennis, or things like that. Because they don't have money to buy the rackets and the golf clubs. But we was great runners. Why?
Because it don't cost you nothin' to run.
(laugh)

You know what I mean? And the sports like running. We were in basketball, or we were in football before we were in basketball, because all you had to do was buy a five cent rocket in those days, and you were in baseball. You could get a stick anywhere to hit the ball.

See, but of course, we didn't have the money. That's the one thing that interfered with a lot of things that we didn't take advanced courses. We couldn't go to the New England Conservatory in those days, because we didn't have the money to do those things.

So, a lot of times, maybe if I had gone to the New England Conservatory, I would have been on the classical kick. But I didn't have any money, I had to get it the best way I could because I certainly didn't want to go into church and play for the church. I didn't want to do that, because I didn't like the church.
But, did you ever get paid for playing at the rent parties?

Yeah, you'd get a dollar and a quarter. It was a whole lot of money. With a dollar and a quarter, I'd be able to take my girl and buy her a dish of ice cream. Or if I got enough money, I could go and buy her oyster stew. There was a fellow on South Street that had a place they called Early's.

And we went there so often that we could have fun there. And we were big timers there. And Herman's, who was the baker shop across the street, we would go there and if we didn't have any money we could go there and say, "I'll pay you at the end of the week, Mr. Herman." Or, Mr. Early. And they'd let it go and the little girl would stretch her eyes, her eyes would pop open, and she'd say, "Oh, they're big timers." See?
(laugh)
That's the way it went.
So, okay, so we're in Philadelphia and you're playing these rent parties and this is around, what? 1914, still?

I want to tell you an incident that happened, this was about -- I was just goin' to the high school, now let's see, that must have been '15, or '14 or '15. Anyhow, it was in there somewhere. Anyhow, we'd just started to smoke. Because we had been goin' to rent parties, and I had had a little taste of liquor, but, blackberry and gin we used to go for, see. We thought that really helped you, sexually. We went for that strongly, see we thought that would give you the kick that you needed to please the little girls.
(laugh)
So we, as we were goin' up the street, we had two cigarettes that we had hooked in school. I had

started to hook in school, now. That we'd hooked in school, and we were goin' up the street and all of a sudden, Mayfield said to me, he said, "Jesus, there comes your father. There's your old man down the street." Well, we nearly choked these cigarettes, we choked them right quick and we put them in our pockets. And he come on down there, and he said, "Hiya boys, where you all goin'?" And we said, "Oh, we didn't have any class, so we were goin' up to -- up on Market Street to the Nickelle." Well, we did have a class, but we had hooked it. We had jumped the class. Anyhow, so we lied about it and he said, "Alright, go ahead, but don't get into any trouble." He went on about his business and we kept on goin'. Well, I told Maceo Mayfield, "I'm very happy that we got in, and he didn't see us smokin' those cigarettes." Because he'd always told me, "Well, now look (unintelligible), if you're going to be an athlete, you can't be smokin'. And goin' on like that, see, so I was very happy. I got home that night. We had supper, and I was smug in as a rug. I thought I had fooled him. Well, he reached into his pocket and took two Cinco cigars out. And said, well, he called me David, that's my middle name, he said, "Listen, David," he said, "I see you're goin' to smoke, anyhow. So, if you're goin' to smoke, smoke cigars. Don't smoke cigarettes, they're bad for your lungs and all of that." Don't you know, I've never smoked a cigarette since that day.
(laugh)
But, it was not the thought of the cigarette, but the thought that I'd fooled him, and I hadn't fooled him.
Right.
And when he worked that, my old man was brilliant. He was brilliant. And he's just out of slavery.

When he left Virginia, his mother had one -- my uncle was born just in slavery. Just, he was about a year old. And my father was just born out of slavery, see. And she had these two kids, she had them, one, pullin' my uncle along, and she had my father over her shoulder and she didn't -- over her shoulder, and she didn't know even which way she was goin', even. But she followed the crowd and we got to Pennsylvania, to Philadelphia. She said she didn't know whether she was goin' up, north, or goin' west or east. So that's what my grandmother said, that everybody was making it up north, so she made it up north with them, see.

But, he had done a lot of studyin', and after he studied, he, then he went with the Biddles, I told you. And when he had time off, between meals or anything like that, he'd sit down and read those books. And, you know, they had a big library there because old Colonel Biddle was the head of the Pennsylvania National Guard, see. So he'd read those books, well, he'd come up with
Uh, huh.
You see, we tried to carry on, but in a poor way, we carried on.
So what happened now, after that. We're, uh, the rent parties.

Well, we were doin' pretty good at the rent parties.
Well, now, I met a little girl, and this little girl was tryin' to be a singer, too. And Maceo had one, too. So, we used to go up to her house. And she was a little older than we were, and we would play and they would sing.
Well, now, we were beginning to learn keys. But not fast, you know what I mean? The way we played, we was playin' F-sharp and C-sharp, and you couldn't put no singers up there, you see. So, we were getting a little better, now, see. So, at the end of the term I met a woman that was, her name was Josephine Berkeley. She was a dancer, a cakewalk dancer. She was a cakewalker. You know about cakewalk dancers. Do you know about it?
Well, I know about it, yes. Tell me.
Well, cakewalking -- a lot of people, you've heard them say, 'that takes the cake.' A lot of black people say that a lot. 'Man that takes the cake.' Well, where it come from,
they had, they'd do this walkin' dance, and the girls prancin', and the fellow struttin' and all like that. The same thing that George Walker used to do in the show.
Well, the winner would get a big cake. And that was the winner. And maybe a few dollars, maybe ten dollars or something on the side, because that was a lot of money in those days.

So, they would, well this little Josephine, this lady, won the cake. She was a little older than I was. She won the cake, and she was just comin' up, just goin' up the steps in this ball, when it was the Greenwaiters' Ball, One of those musical fun halls. (unintelligible) And she almost dropped this cake. And I grabbed it just in time. Well, we formed a friendship there, see. And, later on, I wanted to get into show business and this lady was in show business, see, so we fell in love. As you'd call it, at least, a fascination, see.

So, anyhow, that summer she went to my school, and I was droppin' out of school regular, now. And so far, I was droppin' out of school, but my parents didn't know it because I was leavin' the house with my lunch. And they didn't know I was dropping out, but I was droppin' out, see. And so, that summer, I went with her to Atlantic City. Because that year, my father didn't go to Atlantic City. I went with her to Atlantic City. And that's where I met such fellows like Jack the Bear, playin' the piano. I thought he was good until after I had got another good look at Eubie Blake, I found that Jack the Bear was asleep on the piano stool.
(laugh)
Because Eubie was very good, you see, and he was getting better all the time.

So, now, Jack the Bear, she worked with Jack the Bear. That's when they first heard this piece, 'You Made Me Love You, I Didn't Want to Do It'. Well, Jack the Bear was very good. He was good for hokum, but he wasn't in no comparison with Eubie Blake.

Anyhow, so I stayed with this girl, but I had a chance now of meeting one of the greatest men that helped me in my life. That was a fellow called Charlie Johnson. Charlie Johnson was about three or four years older than I was, but he come from Boston. He taught me a lot of things. The fact that I hadn't had before, in the early years, before, you know.
Did he have a band at that time?
Oh, at that time didn't nobody have a band in Atlantic City. They had some combinations. I think he was working with a tenor banjo player and a drummer, you see.
Was the Paradise open at that point?
No, no, this was way before that.
It was before the Paradise, huh?
Just played around any way he could, you know? And, afterwards, he got with Ray Weloff, and they opened the Paradise. But, at that time, there wasn't any Paradise, see?
What year are we talking about, now?
This was just before the war, '15 or '16, now.
Uh, huh.

We're up there, see. Now, we used to come down there to play a little piano. So, in Atlantic City, the only way I could make a living, I used to, to eat and sleep, after trying to be a little pimp or something around there. See, was to stand on the corner of North Carolina and Baltic and, up North Carolina Avenue, going towards the beach, were the white bawdy houses. And going south from Arctic Avenue, Baltic Avenue, was the black bawdy houses, you see. Well, we used to stand on the corner, and when, if they got a red hot John came in there, they would come down and say, get a piano player, a professor. Say, get one of the professors. Now, that's one word that later on in life I didn't want nobody to call me a professor. When I got to be a professor, I didn't want nobody ever to call me. But, we use to stand on the corner, and we used to see some awful sights in those houses, you know? No use to me mention them, but I can tell you some pretty funny things happened.
Tell me about them.
UNIDENTIFIED: Love. ALBERTSON: Love?
You see, there was a screen around us, see? But the maid would know us. It was a colored maid, mostly. The maids were colored. The prostitutes were white, see. And

their only visitors were white people, see. So, they'd fixed the screen so that, you know the crack, they'd fixed the screen so that you could see through the crack. And sometimes we'd be playing and look and some awful things used to happen, see. So.
What -- these, sexual acts, huh?

Yeah, sexual acts. But, you see so, they had to do everything sometimes. A fellow would come in there and bark like a dog. And they'd all run around smelling each other, like this. And such tricks like that, you know what I mean? Such things as --
All to music.

Yeah, well we were supposed to keep the music going. And when they got through, they would say, 'Give the professor something.' Well, maybe he was slow, so some of these girls would reach into his pocket, and get some, 'Oh, come on, give him something.' And maybe the man would take out a dollar, or some change or something, and they'd grab it all and say, 'Here, take it professor.' You know what I mean? And so, we did very well for ourselves out there. You see, out in the summertime.
Uh, huh.

Now, when the winter come, it was a different story. You see what I mean, because there were things that would happen, that we were going, the people that supported these houses were all gone away, and some of the white bawdy houses
closed, see? Because Atlantic City, now, was the playground of the world. And from May to September it was good. Now...
Okay, so you're talking about Atlantic City after the summer's over in September. At this point were you staying in Atlantic City in the winter time, too? Were you living there?

Well, no. I'm trying to live there. 'Cause see, I don't want to go back to school, and I don't want to go back to Philadelphia where my people are and all, you see. I'm lost. I don't know what to do. That's right, I'm really lost. I don't know what it's all about. I jumped out of school and followed this girl, you know what I mean. And I got down there, and it was like that song said, 'After you get what you want, you don't want it.' Now I've got it and I run into Charlie Johnson and I think he's the greatest, you know what I mean, and he's struggling to get better and he turned out to be one of the greatest cabaret pianists and band leaders that we had. But, he died very poor because he would do one thing, he'd gamble. He and I -- I used to gamble with him, you know. I used to stay out all night to get this money and I'd wait, and then on Saturday night when I got the job, working, we'd go to a gambling joint.

But let me tell you about that. There got to be a place right across from where Eubie Blake and Madison Reid and I worked, called the Bucket of Blood. Now I've got this job in the Bucket of Blood. And this is where, in the wintertime, it

was wintertime, and where they would -- if the bartender let the fire go out in the back, because he was the boss of the whole room. They'd beat him up. See, cause the girls used to come in there to get warm. And I was the pianist there, and I did have a drummer there, and neither one of us could play enough to keep us warm. See what I mean? We couldn't play for singers yet, because I don't know how to play for singers, you know.

Every singer would sing in F or C, or keys like that, and I couldn't change no keys, you know what I mean, there's only just playing, I was only just playing, you see? So this was something the youngsters nowadays don't get this practice, to play, you know what I mean? To learn how to play for singers because you can't get that in a conservatory.
Right.

You can't get that. You have to get that from only the practicality. It's just like, like a doctor. He can study for four or five years, he can study for ten years, but he comes out and be an intern and know medicine like it should be, know from the actual meeting with the patient and all like that. And understand the symptoms, because later on -- that comes from, I knew from school, the individual differences of people. And some people, like if they've got a -- pneumonia or something like that, they carry an aroma that a doctor can tell
that they -- that this person -- just what disease. Some of them can tell, may even smell cancer. But see, the different diseases.

But, now, not everybody. Cause this person may have it and one would be so faint that you couldn't see it. Anyhow, in Atlantic City at this time, why, this was the greatest school. Because they had about 15 cabarets in the black belt, see, but most of them were patronized by white people. And this was the real age of the ragtime, you see. But in the east we didn't have the whole full bands, yet. We had maybe three or four pieces, and that's the way it went on, you see. So, I did luck up to this Bucket of Blood job, and I got this Bucket of Blood job. And they called it the Bucket of Blood because, outside of the fighting over the fire with the bartender, there used to be somebody's blood would be spilt on the steps every night, see what I mean? Because they'd drag out somebody or drag in somebody, so that's what it was.
So, well, you played -- how much did you get paid for playing there?
Huh?
At the Bucket of Blood.

At the Bucket of Blood? Well, I was lucky if I got twenty-five dollars, or twenty dollars. But, and I didn't get all of that, because we'd tab half of that up because the rest of your friends would all come in and say, alright what

do you want, and you'd set them up with a drink because you were known as so happy to be a big timer, you'd spend that twenty dollars. Sometimes I'd get paid, with a whole lot of checks that I done signed, and maybe four dollars, sometimes it would be ten dollars. And so I had to quit that. I couldn't make it.
I'd bought a piano for a hundred dollars, and lived where I paid a dollar and a quarter rent. I tried to...
A dollar and a quarter a --
A week.
A week.

Yeah, so see I tried to, tried to get a couple of girls to do it for me, but they didn't work out so good. So, I didn't say -- I would say that they didn't work out so good. So I had to go to work. Well, I knew how to wait.
So you almost became a pimp.
Yeah, well, only I was a pimple. You see, I couldn't be a pimp because I didn't know what the devil I was doing.
(laugh)
But I was just trying to exist so that I could play.
Right.
You know what I mean? I was in it, but I wasn't a part of it, you see what I mean?
Um, hunh.

And so I went on, and at last I got this job. And there was a lot of others around there, more unfortunate than I was. So, I was working in this hotel. I learned how to wait good then, because I used to go up and help my father, so I knew something about waiting, anyway.

So, what happened was that these guys would say, "Sam, hey, we haven't had nothing to eat today, we haven't scoffed today.", they said, "can't you pick up a couple of pork chops up there or something and bring down here?" Well, one of the waiters, I told him, I said, "How do you get something out of here?", I said to one of the older waiters, and he said, "Well, you know the way I do, I got a leather pocket put inside of my waiter's jacket. And so won't no grease come through, you put this leather pocket in there, and when"-- we served the American Plan, you know, in the hotel -- "well, you go in there and say, 'five orders of chicken'". Well, maybe you only got three people out there, wasn't nobody'd bother you. So, two orders, you shoved in your pocket, see. And I'd take food across to the guys all the time. I'd be takin' them food. I didn't charge them nothin' for it, because I'm trying to be a big time man and be somebody, you know what I mean?

And so, we were getting along fine, until business started falling off in the hotel, and there wasn't no chicken, and they got a new steward or something. And he's been buying just enough for the people. There wasn't nothing left over.

So, one guy called me and said, "Man, you don't bring nothing no more. What's the matter? You must be selling that or doing -- what are you doing with the food?" And the guy said, "Oh, he been stealing that food and selling it to somebody." Well, that made me angry, cause I didn't want to be called a thief. So I said, "Look --", I used some four letter words, a couple of them, I said, "Look, you get your own damned chicken, I'm not getting nothing more.", I said, see? And I quit that stuff and I stopped that, see? Well, because, sooner or later I'd have been caught at it anyhow. And then this guy woke me up by calling me a thief, cause that's the last thing -- I had a good home and I was well raised, you know what I mean? And I couldn't stand nobody calling me no thief, so. And I'm feeding him, too. So I said, "Forget it, we're through with that." So I went on and just -- I was getting better, anyhow, with the music, and I got, then I got a job. And I got a chance to substitute for Eubie Blake was sick. And I got to substitute for him, and I was gettin' into the big time, then.
And, well, first of all, the Bucket of Blood, now, what about tips. Because a lot of performers in those days told me they made more money in tips than in salary.
Oh, you mean in the cabaret.
Yeah.
OH. Well, we hadn't worked up to no singers.
Oh, I see.
I still wasnt playing for singing yet, Because I couldnt play that well.
(unintelligible)
So, when you worked for a singer, the singer collected the tips and shared them with you, right?
Oh, yes, then they split it up with the band.

Now, how that happened was that a fellow called Freddy Tunstall. Tomsill. He played at the Belmont for Mr. Brown. And he got mad one night, one Sunday night, and left. And Brown knew that I was around there and wasn't working at the time. So he said send somebody and tell them to send for me and I'd come there. He said, "Son, how would you like to go upstairs and play for me?" Cause, he said, "you see, I'm stuck. Freddy's gone back to New York and left me." I told him that, "Mr. Brown, you know I can't play for this, good enough for this cabaret." This was a first class cabaret, it had four singers, something like that." And they had a drummer and a piano. That's all they could have, you see. And the drum stopped at twelve o'clock, anyway, because the windows were open and the people in the neighborhood would squawk on it, you know what I mean? So, that left you with the piano alone. And sometimes it was alright to play, to get through with the song. But then, when the girls pulled up their dresses and started to dancing, you know what I mean? Like they were doing their prancing, they did a funny dance, a cabaret dance. You had to beat it out, all by yourself. No

drum. You just had to beat it out and play enough for the dancing. But, I could do that, because I had all that training at playing for house parties. And I handled that I could kind of swing good, then, you see?
Uh, huh.
I stopped swinging a long time ago, because it's bad on the heart.

But, anyhow, so I told him, he said, "I can't do it, Mr. Brown." And he said, I said, "I'm frank with you -- well, I wouldn't make it." He said, "Look --", this was a colored man, and he was a real race man, too, and he said, "Look, if I send you upstairs and it's my place, who's gonna fire you?" And that gave me my start. I went upstairs, I didn't sleep for maybe an hour or two, for over two weeks. Learning the songs and how to play them in the different keys. I knew the songs, if I was gonna play them in the original keys. But most of those singers didn't sing them in the original key. So I had to transpose it into the key that -- well, the pairs I'd get, first I'd have one or two, then I'd have four, then I'd get the keys of the pieces until I had a repertoire. I could play for them. But I went up there and that night was miserable. Because I had to come up and say, "Do you know I Lost you so why should or What Do I Care'?" Well, what key? "Well, put that in D." Oh, Jesus.
(laugh)
What a hard time it was. I was watching

the clock every minute, worse than a prizefighter in the ring when he's supposed to be knocked out and he's looking at it to see if his round's up yet. Well, I was watching the clock. When it got to three o'clock, he closed down around three o'clock. I was a happy man. Happy boy, rather, because I wasn't a man.
Anyhow, well we made it. I stayed there for two or three months.
What was the name of this place, again?
Belmont. That was on the corner of North Carolina and Mediterranean Avenue.
Do you remember any of the singers there, who they were?

Yes, there was a woman called Mabel Richardson. She was from Washington or Baltimore. She was very good. And there was another one named Alice Jackson, I think, yeah, Alice Jackson. And there was nobody, of course, the ones that you would know more than her, but she was working more with Madison Reed, but that was Mary Stafford, she was with him. Mabel Richardson was almost as good as Mary Stafford, though. And there was another woman called Teddy Peters from out in Chicago, I mean, out along the coast. I asked when I was with Rae, And I remember, once I asked this woman, the Peters Sisters in Paris, did they have a relative named -- but they said she wasn't any kin to them, but she looked just like the Peters Sisters. She was big, just like they are, and all. And so, she was up there. And then, well
naturally,
I had an eye for her for somehow, but she didn't have no eye for me and she said, "Go on, boy, you don't know what you're talking about."

Anyhow, because, I always carried my sex along with my music, because I think that's one thing that made me be a piano player, so that there wouldn't be so many that refused me. At the time, it bothered me. If I was a piano player, they said, "Well, let's give him a break."
(laugh)
I got a break in a lot of places that it wasn't expected.
Well, that's what happened there. So, we did alright there. And from then on, I was on my way. That's where I got my start. When this man gave me my start, Old Man Brown.
But do you remember what kind of songs they were singing? Were they singing sweet songs? The girls?

Well, they sang all kinds of songs. There was a song they called 'Shimme-Sha-Wobble'. And there was a song called, "I Wish I could Shimmy Like My Sister Kate". And then there was songs called, "I Lost You, So Why Should I Care". And then, we had the others, you know, different types of songs, and that's one thing Old Man Brown told me, too, he said -- and I never forgot it. Later on, I told a little lady working with me, Rae Harrison, I told her the same thing. He said, "Sam, don't set up on that piano and play like a gawk. Turn around and look at your

audience and see what condition they're in. Now, if you see a lot of people sitting around there like they're moonstruck or something like that, what are you going to play the "Strutters' Ball" for, what are you going to play like that? You want to go into something like, "I Lost You, So Why Should I Care", or something like that." You know what I mean?
Um, hunh.
Now, if they come in there lively, you don't want to play, "I Lost You, So Why Should I Care", or , "The Rosary".
(laugh)

You've got to watch your audience and see what they want. And you'll catch them at a different time, and you might they come in there and want, "Toot, Toot, Tootsie, Goodbye". You've got an audience like that, you want to give them how they feel. And I've found that that can be used today. A lot of times, a lot of people use the wrong things on the wrong people at the time.

Like, I heard Barbra Streisand sing "Mon Homme". But, where it was, it was the wrong place for it, you know what I mean? And then, she was singing a song that wasn't very good for her, anyhow. For this reason. French people, Edith Piaf and all of them, they like to sing low. And [Streisand] she was too high. Like in, "Mon Homme", she has a nice beautiful voice, but that was a question of the wrong song, what I'm trying to bring out.

You can give them the wrong song, and a person has the wrong tune, and they wonder why they're not a success. It's because they're not giving -- because, do you know, at one time, the great act of Williams and Walker // Williams was the straight man, he was a better looking man than Walker. George Walker was the comedian. And, then, suddenly, some fellow that knew them, like in the show business, turned around and said, "Look, you fellows are hooked up wrong. Why don't you turn it around, and then let Bert Williams do the comedy and then put cork on, and George Walker, you be straight." Because they had it around the wrong way.

Now, that was the greatest team we had. We've ever had. Bert Williams and George Walker. And they turned it around, they went over there, they had a Command Performance for the Queen of England. And he had diamonds, they gave him diamonds and everything.
But, before that, they didn't go no place. They couldn't even get in the Rabbit's Foot Minstrels (unintelligible).
(laugh)

They couldn't do nothing. But they were hooked wrong, you see? And, I know in the Army once ~~Strug~~ gling -- we had a fellow struggling around there - a fellow named Lionel. He was struggling around there with trying to play trombone. Wasn't going no place. He was a pianist, had been a church organist, you see. And they had switched him --

Bill Vodery had switched him to the saxophone, and in four or five days, he was playing the saxophone. And he was fooling around there with the trombone. I mean, you can get there in the wrong place, you know what I mean?
Right.
And be cast wrong.
What about, now, this Mr. Brown's place. Is that the place where you replaced Eubie Blake.
Oh, no. That was in Kelly's.
That was before you went to Mr. Brown's place.
No. After.
That was after. When you left Mr. Brown's place?

After I left Mr. Brown's place, I went to Newark. That's where I met another friend. A very good man that helped me so much. He's dead now. Willy Smith. But he was later known, (unintelligible). He gave him the title himself. Willy, 'the Lion', Smith. I used to go up there and play jobs for him. Because he -- he had a -- he worked there on the street there. In a cabaret.

But, Willy was a great pianist. But Willy, he didn't give a darn. I'd come in and he'd say, 'Hey, kid, hold me down. Play a couple of tunes for me, until I come back.' Well, he'd come back two or three hours later.
(laugh)
So, I had to sit there and hold it down, you know. Because I wouldn't leave as long as he was there, you know, til he come back.
Well, the man wanted to hire me. And I told them, I said, 'Hire me to play behind Willy Smith? What am I gonna play?'
And, when was this? This was in Newark, New Jersey?
Yeah. Newark.
And when was this? Was this right after you left --
Yeah. Right after I left Brown.
I see.
I went up there in Newark, you see.
And what was the name of the place? Do you remember?
Oh, Keeney's Hall. But he didn't play at Keeney's Hall. He played at a place called Janers. Janers. Keeney's Hall, I played in Keeney's Hall later.
How do you spell Keeney?
K - i - n - n - e - y - s.
Oh, Kinneys, um hunh.
Kinney's Hall. That was Arlington and Augustus. That's remembering pretty good, now. That was in 1917. Arlington and Augustus was where this place was, see.
Um hunh. This was during the war.
Hum?
This was during the war.
The war started then, see?
Um hunh.
And I remember when I came back to Atlantic City, afterwards. I come back to Atlantic City. The gal [girl] I had, she done gone off with somebody else. I didn't have no girl.
Josephine?
Huh?
Josephine?
No. I'd left Josephine a long time ago. Man, I'd had four or five since Josephine.
(laugh)
So what made you go to Newark, New Jersey? How did --
Well I was brought to New York later on. I was brought to New York with by old man Baron.
He's asking you about Newark.
Yeah, I said what made you go from
Atlantic City to Newark, New Jersey?

Oh, Newark. I didn't get that. Well, the reason that I went to Newark was that Charley Johnson had been there. And he worked at someplace there. And, when he was leaving to come back to Atlantic City, and they wanted somebody else there. So he was hoping that I could make it. So he had me to come up there and take his job. See?
Um hunh.
And, but the funny thing, the first time I'd ever seen a dope fiend, too. I didn't know nothing about the dope fiends or nothing like that.

But Charley said to me one night, he said, 'You see this fellow coming in here? Watch him. He'll lean right on this piano and go sound to sleep.' And he told me and sure enough, he walked right in there, went sound to sleep and his knees bent, he went on down, instead of holding on the piano, and he come on up and sat there. And after a little while, he said, 'Hello, Charley', and turned around and walked on out.
Well, this was all new to me, see. You know, I'm still a kid in a way of speaking. Of course, I'm not of age yet, see. So now we're getting ready to go to war.
But, you must have -- well, we're talking about 1918, right? So you were twenty-three at that time, weren't you?
No, I wasn't even twenty.
When were you born?
Eighteen ninety-five.
Yeah, so you'd have to have been --
When we were drafted in 1917, and I went in in 1918, I wasn't twenty-one. And it was the draft, at that time --
But, you had to be --
Was from twenty-one to thirty-five, you see?
But, Sammy, you'd have to be if you were born in 1895.
Yeah. Now, you figure.
Yeah. And 1918, that's eighteen plus five. That's twenty-three.
No. I wasn't.
Well, how could you. Then -- there's something wrong somewhere.
I wasn't of age until -- in fact, you know how I got of age. Let's see, let's see now. Eighteen ninety-five and ten is 1905. And, that's nineteen five, isn't it?
Yeah. You're ten.
And eight would be what?
And eight? That's eighteen.
That's eighteen.
Yeah.
Well, then I'm eighteen.
No, no, no. See, 1895, okay? The year 1900, you were five years old, right?
Yeah.
So, in 1910, you were fifteen years old. In 1918, you were fifteen plus eight, you were twenty-three.
No.
You have to be.

No, I couldn't be. What, see, I'll tell you why I couldn't. When I registered, I had no right to register for the draft. Because, the reason I had no right to register for the draft was, I had been voting, from 1916 I had been voting. And posing as a man. Then, when I went up to, when I was called in the service, I wasn't, I wouldn't have turned twenty-one until I had been there five or six months.
Well, you would have to, in 1916, you'd have to be 21. Right?
Well, we registered for the draft, it was 1916.
Yeah. Well, then you were 21 years old.
Yeah, well I had to be, but I wasn't -- I hadn't turned it. I know it, for the draft, I hadn't turned quite.
Oh, I see, well when's your birthday, what month?
June.
June.
Yeah.
Um hunh.
See, I hadn't turned the year.
So you were 20. You were about to be 21.
Yeah. But I wasn't -- I had been already voting now.
Um hunh.
I can't back out of it, you know, because they'll say, well I can't register because I'm not 21.
But then, you see, by 1918, you'd have to be 23.
Well, that was. Well, I'm already registered now, in the draft, now. But, when they put the call out, I wasn't 21.
No, no. But what I'm saying is that by 1918, you were twenty-three.
Well, well.
You had to be.
Well, because, it was two years that I hadn't registered yet.
Right.
I mean I had registered, but I -- four or five months behind the time that I should have been 21.
Right.
Because from 18 to 35. That's how it happened. But, because, well, I'm in there, then so I may as well go on.
Um hunh.
I couldn't say, well I'm not of age. When I've got four or five more months. And I was anxious to go, anyhow.
Right. No, but we were talking about 1918, before, when this all came up. And you said you weren't of age yet. But you had to have been.
When I -- when I made the call, I wasn't of age. When I was drafted, I wasn't.
No, but what were we saying about 1918?
Well, that was when -- what were we saying, I don't know.
You got to Newark.
Huh?
Newark, New Jersey. We were talking about how you got to Newark, New Jersey.
Well, I got to New York, Charley sent me to New York.
No, no. Newark. In 19 --
Yeah, Charley sent me to take his place. I had come up there and we was talking about the dope fiends.
Yeah.
And the first time I had seen a dope fiend.
Right.
And that's the first time I met my first wife, up there. And then when the season was over, I came back to Atlantic City. I played about three or four months there.
I see. Were people smoking marijuana in those days?
No marijuana.
No?
Hop.
Hop? Smoking hop.
Yeah. And then they had a -- sniffing cocaine.
Uh hunh.
There wasn't no such thing as marijuana. I didn't hear of marijuana until after Louis Armstrong got on
the scene, you know?
Uh hunh.
See, and then they used to call it loco weed, or something like that. They used to -- the cows used to use that out west and go crazy about it, you know?
Well, cocaine was very expensive, were black people sniffing cocaine, too?
Sniffing cocaine.
Yeah.
Johnny Vikal. He had a big act on that and he did very well with that. And what he used was, 'Chinatown' for his music, you know, and he did a dope fiend act.
(unintelligible)
There were a lot of songs about that. About dope.
(unintelligible) -- blacks using cocaine at that time because it was very expensive. Nothing but the sports.
Oh, the blacks that were using the cocaine were the sports. The pimps and the --
Yeah. Well, you see, when I was in Newark, Newark was a sporting town.
Uh hunh.

There was a hundred and one girls in there. Well, these pimps were all around there, some of them had five and six girls. Well, they had a pipe. A hop pipe they called Black Diamond, they used to call Black Diamond. They tried to get me to come up there and use that pipe, but you know, there was a kid, they wanted to break me in to that. Because I was young and, I mean, I liked them because, you know, I'd give them anything they wanted when they come into the cabaret, like if they wanted a certain song or something like that, I'd play it.

Well, anyhow, what happened is that I've been up there and I've seen them and to, and they used it, and they thought it was a great thing. As I say, they were hop fiends and they only used fruit and milk, you know what I mean? And they were big timers, so they thought, you know?
Uh hunh.

Like the Sioux Indians or somebody, see. Anyhow, I never went for that, because, in fact I didn't even smoke any more cigarettes after that episode with my father. You know what I mean? I've been smoking cigars and everything ever since that.
Now, okay, how long did you stay in Newark?
About three months.
And then you went back to Atlantic City.
I went back to Atlantic City, yeah.
That's when you went to --
That's when I substituted for Madison Reed for Eubie Blake, when Eubie Blake had me come up there. He was sick in Baltimore.
Uh hunh.
And the reason why I substituted for him, was there wasn't nobody else around there. Because I wasn't raising no hell on the piano, you know.
No?
No. So, what I substituted for him, and I tell you, to give you an episode, an incident of that which taught me another thing about music.

He asked me to play a song for him, 'All That Worries Me is Someone Else Will Be There When I'm Gone'. You see, a song, on account of the war, people sang, they used this song because it was the draft dodgers, you know, and that was the reason why the guy wrote this song. Well, Madison told me, he said, 'I sing that in E-natural.' Well, as I told you, the colored keys were still a nuisance to me. So, E-natural, I had never bothered, I'd rather not play it. Rather play, put in in E-Flat or F, see what I mean? So I put the song in E-Flat, you see?
Uh hunh.
And he went on through the song, he
struggled through the song, but when he'd finished, he comes to the piano and says, "Listen, Sam, when I tell you I want a song in a key, please play it in that key."
Well, I didn't know about absolute pitch. I didn't know that this man would know where he was, you see? Well, I stayed up all night to learn that song in E-natural.
Uh hunh.

But, I never forgot that. Because that was such a slap in the face, that's another one that's like the other -- see, I remembered that, like, I felt about this big. Of course -- because I had had it -- I thought I'd fooled him. Like a lot of other singers, you know what I mean, when you say, "Play that in E-Flat." Well, if you've been used to playing it in F, you want to play it in F. They don't know the difference, it seems a little high. And I say, "Well, maybe your throat's choking you a little bit." Anything, you know. But this man had absolute pitch, as Willy, "the Lion," Smith had absolute pitch.
But, that is not -- that's a gift. You don't have to study for that, or all the studying in the world don't give it to you if you ain't got it. That's a gift, you see what I mean?
Right.

So I went on and I followed this thing through. But after that, I played his songs the way he wanted me to. If I didn't know them, I'd say, "Mr. Reed, give me another day on that song, will you?" Well, if he wanted a special

song and he didn't have to have it that day, I'd work on it all the next day. Unless, there's one time, I was broken down, so tired and worn out, from trying to catch up. But it was building me all the time, you know what I mean? I was scramblin', but it was building me. So that's how those things happened.
Did you work at all from sheet music? Or did you have to memorize all the songs?

Oh, no. You had to memorize them. I mean, you'd look out of date, putting up sheet music up there. You know, you'd memorize them. In fact, you'd memorize the words too, because the singers like Mary Stafford, and all like that, you were there, you'd be considered the biggest ham in the world if you put up a piece of sheet music, you know, like the P & R copy, you'd better not have those on there.
Oh.

You'd have to memorize it. And, then, we learned how to improvise, too. See, and it got so that you could -- if somebody come up to the piano and said, "Do you know, 'Hallelujah, I'm Home'"? You'd say -- we'd never say no, because maybe he had a dollar or fifty cents. You'd say, "Yes, I know it." I'd say, "What key do you sing it in?" He'd say, "Well, give me a key." Well, you would follow him -- you don't know the song, but you know the chords, and when he'd say, "I'm goin downtown --", you'd sing, "I'm going downtown --", you know

what I mean? But now, you don't know what is next, and you have to wait. You're just a little behind him. And he says, "That's good, that's good." But you don't know the song at all. I tell you. So you got away with it because -- that's what I mean when I say that nowadays, kids don't have that chance. Unless they're way down in BIP-BOP somewhere, where they just use the piano and people come in and say -- but around here and everything is high powered, New York, (unintelligible).
Yeah.
Where you going to get that practice anymore. That's one thing that's against us.
Uh hunh.
I mean, that's bad for the musicians that want to be really -- to be a THOROUGH musician, you have to know those things.
Now, around 1918 in Atlantic City. There were a lot of singers there, and you played for some of them. Did any of them sing blues, had that come in yet.
Oh, yes.
They were singing --

In fact, at that time, there was quite a lot of singers, and a lot of men sang the blues. At that time. At that time, you'll find out that -- 1918 -- of course that, someone said the other night was all wrong, said Benny

Goodman, said he did the "Bugle Blues". Well, that wasn't so. Jim Muir started the Bugle Blues in Europe, in 1917, during the war. See, one of his trumpets would play, (imitates trumpet), they did that in 1917, before Benny was born.
Right. Uh hunh.
So whoever said that was incorrect.
Now, we had a blues, but it was different types of blues. We had the blues coming from the South, was a little different from the Western blues.
How so?

Well, it was slower, and -- well, it was all blues, all twelve bars, like that, it was all blues, but there seemed to be more of a wail coming from North Carolina and Virginia and Georgia and like that. The guys would walk along the railroad track. They used to sing songs like, "Honey Let Your DRAWERS Hang Low", you see.
Uh, hunh.

(sings) "La de de de dah, dah, dah. La de de de dah, dah, dah. Was the last time you're going to shake it in the sheets with me." You see what I mean, those old low down blues. But in the West, it was a different type of blues. It was a blues -- were built more up. Because Chicago surpassed New York, in bands. And so did Detroit. Because they had big bands when we only had two and three pieces, you know? So

that's the reason why they got a better grip on the music. And a lot of the best jazz musicians would come from -- and Ohio was another place. Ohio, Toledo in Ohio, and Columbus, they had musicians. And Detroit, and Chicago. St. Louis, they had musicians on their instruments long before we had them in New York.
When was the first time you recall hearing the term 'jazz' used?
Jazz?
Yeah.

Well, the first time that I ever heard of jazz was after we come back here, let's see -- well, in Atlantic City, we started playing it. Because I opened up with a -- I opened down there and then there were -- Ed Major who was with Charley Johnson -- they played quite a lot of jazz. They played jazz -- it wasn't the livery stable jazz, not Dixieland Jazzband. We had a lot of jazz before that.
But I mean the use of the term, 'jazz'. Was it called, 'jazz'?
Well, it was begin to be called jazz. Because jazz has a funny word -- jazz means nothing.
Right, but what I'm trying to get at is, for instance, that the word 'jazz', before it was applied to music, was it used for other things, did it have another
Well, a lot of people used 'jazz' because they sounded old timey if they said, 'ragtime'. Because that was the next term thing in.
Right. Did they talk about, 'jazzing things up' ?

Absolutely, it meant just playing around, butterflying around, or a bunch of guys together, whooping it up or something like that, and they'd say, "Man, all that jazz." Jazz, it meant nothing. There was nothing going on worth a quarter. But a lot of guys just beating up their gums and things like that, you know what I mean?
And then they got so they applied it to jazz. It's just like the word, 'gutbucket', and 'funk'.
Uh hunh.
Funk, at one time, meant stinking.
I think it still does.

(unintelligible) -- man, the funk was so thick you could cut it with a knife. Meaning, at a house rent party, or something like that, the women and all was dancing running around and screwing around, and you see, everything was all mixed up,

and, you know what I mean? I don't mean that they would do anything sexually. They're screwing around. You know, everybody was just having a good time and so, the guy would come in door and say, "Whew, open the window in here, it smells funky in here." But now, it has a different meaning. It has the meaning, with reference to music, taking the place of jazz. Lil
Like Louis Armstrong told me, the first blues he had ever heard was called, "Funky Butt", which later became, "Stinky Butt", and different names.

Yeah, well you know where that come from, Lil Unintelligible could have been saying that from a word, when you come into a place. There's a little song that's called, I thought I heard somebody say, 9 Funky Butt, Funky Butt, take it away.", you know what I mean? Well, it meant that you didn't smell good.
Right.
You see what I mean? And she was standing around and maybe she hadn't taken proper douches or (laugh), whatever it was. So that's what that happened from.

But now, then it got to be a -- and I was wondering about that, because in Germany, funk means, in reference to the radio. Well, I wondered if some people took it and identified that as a -- to make funk, you know what I mean. Cause I, even now, I tell some of the guys now, "Look make that song Sound funky."
Right.
But, that's not it. You know what I mean? So, maybe that's the wrong way to look at it. You see? But that's the way those things started. Like you said, we used to say 'jazz it up'.
Right.
Then, and then, we go -- the first word was, "Get hot, boys."
Um hunh.

The we got to say, "Jazz it." And now they say, "Put some funk in it. Make it, you know what I mean." These are just words, and somebody coined them, and made them step into the English exagerrated and they stuck into the language.
Right.
You see, I think that's where that started.
So, why don't we leave it today that we're in Atlantic City around 1918. You've replaced Eubie Blake. We'll pick it up there.
Yeah. Because, the reason I say that's good is that now I'm getting ready to go to war. And that was a -- and then we have a different story altogether.
Alright.
Okay.
This is Chris Albertson with Sam Wooding. Interview number 2, April 24, 1975.
We are in Atlantic City and it's about what, Sam, what year?

Well, this was around the latter part of 1915. And I was just in the practice of being a pianist. I didn't know how it was going to turn out because I was really lost. I'd dropped out of high school and now I was trying to make it on my own because I was going against the wishes of my parents.
Uh hunh. So what did you -- you were living by yourself then.
Yes.
Yes.

I'd gone to Atlantic City with a lady that was an entertainer. And she was older than I was and she was trying to run things like she wanted. She said, 'Well, here I got my stooge and I'll take him on with me and we'll have a good time together. And when I get tired, I'll toss him off.' But, in the meantime, I met two or three fellows down there. Especially one, Charley Johnson, that was a great help to me and showed me the ropes and how to go about it, and all. So, he showed me how to do a lot of things. In fact, he taught me how to gamble. And every Saturday night we both would get
broke in the place. Because these fellows were waiting for us. Well, we come in.

So, one Sunday morning I was standing on the corner eating a ten cent can of salmon. Which the same salmon nowadays costs around $2.50. It was ten cents then, see? And I said, "Look here, Charley. I'm tired of standing around on the road getting broke ever time." I had a little job. I was working at a little place called the Bucket of Blood. And I wasn't making much, and half that was going, a lot of times, in tabs for my friends coming in there. So I said, "Charley, I'm going to stop gambling. If I've got any money to waste, I'm going to spend it on these chicks around here." "Cause", I said, "I don't have no fun just taking my money that's in my hand, it's the only time about an hour and a half, and then the other fellow's got it." So, I was through. That's the last time I gambled. But Charley went on gambling and didn't come out to no good for him. You see, so that's one habit I broke up.
Uh hunh. But, Charley Johnson, at that point didn't have a band, he was just working as a pianist. Is that right?
Yeah, he was working as a pianist. But he had charge of -- now he, Charley, this was one of our great-est cabaret runners. He's the one that made the name "Paradise".
Right.

Cause there was an owner down there named Max Weloff, Ray Weloff. And Ray Weloff had this Paradise down at Atlantic City. And Charley made it into a legend. And people come from all over to go to the Ray Weloff's Paradise. And for Charley Johnson. Then when Ray went out of the business, Charley came to New York with Smalls, and they again used the name Paradise. And so, now he's got a new life, and 'til today people speak of Small's Paradise. But it really should have been Charley Johnson's Paradise.
Right.
Because he's the one that made it, see.
Uh hunh. But what did you think of him as a pianist?

Not a great pianist. But a great gentleman. You know, every great gentleman can't fight. I mean as for prizefighting or physically fighting an enemy. But he had the brains. Noone has ever, Eubie Blake or nobody else has never been comparable to Charley Johnson for knowing how to engineer a successful cabaret, and with entertainers and all.
So he was a good businessman.
And he had a good band too.
Right.
His band was one of the greatest.
Now you, so you ran into Charley Johnson, and you became friends, I guess.
Yes.
And what was the next step for you?

Well, Charley's step led me right up into the war. I think that's the one mistake that Charley made. He was lucky enough for somebody to get him out of the draft. But that was the worst thing that ever happened to him. And it was the greatest thing that ever happened to me, that I didn't have sense enough to get out of the draft. Because, if I'd have could, no doubt I would have gotten out. As the guy said, "I fought and I fought, but they kept me anyhow." See?
(laugh)
But that's one thing was in my favor, that I didn't get out of it.
Now, how was that in your favor?
Well, I learnt men.
Uh hunh.

I learned how to deal with other people. I learnt how to obey the authorities, and how to respect those that are over you and how to know how to get out of those under you. Those are the things I learnt. I learnt manhood, I learnt to be a man and how to be a man. Which a lot of people don't know today.
And what was your function in the Army?
Well, I was a -- I started in as a Third

and ended up as a Second Class musician. I played in the band. But, I wasn't any kind of non-commissioned officer for the simple reason why, every day I was in the Y.M.C.A. practicing, playing. And I was also watching my friend I took so much off of. Old Bill Vodey. Old Bill Vodey was the rage for Ziegfeld. He was a man that came from Philadelphia. But he done quite a lot of arranging. He was such an arranger, that for some time, George Gershwin worked in his office as a copyist.
Bill Vodery, that's V-o-d-e-r-y.
V-o-d-e-r-y, right. Bill Vodery.
He was the leader of the military band that you were in?

Right, he was lieutenant. Bill Vodery. He took the examination in CHAUMONT and he was supposed to have two hours to do it, he did it in twenty minutes. Because he'd been on Broadway, working with Ziegfeld. So that's what happened.
Now, where did you go with Vodery and the band? You went to Europe, right?

Yeah, we went to war. We went to, we landed in St. Nazare. We was -- when we came back to St. Nazare, we were deloused there. But it was a wonderful experience. When we came to America from there, we came in at Hampton Road, and the guys actually cried on each other's shoulders. We had some great guys in our band. A lot of them are

dead now, but there was Feber there, we had Charley, Tom Whaley, we had Louis Jones. And there was a Bill Byrd, Sergeant Thorpe. In fact, it was a great collection of mostly all New York musicians. I was about the only one that came from New Jersey. I tried three times before I got in that band, you know? That was the last band that was going over that wouldn't be a labor battalion, as far as the blacks were concerned, see?

So, I tried three times, and the last time I -- the second time, I was up there a lieutenant asked me, he said, "Hey young man, what do you want to do? Do you want to get shot? You'll get shot right here. Why you going over there?" Well, I said I wanted to get into the band. Well I got into the band, see, and I played baritone horn in there. I started out with the alto and then I went to the baritone. That's as far as I got, because I didn't want to -- I wanted to be in there to learn the art of music, which I didn't know, see? There was a lot of things I got from Charley, but a lot of things that he didn't even know.
But, what kind of music did you play? Of course, you played marches, but did you play anything else?

Oh yeah, Sousa marches, and then they started -- we tried to imitate, one thing that we tried to imitate was Jim Europe, at the Fifteenth, they had a fellow named Fats. And Fats played -- from Chicago -- and he played this "Bugle Blues." That's the first time I heard the Bugle Blues, and

so -- but I know some fellows later on have claimed that they originated the 'Bugle Blues', but they didn't. It was originated in the Army, in the Fifteenth Regiment. And, see, we tried to copy it from them because we had a chance to hear them once. We played it, we was the only outfit that played guard mount for the Marines. We was connected with the First Army Headquarters and the -- and we had some awful experiences over there because -- one of the experiences we had, the boys got kind of gay one time, so they gave us some saltpetre, and all the guys got diarrhea.
(laugh)

So one fellow, he tells a funny case. He was making it across to the latrine, as we called them, and as he got half way across there, the pain struck him. And he couldn't go no farther, so he was trying to hold himself, and he raised one leg. And there was two nurses and an officer that came by, and they said, 'Oh, look at that poor fellow, he's been shell shocked.'
(laugh)

And he said, 'If I'd put that leg down, something would have happened.' And the other fellow, he was going there so fast, fellow named Chick Johnson, he was gone there so fast that he run down in the latrine, and he come up with all this mess on him, and he wanted to get into the barracks
