and so the guys all took off their side ARMS and said, "If you come in here, we'll kill you."
(laugh)

He had to stand up there and take off all his clothes MR. WOODING: It was the wintertime. It was up in a place called Somme. So, we were right in the middle. Meuse But we got the citation on our discharge, for Musse Argonne, we were in the Musse Argonne offensive. See, I have a lot of things, some shells and things that were from the French 75, that -- when we got shot over there. Once we was out there rehearsing, and an airplane came over, a German airplane came over, and he was ready, and he could have destroyed all of us, or most of us. if he had. And see, he just waved at us and went on. And it was a shame that he got shot down later on. By an American, when he was trying to -- he came over to raid an ammunition dump, see. And I think that's the reason why he didn't bother us. Because he didn't want them to know he was up there.
Right.
But, they got him anyhow.
Getting back to the music, the 'Bugle Blues' that you mentioned before is, of course, the same as the 'Bugle Call Rag', right?
Yeah.
The same tune.
The 'Bugle Call Rag'.
Right, which Benny Goodman did and a
Many of our dancers used to dance to that.
Right.
You see, so that's how that happened.
But, but the music you played, that your band played in the Army, did you play for dances, for instance?
Oh, yeah, but they didn't play nothing. (Habernola), and some other pieces. And I didn't play much with that.
But there was no jazz involved in that?

No, no, there wasn't no jazz. Cause they didn't have any jazz, then. Not those boys. They were -- we had some of them there, and some of them are still living around here. But what they had, they called Ragtime.
Yeah, so did you play Ragtime melodies with that band?
Yeah, we played some. We used to swing up, jazz up, over there and keep the home fires burning, and things like that, but it was nothing of what we call jazz today, you know?
I see. But, did Europeans hear you too?
Oh, yes.
So, what you did with the Ragtime
melodies must have been something new to them.

Yes, it was new to them. Because we had to play guard mount every evening, see? And so, when we played guard mount, and retreat, and after the retreat, they'd close it up, and the boys would stay there and play a couple.

In Barcelaubc, one place there in France, we were stationed there for about four or five months. Well, we used to play there and the French youngsters used to come out and the old people enjoyed it, too. We'd give them two or three numbers and then we'd march on back.
Was there any improvisation involved in what you played over there?
Yeah, but we didn't have too much over there.
Right.

You see, because really, that's what jazz is. It's the rhythmic improvisation on any piece. You can take -- I know, years before that, I think I told you there was a fellow by the name of Duke, and he took "Onward Christian Soldiers". When they got through with it, swinging it with the stride, like he used to, like he used to play like that. And the improvisation is when you don't give a note all its beats, you see? You cut it short, like, (sings), you know what I mean?
Right.
It's the improvisation plus the rhythmic
pattern that you put to any melody. You can play anything you want. And that's all that jazz is really, that is.

And the reason why we are in the front in it is because we have more rhythm than the other groups, the blacks do. That's the only reason why. It isn't that we are creating anything more than anybody else, but it's the rhythmic effect.
Well, let me ask you this. The Sousa marches you played.
Oh, we played them straight.
You played them straight like the white bands. There was no difference?
Oh yeah, because it was necessary. It would have been a crime to take a Sousa march, like "Stars and Stripes", or one of those other marches and mess with it.
Right. So in other words, your Army experience was more influential on you and your personality than it was -- it had no influence on your music.

Oh, absolutely, absolutely. It taught us that system was comfort. And how to obey, as well as be obeyed. You see. And it also taught us the value of things. Of leaving home. When you was over there and you couldn't get home, it taught you how to appreciate home.
Right. And, how long were you in the Army?
About a year and two months, I guess.
So, you went into the Army in 1917, I gather.
No, the beginning, the first part of 1918.
Oh.
Then we were mustered out in 1919, and we come back.
So, in other words, the war was over by the time you got out.

Oh, when the war was -- we was in the Meuse Argonne offensive. And at the time, the Meuse Argonne section, and that's the first time I heard the words, 'fini la guerre, la guerre est fini'. Well, we didn't hardly know what it meant, at the time, see?
I see. So, anyway, when you got out, the war was over, it was over in November of 1918, right?
Yeah.
And --
That's when we heard this.
Right. And when you came back to -- where?
Came back to Philadelphia.
Philadelphia.

See, before I left, I told you, the last days of '18, before we went in, the beginning of '18, the last days of '17, rather, I worked in the -- had a job in Philadelphia at a place called the Madhouse. Jake Gillum's Madhouse, it was Jessup and Poplar Streets in Philadelphia. Cause I wanted to be home, see. And in being there, so when I went to war, I come out and went back there to see Jake Gillum, and ask him, "Well, I've just been in the war, and could I get my job back." And he said, "Well, sure, anytime a man goes over there for his country, he should have his job back." So he gave me this job back. Now this is my first organization of having an outfit together that would sound something like a band.
I see. But let's go back, then, because you were at the Madhouse before you went into the service.
Yeah.
What was the Madhouse like? What did it look like, and what kind of people were there, music and --
The only way I can explain that is, "confusion".
It was a madhouse, huh?

Yeah. It was almost as bad as the Bucket of Blood, but it was one step higher. But it was confusion. And, well I can tell you one thing about the Madhouse. Well, we did an awful lot of -- we played for a lot of people there, and they liked us very much. Because -- but, one thing about it was that

when you come into the Madhouse, every waiter on the floor was a prizefighter. All one punch men. And, when they used to throw you out, Jake, being a very good politician, they come to lock you up for disturbing the peace. And you hadn't done anything. That was the way of doing things.

But, one thing, you had a chance, you had plenty of entertainers there. And I really learnt more about playing for singers, because, singers -- and they had plenty of them coming in there, and they were liable to sing in any key. Sometimes one of the would come in to sing and it's A, and another one B, and E, and another one would be in E-flat. And so, you got something that the kids nowadays cannot get, unless they're way down in Virginia someplace or in North Carolina. Because here there's no place on that lower status now. Everything is built up, so they lose that experience. They'll never get it.
What about -- was the Madhouse -- the audience, the clientele in there, was it black place?
Black and white.
Black and white customers.
Yeah, you see --
But black entertainment.

Yeah. It was like black and tan. See, and everybody held on together and everything was pretty good. A white party would sit down, a black party here, and all, you know, and they all -- they asked for everything at that time.
Right.

The blues was coming and going. The blues was really beginning to come out in 1918, or 1919, the blues began to move on. And when we had singers on the scene, like Ma Rainey, and Lucille Hegamin. And we haven't quite got to that -- I don't know much about Bessie. I didn't meet Bessie until I come to New York.

Yeah, well, Bessie, I think, was at that point, was down around Baltimore, and Atlantic City, but did -- you mentioned Lucille Hegamin and Ma Rainey -- you were just talking about, they were in. But they weren't in the Madhouse? They didn't perform there, did they?
No.
Who did? Who did perform at the Madhouse, do you remember?
Well, we had a kind of people -- I don't remember some of them, because they were nobody of any consequence. They were nobody of any consequence, and I don't really remember their names.
So, when you came back from the war, you went back into the Madhouse. Had it changed in the year and a half or so, or was it the same?
No, no. I think it run on the same. They don't change things. They still knock people in their heads and
rob them.
(laugh)
And sang, and drink their liquor and have a good time and everybody thought it was going to go on forever.
But this time, you got a band together.
Yeah.
Yes, but what, before that.

Not a real large band, let's see, I had a guitar, I had a tenor banjo -- no, a banjereen, the short necked banjo. See, it wasn't a long one, but I had a guitar, a bass, and I had a drum. And the piano. Those five people were there.
Do you remember any of the musicians who were with you?

Oh, yes. I remember Harold Waters, and then there was, what was his name, the very good drummer -- in fact this drummer came along with me. Harry Morris. Harry Morris was one of the greatest drummers. I don't know, he loved Philadelphia so much he never got to New York. But, there was nothing in New York, Chick Webb or nobody else, that was any better than he in those days, you see what I mean.
Uh hunh.
He was very good, but he loved Philadelphia and he started raising a family there and then he never got out.

Then there was a fellow, he's still in Philadelphia, he's still living, was, Henry Branch. Henry Branch played the guitar. But, Unc, as we called him, Harry Waters. He was supposed to be some kin to Ethel Waters. He was an older man then, and I guess he's passed on.
Well, in 1918, when you were back at the Madhouse, the first jazz recordings have come out by then. By the Original Dixieland Jazz Band. This white group from New Orleans, do you remember?
I didn't hear that until I went to Atlantic City.
I see.
You see, I didn't stay there no longer than -- you know, when it got to be May, Atlantic City was a great place in those days. What Las Vegas is today.
Right.

What they're trying to do at Ocean City, Maryland. And, Atlantic City -- and, we had so much fun in Atlantic City. And there was always newcomers there. It was -- so, right away I chucked Jake's place. I told Jake I was very thankful for having the job. But, now it was time for me to go to Atlantic City. I didn't have anything to go to. But you never needed anything to go to in Atlantic City.
So, was that the summer of 1918, that
you went back to Atlantic City?
No, this was the ending of '19, because I came back in '19 from --
Oh, right. Right. So it was really at the end of the season, when you came back.
Uh hunh. No, that was twenty when I went back to Atlantic City.
Yeah.
So, what did you do when you got back to Atlantic City?

I looked for a job. The first thing, I looked up my old buddies and was looking for a job. And we organized a band. It was the first jazz band I had. It was a really -- and we played such pieces as "Margie". And, in the course of that summer, I run into a couple of records I heard, of the Original Dixieland Jazz Band.
Well, one of them was "Margie", that they'd recorded, right?
Yeah. They played "Margie", "Bright Eyes", they played things like that. And some other numbers of that day and time.
Because we had a band now, we had to organize, and I began to think in terms of organizing the band right, see? Now, we had Jimmy Thomas. Jimmy Thomas, no. Jimmy
Harrison.
Trombone.
Trombone. I sent and got Elmer Chambers and Charley Dixon from up in Jersey. And Elmer Chambers was from Bayonne and Charley Dixon was from Jersey City. And I got them, and then I had my own --
Elmer Chambers played the what, the tuba, or what?
No, he was a trumpet player.
Oh, that's right, he was a trumpet player. And Dixon on banjo, right?
Yeah. And he was the guitar up there, and the tenor banjo.
Right.

And then, Jimmy Harrison was trombone. And then I had a fellow in there called Fats. I don't know what Fats' name was. He was a friend of Jimmy's. But, anyhow, Fats, we went out to, after the season was finished.
What did Fats play?
Drum.
Drums.
And that was the five of us. After that, the season was finished, we went out to Detroit. We stayed out there in Detroit and I had a chance to see -- bands in the west

at that time had more instruments than the bands in the east. Because we was just beginning to take them on in the east. Because we had so much trouble with the -- oh, on account of the people in the summertime in Atlantic City, they stayed up and there was so many people. The cabarets were right in the neighborhood where some legitimate people lived, you see. And when they raised the windows in the summertime, and you could hear all kinds of noise. So, while I was in Atlantic City, I renewed my friendship with Charley Johnson again. And that's when he -- through Charley Johnson, I had a chance to meet men like Lucky Roberts. Lucky Roberts came down there with a show. And, well, that's one of the greatest guys that I've known to play a piano. What happened, Lucky had a great big hand, and he had two big hands, like some of these, Rachmaninoff, for instance. He has big hands like that. And he stretched the keys. And when he played, especially one piece called, "The Junkman Rag", it sounded like he was a whole band playing.
Do you remember that song?

I don't remember much, but I remember he used to do something like this. (plays piano). Well, he used to do something like that. And then he had another thing he used to throw his hands in the air, you know, like this. And so, when he threw those hands in the air, I was trying to get that. I didn't have that at the time, because another friend

of mine discouraged me from doing that. And that was Eubie Blake. He said, "Kid, you can't play with your hands in the air. Keep them on the piano. You can hardly play with them on the piano, so what are you throwing your hands in the air for?" See, one reason I think Eubie was saying that, was sometimes, because I don't think he could do that.
(laugh)
But, I had the chance to meet all the great piano players down there. And that was a -- and then there was another one, James P. Johnson.
Uh hunh.

At one little affair -- they were all having a great affair, and James P. Johnson came down there with his wife. And he was -- and his wife was a dancer, I don't recall what her name was then, her professional name was Lily Wright. And so she asked Jimmy to play for her, a piece, and she danced. And after she finished, she said, "Jimmy, would you like to play a piece?" Well, Jimmy played a piece. And that broke up the matinee. Because nobody wanted to go near that piano after Jimmy got through playing. The piano was burning up. It was just steaming, see? And so -- and I'll always remember that he played a piece called, "The Bells", or something like that, he called it. But I never heard someone -- Well, all these things intrigued me, you see? Between

Lucky Roberts and James P. Johnson. Oh, they were the greatest for playing, now, for handling a song -- Eubie Blake could play a song behind a singer more legitimately. Along the lines of, but naturally (banging out a rag) for just nicely, (unintelligible), [there] was no comparison, because Art Tatum wasn't on the scene then.
Right.

But then, Willy Smith was good, but the only fault with Willy 'the Lion' Smith, was he sometimes -- he loaded the thing so much, that even the singer didn't know where she was half the time. Because he got so far away from the melody, and he was playing these off-chords, that they didn't know where he was. But, on the whole, I got a wealth of knowledge which, I say today, the youngsters can't get. Because, they need to have some more places like that, where things are ad libbed more often, because everything is so formal now, they don't give you a chance to really, you know, get into it and know the bottom of it. And so, that's a failure of the time.
Well --

Which, I wanted to say one thing here. The American musician is losing out, because the impresarios and the cabaret owners are too stingy to hire a band, but when we played -- when Miss Rae Ray Harrison and I played in Tokyo and all over Japan, they had bands that had eighteen pieces. And I know they don't have the money comparable to American cabaret goers and

theater goers. Now, they had everything there. Now, these boys are learning to play with big bands, while we are here -- the only thing that's saving the American musician against these foreign musicians, like in Japan, is because -- and some of the other Oriental countries -- is because they cannot im-provise, but they're good copyists. And they're good musicians. They can read and then they can copy a solo, an American solo, off the tape, or off the record. But they can't produce them themselves, yet. But, in time, that will come.
Right.

And then we'll be number two in bands, even with the stuff that we created. Because their jazz is an American product. I know that some people will say that 60% of it is black. But it still is an American product. And, you know, we're all, it's part of the melting pot. It came out of the melting pot where everybody contributed something to it. But we, we contributed the most part. That's why we feel that we should have a chance to work at it. Is because we have created the most of it and it was through us that it got started.
Well, let's get back now to Atlantic City in 1920. It was in 1920 that you left to go to Detroit, right?
Yeah.
Why Detroit? How did that come about?

Well, Jimmy Harrison was from Detroit. And so was Fats. And they built up this great picture, how things was going to be out there, and you could walk down the street and pick up a hundred dollars in the street, see. And they had everything there, but there wasn't no mines in town, but it was almost as bad as the gold miners.

So we went out there and we did alright. We went out there and worked for a man called "Bony" Allen. And this man had a cabaret, but he was in bad health and he had to go to Hot Springs for his health. And he had -- he owed us about two thousand dollars, or fifteen hundred dollars, I guess, for the band. Because he was half sick, so he said, "Boys, I ain't got any money, but I've got a cabaret here and I've got to go away. I'll give you this cabaret and tell you what overhead means and everything else." Cause I didn't even know what overhead meant at that time, you see. And he sat down and he explained to us and everything and he said, "Now, take the cabaret and go for yourself," he said, "because I can't pay you and I'm not going to jump up and run out of town." He was one of the finest guys I know. See, he wasn't going to run out of town and don't pay or nothing, and just have you come looking for him, so he just -- well, we did very nicely with the cabaret.
What was it called?
Huh?
What was it called?
Well, just Cabaret.
(laugh)

It wasn't called much of nothing. But I don't know what we named it. Anyhow, it was in St. Catherine Street, right down the street from the Royal Garden. Everybody who's been to Detroit know where St. Catherine Street -- right off of -- I don't even remember the street, now. A big street. I don't know. Anyhow, so when we took this cabaret we had seven entertainers and there was five of us in the band. And of course, Charley Dixon and Elmer Albert Chambers and I took the cabaret because the other two boys said, "Look, we don't want to bother, just pay us a salary." So we paid them a salary and we took the cabaret over. And we were doing very nicely.

But at the same time, we were losing money. Because I found out one thing, you can't play and watch the cash register, too. So we couldn't do that, we found that we couldn't do that. So we played good music. Jimmy was a good piano player, I mean a good trombone player. And Elmer Chambers, incidentally, was in the war with me. And Charley Dixon played very well. Later on he was an arranger with Chick Webb. And Elmer Chambers worked with Fletcher Henderson after he left me, see. Because I had a boy fellow from Philadelphia came in there named Charley Gaines, see, and he worked with me until, in fact until I finished that job.
But, after we came back --
But now, prohibition came in around this time.
Well, prohibition was already in.
When you got to -- all over, yes.

So what happened -- how we handled that prohibition situation was that we had a man that walked around with the whiskey in his pocket -- flask in his pocket. And he sat down at a table and he said, 'Hello, Joe.', or something like that. And then, they had ginger ale on the table or something like that and he'd just pour so much in each drink, see?
Uh hunh.
And they paid him. But we come to find out later that he had two bottles. One was ours, which he very seldom used, and he had his own bottle, see, so we were losing that.

So now, when one of the ladies that I was with, one of the waitresses, she come to me and she said, 'Sam, how's business?' Well, I was a little guy and I thought I knew everything, and I told her, 'Look, business is business and pleasure is pleasure. We are together for pleasure. Now stay out of my business, see?' And she said this two or three times and then I didn't catch on, say nothin' back to her. So, at last she said, used a four letter word, and said, 'What the so and so do you think you are?' 'I'm trying to tell you something.' See, and I didn't

know that she was trying to tell me something. I didn't have sense enough to know then. And what she was trying to tell me, the bartender was trying to get her to work along with him with the other -- course, they don't know that I'm going with her.
I see.
For the simple

Tell you the reason why, because I've got my wife out there. // See, and I'm trying to run a harem on the side, see, so anyhow, what happened, she told me, at last I let her talk. I'd been stopping her from talking because I thought she was trying to put her hand in my pocket, see. So, anyhow, I let her talk and she told me the setup that was happening. Well after Charley and I and Elman got together, we said, "Look, we're not making the money we should make. And we're out here and if we get into any trouble, we're way away from home, and we don't know how much money they've got at home to send us to get us out of trouble. Let's break up this thing and go back East." So we broke up the cabaret and went back to Atlantic City.
I see. Now, before we leave Detroit, I just wanted to ask you what was going on in Detroit at that time, musically?

Well, they had four or five great bands. One fellow that had a great band was named Bart Howard. Now, they had large bands there. They had bands of 12 pieces, and like that. I don't think there was any larger than
END OF REEL 2
that. There was another fellow that had a band there, but I can't think of the name, you know? It's been quite a many years.
Uh hunh.
See, but they had some nice bands out there.
But we had a Dixieland combination, see. And we stood up there with men like Elma Chambers and Jimmy Harrison, and I could play fairly good then, you know? And we were doing all right.
So you were still playing things like "Margie" and some of the --
Well, we was playing those.
The pop tunes of the days.
Yeah, well most of the things were. And then we used such numbers as "St. Louis Blues" and things like that, you know.
Uh hunh.

And we didn't have any arrangement on them, but I used to try to make endings, you know? A new ending or give it a little introduction to try to make it sound like something. And when we got back East, I still improved on that. Because, now when we got back East, I had a clarinet. And a saxophone. Saxophone and I played clarinet. And I had the trumpet and I had a regular Dixieland band then, see.
Who was the clarinet and saxophone player?
Well, I had a fellow -- no, I had a fellow [WALTER] a West Indian fellow named Edwards. He was good.
Uh hunh.
In a way, but he didn't have the swing that men like Buster Bailey -- he knew his instrument, but he didn't have the swing.
See, Jimmy Harrison didn't come back with us. And I wasn't particular about Jimmy Harrison, either, because now I was thinking seriously about having a band and Jimmy didn't read well.
I see. But when you then went back to Atlantic City, was it still 1920, or was it now 1921?
Well, I think it was the beginning of 1921. It was in the Spring.
Okay, well around that time, I guess, the Paradise Cafe was in business, right?

Well, at that time, let's see. No, Charley was working on the Boardwalk. And the man had the -- Al Branch had a place there where the Paradise was. But Ralph (Wheelock) hadn't taken it over. He took it over that summer, or the end of that summer. Cause Charley lived the year round at Atlantic City at that time, see. And I think that Ralph
Wheeloff
Wheelock -- and he was really going -- wait, yeah, that was about '21, because then Charley left and came to New York.
Yeah. But now, Atlantic City during prohibition must have been a little wilder, a little different from what it was before that, in 1918 for instance.
Oh yes. Because, you see, a lot of people started drinking in prohibition, even myself, that didn't drink at all..
Uh hunh.
Because Charley was another one. I guess the biggest thing I could get for me was a glass of sherry, maybe. And I copied that from Charley.

But now that prohibition was in, everybody thought that they were doing something to spite the government by pouring a lot of liquor in themselves. So that liquor was now jumping. There was more liquor around now than there was before prohibition.
Right.
And then, a lot of times, we got a lot of bad liquor, see?
Well, where did you then, when you got back to Atlantic City, where did you perform?
Well, when I come back to Atlantic City I was getting a band together and a man named Ben Allen had a

place at Kentucky and Arctic Avenue. And then he was just turning his place over to another MAN called Charley, um, anyhow this fellow was Charley, I can't think of Charley's name, but, anyhow, this fellow was a very good friend. And I worked a season there. That was when I worked with the two Ethels and there was a fellow named Snow Fisher, he was a great strutter, and a girl named Izzy Ringgold was a great dancer, come from a dancing family.
Okay, now, the two Ethels were Ethel Waters and Ethel White.
Ethel Williams.
Ethel Williams and Ethel Waters. Right.
They were the two Ethels. And at that time they were good friends and they were even -- and they had a like a sister team, and they even had their clothes alike, you know?
And they sang together, huh?
Yeah. And Ethel Waters -- er, Williams was the dancer and Ethel Williams, I mean Ethel Waters, was the singer.
Uh hunh.
Ethel Waters was never a great singer. But she was a -- more of an entertainer.
ISOLA RINGGOLD
Ethel Williams, you mean.
No, Ethel Waters was a singer, but not much of a singer. And Ethel Williams was a good, very good dancer. Eccentric dancer, like.
But you don't think Ethel Waters was much of a singer.
I know she wasn't.
(laugh)
And she had never been. And she ain't much of a singer. But she's been an entertainer with a very pleasing voice, but she wasn't any singer.

The way I know as singing, that somebody can sing -- she may have been what we call a crooner. At that time there wasn't no name for it. There wasn't no name, 'crooner', but she'd never been a great singer.

Now, when I come back from Detroit, a man, a fellow come to me and he said, "Sam, what are you doing?" And I said, "We just got back into town. We're not doing anything." Well, he said, "Charlie Reynolds is taking over old man Baron's, Ben Allen's, rather, old man Ben Allen's place." Now let me tell you about Ben Allen. Ben Allen was a -- there was two negroes in Atlantic City at that time that controlled the whole negro section. One was Ben Allen, and then, up North, up in the other part of the town, there was another fellow named Mike Green.

Now, these two fellows could HANDLE on any part of the sporting world and they could control anything that went on down there. But Ben Allen was getting old now, and he was tired of this business, so he turned the place over to Charley Reynolds. But Charley Reynolds was a younger fellow and he had his gambling going there and everything, so he wanted a good show. He figured that being at Kentucky and Arctic Avenue, that was the hub of the black belt. Where everybody, both the people who were good and the people who were bad, everybody circulated around there.

See, so, he said, 'Sam, you can bring a band in here.' I had about, let's see, I had five, six musicians at that time. He said, 'Come on in here and find me some girls that are good entertainers. And a man to go along with them.' So, that's when I picked up the two Ethels and another girl named Izzy Ringgold, which was a very good dancer and singer. In fact, she outsung most of the girls at that time. She was very good. And then I had a fellow called Snow Fisher.

Well, we worked all the summer. And, of course, being in the heart of town, there wasn't no laying off. You had to keep the music going all the time. Often, I'd keep the music going. So one night we started in at 9 o'clock. About 12 o'clock Ethel Waters got tired of jumping up every now and then, doing a song. So she said to Sam, 'Why don't you go an' urinate,
relieve yourself." She said, because, "And take a rest, because I'm tired of singing."

So, anyhow, we got along very nicely. But before the season was over, a man came down from New York, which everybody knew at that time was the boss of Harlem, was Baron Wilkins. Baron Wilkins come down and said he was looking for a band. And he asked Charley Reynolds, "What about the band you've got?" Because the season was about to close down there. So, Charley Reynolds said, "Hey this guy is good. He's a young kid, he's trying to get going and one thing, he tends to business. I don't know what he does after the business, but he really tends to business while he's on the job." See, so Baron come in and said to me, "Son, would you like to come to New York?" Well, that's where I wanted to go. I'd been wanting to go there. It was my Mecca. So, I told him, "Sure, what job do you have there", and he said, "In my cabaret." So I said, "Well, I'd be delighted, Mr. Baron, so we get together on the price. Well, we did get together on the price. I got something like $40.00 a week, and the men got something like $25. or $30. a week. Anyhow, I came to New York.
Now, before we leave Atlantic City, I wanted to ask you about some of the other performers who were around when you got back there. Was like, Frankie, 'half-pint', Jackson, was --

Well, Frankie, half-pint, Jackson, Frankie Jackson, I knew him before I left for Newark. Now, he worked up there and there was something I wanted to tell you about him. He said something that was almost a sacrilege. You know how you --he used to talk on the floor between his songs. They all took that from Madison Reed. Madison was the first man used to make up stories on his songs. So he was singing a song, and this was near around Easter time, so he was tellin' the -- preaching. Like a lot of the comedians do in those days. He was preaching this song, and he was preaching about Jesus Christ, see. And he was saying that about Palm Sunday, he said he came into with the crowd all hollering 'Hosanna' and waving palms and all like that. But, he said, 'But these people were sneaky.' He said, 'He come in there on Palm Sunday, and by Wednesday, they put him out.' See, Christ was riding on one of those jackasses. But Frankie didn't say that. He said, 'They put him out, they put his ass out.' See? And I thought this was terrible.
(laugh)

For a man to talk about Jesus Christ like that. And he kept saying it. And a lot of people said, 'Oh!' But it wasn't sacrilege on his part, we thought it. But what he was saying -- they did put him out, and they put his little jackass out. But he didn't say, 'jackass'. He said, 'They put him out and they put his ass out.'
(laugh)
Jaxan

I always remember that Frankie Jackson was nice. He was from Chicago. He was a nice guy. And another guy from Chicago, Billy Leadman. He was very good. And then they had a woman there. Nobody's ever danced like she, since. Was Grace Jackson. Grace Jackson was a terrific dancer, but she got up with one of those pimps around there and he got her on dope, see?
Um.

And then we had such singers as Mary Stafford, worked with Madison Reed and with Eubie Blake. She was one of the greatest. You could hear her four or five blocks away, yelling, when she would sing. I knew her as a kid, as I told you, I used stare and look in the window for her. And I had the nerve to fall in love with her when I was a kid. You see?
(laugh)
And she looked at me and said, 'Get out of the way, you little bugger.'

So, and then there was a woman there called Mabel -- what was her name, Mabel, I can't think of it -- and then we had the great Mattie HITE, was there. There was a woman called A Bee Palmer. These were great singers. These were all great singers.
Now, Bessie Smith was also at the Paradise around this time. But she wasn't really very well known.
Did you hear about her at all?

Well, Bessie Smith was there and she did alright with the people, but a lot of people didn't appreciate Bessie Smith. Not because Bessie Smith wasn't a singer, but because they hadn't had a touch of the Blues.
Right.

They really didn't understand the Blues. And then when anybody -- when Bessie Smith sang the Blues, the Blues was rather depressing in those days, you know what I mean? There used to be people'd say the Blues was when you was going to -- well, somebody was in trouble. And like, we used to say "Blue Monday", when you had a whole lot of work to do or something like that, we sang the Blues. But on the whole, Atlantic City, they were for more joyous things, you know? And most sob songs and sentimental songs, you know?

Right. Well, that leads me to my next question, which is, in 1920, Mamie Smith recorded, you know, the "Crazy Blues", and all of a sudden black singers started recording which they hadn't before. Do you remember, I mean, "Crazy Blues", they say, was a very big hit. Do you remember that being a big hit? Do you remember hearing these records?
Yes, it was a very big hit. But a lot of people don't give the right credit, to the right people. The man that's due credit is Perry Bradford.

Oh, sure. No, no, I'm not talking about that. I know that. But, I wanted to know if you, being in Atlantic City around that time, remember suddenly there being records, and did you for instance, listen to records? Did you have a phonograph or did you know someone who had one. That was a whole new thing for black people, wasn't it?
Well, we didn't listen too much to records, because most blacks, there wasn't a lot of them had phonographs, you know what I mean?
Uh hunh.
And at that time they were the old fashioned phonographs that you'd wind up, you know?
Uh hunh.
No electric phonographs or record players. It was all wind up. And then, some people had them. And the portable ones hadn't taken hold yet, you know?
Right.

So it was only when maybe they'd buy one and run it in a cabaret, like this was a new innovation or something like that, but otherwise it wasn't known. But we heard about the 'Crazy Blues' and Mamie Smith for the simple reason why. So many people was always coming back from New York to Atlantic City all the time, cause now Atlantic City was the summer Mecca, while New York was the winter Mecca, you know what I mean? Of the people in the life.
Because if you wasn't in the life, you didn't go to cabarets in those days.
Right. It was also a sort of playground for rich white people, wasn't it, at that time. Fashionable.
Well, we had plenty of -- Atlantic City was a playground and a lot of the rich people used to come over to Back Bay, for the simple reason that in the summer they got tired of the boardwalk.
The waltzes, and the --
And they'd come over on the -- that's when I started working for Old Man Brown. At twelve o'clock they were all standing outside. And by twelve fifteen, the place was loaded with just white people.

And the same thing happened with Kelly's, where Madison Reed and Eubie Blake worked. Same thing in those places. But they didn't go into places like the Bucket of Blood. And, later on, when Charley opened, he put them all, both of them in the shade. See, for awhile, Charley worked at the Boathouse, then he went with Billy Leadman and Mary Stafford, they had a regular crew. And Grace Jackson. And then he went down to Illinois Avenue to -- Al Branch had a place down there. Well, Al Branch gave up this place, and Ralph Wheelock took it over. And then that's the beginning of the days of the Paradise, see?
Right.
He had it in the summertime and then Ralph Wheelock had it.
And see, and then, and Charley stayed down there in the summertime, and that year, it was '20.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Well, that year Charley went to Baron's, too. And he played --
In New York.
And he preceded me there by a year, or a half a year.
I see, so it was later in 1920 that you came to New York to play for Baron Wilkins.
Yeah.
Was New York referred to then as the 'Big Apple', or did that come later?
Uh --
Did musicians call New York, the 'Big Apple', back in those days.
No, I don't remember that.
That would have been later than --
I don't remember calling it the 'Big Apple'.
Uh hunh.

Because I know there was a place there in New York that we used to all frequent, called the "Big Apple", right across there from Smalls. But I don't remember that statement, that we were in the "Big Apple".
Uh hunh. Well, that Big Apple was still there, on the same corner, 135th and Seventh. Right.

But I don't remember that statement, but I know they came there. Many of them came. But, when we got the word in Atlantic City, Charley had this Matty (Hight) and Mary Stafford, and this other girl I'm talking about. She was a very good singer. She worked with Eubie Blake for awhile. Was also -- was Mabel Richardson. She was from Washington, or down that way. Baltimore and Washington had some terrific girl singers. And a lot of the banjo and guitar players come from there. Washington had good tap dancers. That's where (unintelligible). Philadelphia had piano players.
Okay, so you came to New York and you started working at Baron Wilkins. What was your band at this point. Did you have Charley Gaines with you?
No, I had Elmer Chambers.
Oh, I thought he had left you when you left Detroit.
No, he left me when we got to New York.
Oh, I see, so he came to New York with
you. He had been with you in Atlantic City, then.
He had been with me. He had been in Chicago, in Detroit with me, Atlantic City with me. And now we were going to New York.
Right.
He still played with me.
And Charley Dixon was still with you?
Yeah, Charley Dixon was there.
And who else?
But not Jimmy Harrison. No, Jimmy Harrison stayed out West this time.
Uh hunh.

He didn't come back from Detroit with us. He stayed out there. And I had a fellow called Revis Horton. He was a good trombone player. But, it's like I say with all trombone players, they're half nuts. You see. And he was -- Jimmy Harrison -- you see, nothing vicious about either one of them. But, Revis Horton, at that time, he didn't like white people. And Jimmy Harrison, he couldn't stop laughing. He laughed all the time. He told me he got fired off a job for laughing. The boss would look at him and say, 'You laugh too much. You take your hat and get out of here.'
(laugh)
But, see, they were both of them good trombone players.
So, how big a band did you have at Baron Wilkins?
Well now, let me see. There was a guitar, bass -- guitar, drum, piano, no bass. Clarinet, trumpet, and saxophone.
Uh hunh.
That was six. Six pieces.
Who was the saxophone player? Was that the --
The saxophone player was a fellow named Rollem Roland Smith.
Uh hunh.
And the clarinet player was a man named Edwards. We used to call him Mr. Edwards. [WALTER EDWARDS]
The West Indian.
Yeah, he was the West Indian fellow.
Right.
Yeah, see, so, -- and the rest of them were, you know -- Joey Young, he was on the drums. And Charley Dixon on guitar -- oh, banjoe, tenor banjo, there was no guitar in those days.
Were you playing arrangements at this time?
Yes. I started playing arrangements. A funny thing happened to us there. Well, now we were in Baron's,
that's where I met and we become very good friends, with Bricktop.
Uh hunh.

Bricktop worked there, but later Snow worked with me. But Bricktop was the ruling singer. And they had a man there called Tony Donovan. Well, Tony was good because -- but Bricktop was the queen of the thing. Because Bricktop couldn't sing anything either. But she was a very fine hostess.
Uh hunh.

You know, and she made more money when you know you'd go from table to table. She made more money than anybody because I don't know -- she had a very pleasing disposition. Because we never had no colored people there, you know.
Uh hunh.

It was all white. And it was a funny thing. There was two brothers. Baron and Leroy. Baron Wilkins never had never allowed any of the colored people to come into his place. And Leroy never allowed any white people. But Leroy, -- one white man used to come into his place.
Al Jolson.

Yeah. Al Jolson was the only white man he that had a card to come in there. And nobody stopped him. But, Baron had a lot of the boys around there, a lot of the sportsmen around there, used to come upstairs and playing

and gambling and like that. But, because they sharped the white women, they wouldn't have them down there because the white women were the girl friends and the wives of the gangsters. And the beer barons was going at that time, you see?
Uh hunh.

I know that one time Bricktop was singing a piece on the floor, and that's about the only time I ever seen it. And a guy come up and said, 'Here Sam, sounds good.' And he handed me something, and it was just by chance, I happened to look at it. It was a ten thousand dollar bill. He had given one to the waiter too. You know, he was going to take them back, you know. We knew we wasn't going nowhere with it.
Oh, I see.
Over his dead body. But that was the first time I'd ever seen -- I believe it was the last time I've ever seen a ten thousand dollar bill.
Uh hunh.
But they loved the band, we played dances for them, we had a wonderful time there, see. And we stayed there for quite awhile, til I added another man. So there was seven.
Who did you add?
Bass.
Who was that? Who was the bass player?
Oh. It was a fellow named Edwards, I think. Bass Edwards.
Bass Edwards.
Well, he played around here and he used to put a cigar in his mouth while he was playing. He played the tuba.
Uh hunh.

He'd put a cigar in his mouth, sticking out like this, and at the same time he'd blow the smoke through the horn, and it looked like the band was steaming so that, they were on fire, you know what I mean?
So, when you say Bass, you really mean at this point, Tuba.
Now, you said you were playing arrangements. Were you writing these arrangements?
Yes. Well, the way we did, it wasn't a full arrangement.
Uh hunh.
We had a --
A head arrangement.
Yeah, well like a head. And we'd put an introduction on it, maybe a four bar introduction, and then we'd put maybe a couple of bars to make a first ending or a second ending.

Now, we had a great arrangement on a number called, "Dear Old Southland". So, in the course of a conversation, a fellow walked in there named Sidney Bechet. Well, he didn't look -- he looked just like any other musician in my book. I didn't know who he was. So he come in and he sat down there and so Bricktop said, "Sam, I want you to meet Sidney Bechet." So, I met him and we sat there and talked for a little while, and he said he was from Chicago and just around, you know what I mean. So after we got through playing, Bricktop asked him, "Would you like to play a piece for us?" And he said, "Sure, I'll play something for you. You've got a nice little band here." Or something like that, see. And he said to me, "Hey Sam, do you know 'Dear Old Southland'? Give it to me." I don't know what key it was. And he said, "Give me four beats." Well when Sidney Bechet got through with "Dear Old Southland", I never played my arrangement any more.
Was he playing clarinet then?
No, he was playing soprano.
Soprano then.
Soprano. And when he got through with "Dear Old Southland", I didn't want to hear "Dear Old Southland" no more in life.
Did he say he was from Chicago or New Orleans?
He said he come from Chicago.
Oh, so he'd been in Chicago.
Well, let me tell you about that New Orleans business. Most of those guys -- like I come from Philadelphia, but you hear me talking about Atlantic City.
Right.
Because that's where I got my start.
Yeah.
Now, most of those fellows were pure nothing in New Orleans. Louis Armstrong was another one. And Joe Oliver. And Freddy Koppard. They were nothing until after they come to Chicago.
But they were from New Orleans.

Yeah. But they wasn't nothing. And a lot of people get this thing about -- that jazz originated in -- which is very simple and very elementary to say that jazz originated in New Orleans, because it didn't. It spontaneously originated all over the United States. New Orleans contributed so much to it. But even Louis Armstrong still wouldn't have been anything if it don't be for him coming to New York with Fletcher Henderson. Because Fletcher Henderson gave him the showcase. But nobody -- they mention Louis Armstrong being a great man, but they never say that Louis Armstrong was great on account of he come into New York with Fletcher Henderson.
Now, I missed Louis Armstrong by about two weeks. I tried to get him to go to Europe with me.
We'll get to that later. Because, right now, we're still in 1920 or '21.
Yeah.
And I wanted to ask you what you were playing at Baron Wilkins. Were you doing original compositions then, too?
Well, no, I wasn't.
Just standard things.
I was just playing the songs that were popular in those days, you know what I mean?
Right.
Because, see, mostly when we were playing, we had like five or six entertainers. And we didn't do a whole lot of dancing, because we didn't have a very large place, see?
Uh hunh.
And you'd play some dances, but... because naturally, every time you played for entertainers, there was money coming in the cut-box. Which we used to split up.
Right. Now, how much -- did the tips exceed the amount you got paid regularly? Your salary?
Well, you got paid a regular salary. Like I told you, I think I got $40.00 and the men got $25.00 or $30.00
Uh hunh.

But, you remember one thing. It wasn't the time, for over a year and some months that I was there -- the lowest we ever made for the, something like the twelve or eleven that split up with us, was $4.00. And we made as high as $15,00 or $20.00 apiece.
Were you ever called upon to make any records, to appear in any records during that period?
Not until the next year. I had a chance to go to make records the next year.
Alright, first let's get to that. When did you leave Baron Wilkins? And how, under what circumstances?

I left Baron Wilkins after being there about a year and two or three months. And what happened -- Old Man Baron didn't want me to leave. But what happened, the dude wanted to cut the band down. Well as I knew in those days and as I feel today, the band was more important than me. See, cause I could have been a good pianist. But I stopped thinking about the piano and started working, now, towards having a good band. See, I thought I'd go farther with a band than I would with a piano. I used to be a composer. I used to with a lot of things.

So, when we left there, I didn't have a -- Old Man Baron told me, 'You're foolish for leaving here, son.' And he used a four letter word, but he said, 'Because you won't be out on the street two weeks before you won't know who the first musician

is you're quitting for. And if you stay, I will double your salary, but we'll cut you two men off -- down to five. Because that's what Dude wanted. Dude Adams was his manager. So I said, "No, no Mr. Baron. I appreciate what you're trying to offer me, but my idea is to have a band. Not to make a little more money." You see?
Uh hunh.

So, of course, I'd bought a house there, you see, and I'd paid $14,000. for it. Course, we made good money, no question bout that. But that wasn't important to me. My idea was to be a successful band leader.
Right.

And so, I worked on that line. Well, when I left, I got a new experience, because along comes a man -- was it there? Wait a minute now. No, I'm ahead of my story. Let me tell you something that happened. There was a dancer when we was down at Baron's, named Yonder.
Y-o-n-d-e-r?

Y-o-n-d-e-r. Wait a minute, what was his name? I can't think of his name now. But, this dancer was as good as Bill Robinson. But he made one mistake. He went into -- he left for Waterville to go for the burlesque. And burlesque is a step below vaudeville.. See, instead of going up. So, anyhow, Dancing Dodson was his name. Dancing Dodson. Well, Dodson came to us and here was another experience that we had

that was very good, because he was working at the Regent Theater. And he heard about the band, so we had a nice little band there, so he come down one day to listen to the band and he was talking to Bricktop and a couple of other entertainers there. So he said, "How would you boys like to come on and try to -- have you ever been on stage?" We said "no we hadn't". So he said, "Well, I'll tell you what I'm going to do. I'm going to give you a chance. I'm going to bring you down there and let you do a couple of numbers in my show." He was a single. So he said, "Alright, polish up your horns and get your shoes shined and everything and get yourself together and come on down to the theater." Now the Regent Theater is 116th Street and 7th Avenue. And so, he put us on. He got out there and said -- okay, he introduced us, see, and we were ready to play. See, and the curtain come up -- and, well when we started off, we sounded like a bunch of cats yelling. Well, what happened, everybody was scared to death because all these guys, you know, we had come up from Atlantic City and we had never been into a theater. Elmon Chambers couldn't find his mouth. He couldn't find the embouchure. And the trombone player was just blowing. He didn't know. And to me, it looked just like two keys, one big white key and one big black key. That's all I could see. And I know we must have sounded like the devil. We really sounded like the devil.

And so, we sounded so terrible that Dodson came out on the stage and said, "Wait a minute, that's enough of this foolishness." He said, "Let me straighten you guys out. After all, you're here to play some good music for the people, not to clown and kid like you would in the cabaret." You know? But that settled us. We went on and did very fine for that show. And he kept us there for two or three days, you know. Because it wasn't paid. But that was our first chance.

Now, the second chance I got was an act. The first time I was ever on stage. But, I'm telling you, it was a horrible feeling. The sweat rolled down on us and, (laugh), (unintelligible). And I couldn't find nothing.
Uh hunh.
And then Elmer Chambers, he said, "I tried very hard, but I couldn't find my mouth." And you know, he couldn't get the horn on his chops.
(laugh)
And poor Horton was blowing everything out, you see?
Uh hunh.

So, anyhow, but after he did that -- he coming out and saying that, it changed the whole picture. Then we went into a little number like, "Toot, Toot, Tootsie, Good-bye", something like that. And the people liked it very much, you see. That was my first chance on the stage, see?

And then the next chance was when I was working -- and then there was an act named CHAPPELLE and STINNETTE. They hired us for a week, in the Lafayette. They hired us for a week in a theater, the Lafayette. On account of what they heard that we was doing a very good job down there.
This was around the same period.
And on the same bill -- yeah, this was still in Baron's. I'm still in Baron's. On this bill was -- there was an act that's very good, Clarence Williams was there with Eva Taylor. That was his wife.
Right.

And it was the first time she had ever been on a New York stage too, see? And Clarence Williams -- they had an act, and they was on the same bill, and we played for CHAPPELLE and Stinnette And so we did a very good -- that was the first week we ever been on the stage. From then on I thought I was somebody.
Later on, when I left there, they were looking for -- a second show, "Plantation Days". James P. Johnson had the first show.
Now we're getting into 1924 or 5, aren't we?
No, we're still going into '23.
Going into '23.
Yeah.
I see. Before we get to that, let me just ask you about Harlem in those days. Did you play rent parties there like you had in --
No, I didn't have no need. I was working steady now, above that.
So you're above the rent parties.
Yeah. There were rent parties going on, but they were for youngsters. I called myself a finished musician, now.
What about Buffet Flats.
Well, we'd go up there and drink.
What were the Buffet Flats like?
Well, the Buffet Flats, at this time, they began to have pianolas.
Uh hunh.

And they didn't have any piano players, but they had the pianolas. Put a Lucky Roberts piano roll on, Peter Wedling. And some of the other fellows that had made rolls for the piano roll companies. And then you set there and drink. Because it was prohibition. And they would serve you the liquor in a pitcher and a cup, like you was having tea. And you'd sit there and drink and you'd meet a little lady friend and all like that, see. And they had at the Buffet Flat, it was more like a
motel. They had rooms for you if you got that far.
Yes, well, I've heard that all kinds of things went on there. Everything imaginable that was illegal went on there in the Buffet Flats.
Absolutely, that's what I'm saying. It was like a motel. If you'd get that far. Depending on who your friend was, you could do anything you wanted to. The sky was your limit.
I see.

And they had to make money, that's because the rent would go up for the other people. Because the woman that -- say, this apartment, there's six apartments in this house. Well, the poor people can't afford it there, with $30, $35 a month.
Uh hunh.
But the madam that was running the Buffet Flats, she was supposed to pay $75.00 or $100.00 a month, because she was making that some times in one night.
Right.

You see, so when the real estate agent would say, "Look here, I'm -- I can make enough if I can get a couple of buffet flats in here, I can make more than I'm making on these other people." And so, he'd be ready to dispossess those people if they got anyways back in their rent. And give it to somebody running an illegitimate house, you see?
I see.
The house of flowers, or whatever you want to call it.

You know, see, so that's what went on. But the Buffet Flats were very popular because you couldn't very well do what you wanted in the cabaret, you know. Because, see, most of the people around that time was married or had a girl friend, and if you had a stranger, it would be back even before you could get back home -- somebody'd been there ahead of you and told the people at home, "I just saw your husband, your boyfriend, around the corner with Anna Jones." And it'd be one of those things like Frankie and Johnny, you know.
Right. But did -- why were they called Buffet Flats. Do you know?
Well, Buffet Flats -- the only thing I know, it would come from like you see in a lot of railroads -- porters, like --
Right.
Because they'd be running, have a run from here to Chicago, or Chicago to here, why they'd stop in -- why, they worked in the buffet cars on the train, I think it got --
I've heard that before, you're really just confirming that.
Yes. Well, they'd call it a buffet flat.
Why, because they used to, they were used to that, and that was the biggest trade.
And porters had a high standing, didn't they?
Oh, yeah.
Because they were a good catch.

They were a very good catch, you know, in that time. The girls would go for them. And they didn't stay there either. So they didn't tie them right down. One of the fellows stayin' there all the time, he was doin' them like that, see?
(laugh)
But he thought he wouldn't be back for a -- another seven or eight days on his next run. And they had the freedom.
Right. Okay, now let's get to 1923 and were you still at Baron's?
I quit there at the beginning of 1923.
Uh hunh.

I had quit there and Old Man Baron said that I wouldn't be out for three days, I mean for two weeks before you wouldn't know who any of the boys was. And that's what happened. So, just like the old man said. Because the old man was a very brilliant man. He was a man that was -- it's worth saying a few words about him because he was a man that controlled
all Harlem for blacks.
Uh hunh.

He would not let nobody else in, less it was for the black man, see? He had controlled the Democratic Party and the Republican Party. From the leaders of both parties, and old man, registered but never voted.
Huh.

See, so -- but so, and he controlled both parties. Ferdinand Morton, I think was one, and I forget what the other fellow's name was now.
Anyhow -- and when Connie Carney's Inn opened up, it was called Shuffle Inn. Well, in order to protect another cabaret called Happy Rhone's, Old Man Baron wouldn't let him have a darned dancing license. And wouldn't let Connie Carney have the Shuffle Inn, as it was called then. Wouldn't let him have a dancing license, and he didn't, he wouldn't give -- where the Cotton Club was, later on, he wouldn't let that fellow sell liquor because Happy Rhone was colored cabaret.
He protected the places, he and Connors and Leroy, and all of them protected all the colored cabarets. Harlem was for a black man.
Uh hunh.
But then, the Italians come in, I think it was mostly the Italians. And they tricked the blacks by one

thing. They got hold of a black man that was a dope fiend. Yellow Charleston. They got ahold of Yellow Charleston and they shut him off, isolated him from all dope. Until he was like this. They told him, "Look, if you want to get dope and all the dope you want, you've got to shoot Old Man Baron." And he shot, he killed Old Man Baron. Right in front of his place. Right there at 7th Avenue and 134th Street.
When was this?

After I left. At that time, I was working at the Nest. In 1923. And he killed Old Man Baron, right there. And then they didn't protect him, either. The boys around there, Bob Hewlitt and all of the boys, the sportsmen, or gangsters, or pimps, or whatever you want to call them, that was around there. They run all night, two nights, looking and trying to find, Finally said Yellow Charleston. But the white gangsters had hid him for awhile.
Uh hunh.

But nobody was able, amongst the black boys like Johnny and Mal and Bob Hewlitt, was a legendary character around there. He was a big gangster. And Bully Hall, and these fellows. DESVERNY was one of them, was one of the guys around there that he went to the war in the 15th as a Buck Private. When he came back, was a Second Lieutenant. He got decorated right on the field.

So that's what happened. And then, when I come out of Baron's -- here's another chance in my life, and I'm showing about the chances that they had in those days, it was a show, it was the second company of "Plantation Days". Was being organized. And they were looking for a music director. Well, now, I had never been in a pit in my life.
Uh hunh.
But I had nerve.
(laugh)
They said, if you only needed nerve and carfare, you could go around the world. So I took this job on.
Well, were you on the street then, or were you at the Nest?
I was on the street.
I see.
I was doing nothing.
So this was a touring company.
And I'll show you one little joke about this. I bought this house, I bought a house on 129th Street. I had all my boys in the house, so I was taking their salaries and all like that.

Well, now, when we got out of a job, I paid $275, I had to pay a month when I first got this house. Before I bought this house in the next block. They all got out of work. When we got out of work, the boys all come to me and said, "Well, Sam,

you know we're working with you and you ain't working. So we can't pay no rent." Well, I had an awful time. I remembered that in the future. Anybody that ever hears this interview, don't ever take the men that you're working with on the job, in where you live. Because when you're out of work, they're out of work.
(laugh)
And all of this weight falls on you, because you can't put them out.
Well, anyhow, that's what happened, anyhow, so they all got other job, see? They eventually got jobs.

Well, when I got this show, I had to reorganize the band. The only one I had with me when I reorganized the band was the drummer. The rest of them had left. Now, here's what happened. We take the show out, and for the first time, I was stranded. This was my first strand. We got as far as Indianapolis. And Eddy Green was on this show. He was one of our first-class comedians. He and the man that owned the show, was called Friedenwald, that's 'free forest', Friedenwald.
Right.
Anyhow, he -- they both left and from Indianapolis, went on to Chicago, and took what money. We were stranded out there.
Well, now, there was another fellow there named Gus Smith. Gus Smith knew what to do. I didn't know that to do.

So he said, 'Well we can't leave all our girls out here stranded, like this.' And they were perfectly at home, that's one thing. I know one girl just got a newspaper and covered her head up and laid her head up on the wardrobe, and went right on to sleep.
(laugh)

We was all in the station, waiting. We was supposed to move on to another town. But there wasn't nobody there to move us on to the other town. That was the first strand. I didn't realize that I was stranded. I didn't even know what it meant.
(laugh)
Do you remember, what tunes were in the Plantation revue. And who else was with it. Who was with the show.

Well, we had a quartet of youngsters around there. We had Maude deForrest. Later, Maude deForrest went to Europe with Josephine Baker. She had been chosen by Josephine Baker bein' the first strip teaser. Maude deForrest was a very good blues singer. Because she had a heavy voice. And everybody thought you had to have a heavy voice to sing the blues in those days. The heavier your voice was, the better they thought you could sing the blues. As if that had anything to do with it anyway.
(laugh)
But they felt that way. Somebody was singing way down there, 'I Honey love you baby --', it was hoarse and raspy like that, they thought that was good, see?

And so, anyway, Maude DeForrest's partner was Gus Smith -- the guy was successful with moving. And my bunch. Then, we had a couple of comedians on the show, and the rest was -- two dancers. That's about all. But none of them of any consequence. But Gus Smith and Maude deForrest and myself, and Eddie Green, were the biggest people worth mentioning.

Anyhow, Gus organized this thing. We went about doing tab shows, because he understood all that. All down, Drake and Walker and all those. And all through Indiana and Illinois we did what you call tab shows, you know, where we got the word T-O-B-B-A from. [Theater Owners Booking Agency, aka Tough on Black Actors or Asses.]
Uh hunh.

We had a company, about 12, 15 people. And as the girls would make money, or they'd hear from home, why the show got smaller and smaller. And when it got down to where we had all the girls protected and it was all straightened out, well we went on home. Because we had money, you know what I mean? And so we went on back to New York, ourselves.

And I got back to New York -- now, this is where, where the really, the things start turning over now, see? I got back to New York and I walked into my drummer, the fellow that had been in the Army with me, George Howe. George Howe said, 'Sam,

Johnny Carey and Mal Frazier is looking for"-- that was the Nest -- "they're opening a new club called the Nest Club, and they're looking for somebody to take the band. And I told them that you would be in town and you had worked for Old Man Baron." And they'd been down to Old Man Baron, and Baron'd said that Sam is a good man, get him if you can, see? Said he's a conscientious kid, see? So --
That's how you got into the Nest.
Yeah.
Well, so, should we stop now, or do you want to go on?
No, let's stop now.
And we could pick up, next time, we could pick up from the Nest.
Yes.
It seems like a good way to break it.
Yeah, because --
Okay, this is Chris Albertson interviewing Sam Wooding for the Smithsonian Institution, April 26, 1975. Interview 3.
Sam, we left off where you were about to go into the Nest Club in 1923.
Well, when we come back off the road from

the "Plantation Days" where we got stranded and we had helped and all all the girls get home. I run into an old buddy of mine from the war. And he said, "Sam, what are you doing." And I said, "Doing nothing and going nowhere fast." So, he said to me, "Well, how would you like to go down to Johnny Carey and MAL Frazier, they are opening a new club. And they're looking for an orchestra leader and they'll put a band in there, and I said, "What size band?" And he said, "Well, you come on and see Johnny." And Johnny did more of the business than Mal. They were two sportsmen that had been around there in Harlem. In fact, they were king of that, and they had been under Baron Wilkins' tutelage and they were pretty good. Anyhow, so I went down to see them and they were just putting up a rag decoration in the place. And Johnny said to me, "Well I heard that you didn't have much luck out on the road, and I know you from Old Man Baron's place, how would you like to work for us?" Well, we got together and the money was satisfactory, so I said, "Sure, I'll be happy to come in here." And he said, "Well, we're going to open in about six weeks." "By the time this place is finished and we get a little revue together." And he said, "now, you start getting the band together." And we didn't have no contract. Because in those days, we didn't bother about a contract when you'd know people was straight and all like that and we'd worked together. I worked together with the man that sent me to Europe and never had a contract. You see, in those days,
it was a gentleman's agreement. If you can call them gentlemen.
(laugh)

So anyhow, I started to get a band together. Now, I wasn't trying for sound, I was trying to get a band together to eat and make a living. But, by picking, by looking at the place, I said, well you certainly don't want no trombone in there. And you don't want too big a -- but yet, I had in mind to have a round sound, but without expecting anything out of it. Because I think I was the first one in Harlem to try anything like this. So I had two saxophones, two trumpets, and a full rhythm section. But, of course, I know, if you've got a full rhythm section, it can sound like a big band, you'll get a big band sound.

You see, sometimes when you are short on one side, like if you're short in the reeds, you can take a trumpet and give him the third saxophone part, or sometime when you're short -- or when you need two trumpets and a trombone, then the tenor saxophone will answer the purpose for the general Public that don't really understand the sounds. So I put this TUBE TRIP together and I wasn't sure of it myself, so I used to rehearse at my house. And Johnny and them were beginning to get nervous. They said, "When you coming down here to rehearse?" And I said, "I'm not. I'm rehearsing up here quietly by myself and I don't want anybody to hear it." And on account of the confidence that they had in me from Baron Wilkins' place, and I'd had a nice pretty

band, they said, 'Well, we'll let you go. But you'd better be ready when you come in here, or out you go on your nose.' See, so anyhow, we opened up. Well, I wasn't trying for a sound, I was trying to eat, as I said before. You see, so it worked out. the one thing quiet as it's kept. That's the one thing that made Duke Ellington. The wa-wa and the plunger thing which he took from Bubber Miley, and he made a classic out of it. He using it with the whole band, but it really started - turned it into something by (unintelligible) Johnny Dunn was the first one. Well, anyhow --
Those were the Blackbirds revues.

Yeah. See, so, but Johnny, Johnny, had it a little different from the others, because he was more so- wa-wa-ooed sophisticated wow-wow. In other words, he wow-wowed with-double.* But Tommy Morris and Bubber Miley, it was lowdown. What we called then the gutbucket, you see?
Uh hunh.

A lot of them, see, them standing on the railroad track, waiting for my honey to come back. It'll be the last time I wait around for you.
Well, all those things had a meaning, you know?
Uh hunh.

And the blues. But now, I wanted to say one thing here. Blues was not a new music. Blues come off the ring shout and what you would call the approach to the spiritual. The, the, the word has slipped my mind now. You know, the approach to a spiritual that is not sacred.
Uh hunh.
So, but the blues were, it's a part of the negroe --

So now we come to the age, we just beginning to butt out into the age of the Stomp and real jazz. Because before that it was Dixieland. Right.

Oh, no, it was a mixture.
It was a mixture. As opposed to Baron's.
Yeah, it was different from Baron's -- Baron had -- and then this was a higher clientele than what Baron had. Baron had mostly the gangsters.
I see.
And beer barons, and all like that, see? But these were mostly per -- cause we had millionaires and everything coming up to the Nest, see. And they made a million dollars in one year.

Uh hunh.
In fact, very few of us had arrived at

that time. Edith Wilson used to be there. Florence Mills was about the only one that had actually arrived. And she arrived because on account of the ignorance of Gertie Saunders. When Gertie Saunders walked out of "Shuffle Along", Florence Mills stepped in and that made her.
Yes, right.

You see, so that's the way that went. But, see, I didn't understand in those days what it meant. But I understood later on when towards the end of my days at the club. First place, there was a man, Arthur S. Lyons. He was a fellow -- he was a struggling agent in those days. And he'd come down to the Nest and he'd sit there and he watched the boys and ask for a couple of numbers. I see.

So now, when Arthur come in there for a couple of pieces, he was always speak and he got more friendly, and one day he says, "Listen Sam, how would you like to go down on Broadway?" I said, "That 's what I'm trying for." See, because
I'd had two or three good numbers see, I'd made some arrangements on these numbers myself. I'll tell you, you want to know how I started to do this?
Yeah.

Well, I'll tell you Chris, we went downtown one day and we was trying to get some arrangements, because at that time I was only making introductions and endings. But inside the strain I wasn't doing it, you see.
That was improvised, huh?
Yeah.
Yeah.

And you see, now, so we'd call up, I forget whose arranging office it was. A white arranger's office. And I said, 'We'd like to come down and see about getting some arrangements.' He said, 'Sure, we've got plenty of time.' But he didn't know at the time that we were black musicians. So, when we hit the door, his attitude altogether changed. He said, 'Oh, oh, what do you want?' 'Somebody told us to come down here and get some arrangements.' So he said, 'No, I don't see how nobody could say that, because we've got all the work we can do.' So, and the way he talked, I knew he wasn't telling the truth. So we said, 'Okay buddy, it's alright.' So we come out and went on uptown. And then, from then on, I started thinking in terms of the whole number. And I ended up making numbers like, 'Gee, But I'm Glad to Know It's the Old Gang of

Uh hunh.

And the when the "Covered Wagon", I had it fixed with the Indians in there and all that. Well, this was the beginning. Well, Lyons was very pleased with this, you see. So he said to me, "Well, I'll tell you, Fletcher Henderson is making a mistake. He's going from a cabaret back to a dance hall. And you never step backwards." And he's the first one told me, he said, "Gertie Saunders has made that same mistake. She left a musical comedy to go into burlesque. Which is a step beneath." And you never step backwards, see. And he said, "The only time that you go from that, it's like with the sublime and the ridiculous. The ridiculous never precedes the sublime. It always comes after." You see, so -- and these points he set down and -- and he told me all these points, see. He was a Russian Jewish fellow. I didn't know he was Russian Jewish then. I didn't know what he was. I knew he was Jewish though. And he was a nice guy, see. So he said, "Now, I can get you down this -- in about four or five weeks, Fletcher will be through there, and he's going to the Roseland. And you can go over and follow him in there, if you want to." He said, "I'll put the

show in there, and I'll put the show in this fall." You see, so that was the beginning so, now, we'd worked harder, but we'd lost interest in the Nest. We wasn't interested in the Nest, now. We wasn't working for the Nest now, we was working for when we leave the Nest, you see?
Yes.

And then Johnny and them, one day, Old Barron Man Bryan said, "Sam, I see that you can duplicate yourself, and you have done better. I was betting that you couldn't do it the second time. This is, in a way of speaking, a fluke. And I've hit on something that I really don't know I'm on, see?
Right.
And that's the reason the band now, the band I have today, is different. I hit on the same thing. But this time, I was looking for it.

I see.

And what was the Club Alabam like?

You see, Club Alabam had such audience always as George Olson, Paul Whiteman, Vincent Lopez, Gloria Swanson, Firpo, Jack Dempsey and all, you know what I mean? It was the biggest thing in New York at the time.
It was right in the Times Square area.
Yeah.

Uh hunh.
And you could get anything you wanted in

Was this show called the Chocolate Kitties, or what was it called?

tape anytime. When I got the chance to go to Europe -- I'm a little ahead of my story, but I'll come back. When I got a chance to go to Europe, there was a great man -- which I considered a great man. Rosamund Johnson, a great Negro composer and a student of music, see. And he's written a lot of spirituals, I mean he's edited a lot of spirituals and had some folk songs of his own, I mean, art songs of his own.
J. Rosamund Johnson.
J. Rosamund Johnson.
Right.
So he tried for the job but he didn't have any chance to get it anyhow, because my manager had it, you see. Even though I wasn't no musician compared to Rosamund Johnson in those days.

So, anyhow, but he come to me afterwards, he was leaving. I met him coming in the place. I was coming in the place and he was going out. He said, "Well, Sam, I see you have got this job." Now get these words he said. He said, "Now, you're going to Europe. My advice to you is to watch all the bad bands, listen closely to all the bad bands that you'll hear. Then you'll know what not to do." And he said, "Well good luck to you." I thought he was joking, that'll show you how dizzy I was. And I thought he was joking, and I started laughing, "Yeah that's right." And it suddenly hit me that this man had said

something great. And I turned around to thank him -- next time I saw him he was dead. But I've never had a chance to thank him for that statement that has been with me and should be with all young musicians. In fact, any line you're in. Don't worry about those that are good. Worry about the bad ones. It's a negative approach, but it's a darned good approach for any youngster coming up in the business. Look for the things that are not right. Then you can say, "Well I'm glad that I saw that. Now I will know not to do that." Well that was one of the successes.

But, getting back to this show. We run this show good. We had some legendary people in that show. Because there was Johnny Hodgins and there was Eddie Rector. The "Sound Off"?

But this was in jazz though, you see. White people had done that drill. White artists had done that drill, but like the wooden soldiers, you know? And they're stiff and all like that. But now here's a man comes up and puts it into jazz, you know what I mean?
Uh hunh.

And while he's in the front of them doing all these steps, the girls are doing their drill behind him. Well this was a great thing, so. And then also we had a -- that was the first real production, because Clarence Robinson was another one in that show. He was a great guy in that show. he played the parts. He was the (unintelligible) We had an Oriental number. And it was done by a man, I guess he's dead now, too. Bunny Barney Weldon. Bunny Barney Weldon was one of the white producers on Broadway, and he -- these girls, I guess it was the first time we'd seen girls grind. Because he was one of the kinds where these girls were kind of ashamed to grind, you know? And I remember him saying there one day, and we'd like to die, he said, "God-dam it, girls, grind, grind." And he went on to show them how to grind, and that was more. Now the boys, the band, can't play nothing now.
(laugh)
Everybody's laughing.
How do you spell his name? Bunny, was it Bunny?
Bunny Weldon.
Bunny? Like Bunny Berrigan?
Yeah. Bunny Weldon.
Like James Weldon Johnson.
Yeah. He was white. And a hell of a ,,, gentleman, because he staged a terrific show there.
Uh hunh. Was the music all original, written for that show, or was it other music.
Yeah.
Do you remember any of it?

I can't think of it -- we had a couple of white men, white writers, see? From Tin Pan Alley, they did the show. The only thing I can remember the tune now, I can remember "I Miss My Mississippi Mammy", that's the song we used to open with.
Do you remember how that goes?

Mmm, no I don't think I remember that now. It's got a -- I've even played the thing, you know, but I remember the name of it.

And we had a kid in there too that never amounted to anything later on. Louis Simms. He used to do a dance in it.

But, Abby Mitchell was just like Mistinguette or some of those European stars. Every show, she was quitting.
Uh hunh.

"Mr. Lyons, I will not go on. I will not do it." "Such and such thing has happened and I'm not going on." And Arthur would look at me and say, "Okay, Sam, hit the introduction."

(laugh)
And we just started the introduction and, let's see if I can think of that. (plays piano), (sings), "I miss my Mississippi mammy --", something like that, anyhow.
Uh hunh.
We'd do that, and she'd start in singing. Cause she had to come on first, you know.
Right.

And then everybody would fall in there afterwards, see. And after you'd listened to what she had said, "Okay Sam, let it go." (laugh) And we'd know that she was coming every day and find some fault with something.
Uh hunh.
