"I won't go on, Mr. Lyons. I will not do it." And, "Okay, Sam, let it go."
(laugh)

And then one day Lyons come in and said to me, "How would you like to go to Europe?" I looked at him as if to say, "Are you kidding?" He said no, I've got a man, an impresario from Europe. A man named Leonidoff. Not the one in Radio City. This was, he spelled his name -L-e-n-i-d-o-w, which is the same thing. W is double f in Russian, see? And they were Russian, see.
Uh hunh.

Now, so I said, (unintelligible), and he'll be in here at ten o'clock tonight. Lyons got there first to prepare us so the boys would be all in shape. Well, one thing we only had one fellow drank a lot, a little bit. That was our trombone player. He would only drink when you started talking
to him about home and things like that. He was from Baltimore, and he would start drinking.

So I'll tell you about him after, but let me tell you about this show. Lyons brought this man in and this man heard us and he said, "I think that's what we need. But we've got to have a show." And Lyons said, "Don't worry about that, because I've got a choreographer here. Charles Davis can do that. And all he had to find was the necessary people. And we found some people like Adelaide Hall, Margaret Simms. And Eddie Rector didn't want to go, and neither did Johnny Higgins, see. So, we found others to take their places. Greenlee & Drayton was a big act in vaudeville then, see. And there was some others. Arthur Bryson. So we had a good show. So that was the way it was.

But before that, then Lyons would start playing the Winter Garden. Every Sunday night, we started putting a show into the Winter Garden. I played the Winter Garden I guess, during around a year, I guess about 10 times. Sunday night concerts. And we was doing vaudeville at different times. And we started vaudeville when we was there, at Loew's vaudeville.
See, I never played the Palace, because that was in opposition to Loew's State. And we never could play the Palace, see.
So then we went on at noontime. The only time I ever played the Palace was accompanying Ray Harrison. Ray Harrison later on played the Palace after -- she was one of the first
who went in women to play the Palace. And I was in the pit.
That was much later though.

Yeah. Way later, see. So, anyhow, how I come to find out that Lyons was Russian. Because he talked very -- he was clever and he talked very good English. But we come to find out that he'd gone with Zukor and all those other guys.
Uh hunh.

So anyhow, he had a brother Sam Lyons, Sam Lyons got in an argument with the busboy. And they started fighting. Well, the busboy was Greek and Sam was Russian. So when they started fighting, they forgot their English altogether. One started talking in Greek and the other one started talking in Russian. And I still wouldn't have known, but one of the waiters, one of the white waiters, we had white waiters, see. He said, 'This is a funny argument. Here's one cursing one out in Greek and the other one in Russian.' I said, 'Who's speaking Russian?' He said, 'Sam, Sam Lyons's is a Russian.' And the busboy was Greek. So then, when Arthur said to me, Arthur Lyons wasn't his name. He had a name like Reboski, or something like that, see?
Right.
So, when he was surprised that when I told him that he was Russian, he said, 'How did you know that?' I said, 'Your brother told me.'
(laugh)
He got in this fight and he told us that.
So, anyway, Lenidow came in at ten o'clock, right?
Well, we signed the contract that night about four o'clock in the morning.
This is late 1924, or when was this?
This is late 19 -- well, no, it was the beginning of 1925.
Uh hunh.
Yeah. See, because we went over in that July, or that August, see. And opened up in Berlin in either August or September.
Uh hunh. So, how did the trip go?
The trip? Oh, we had fun going over the water. See that was the first -- well, I'd been in the war, you know.
Uh hunh.

But we had a -- the guys were slipping in and out of other peoples bunks, because we had fun there. Others were gambling all the time. So, we had a wonderful time. The band, see, didn't have to do no rehearsing because we knew what we was going to do . We'd been doing it for a year and a half, you know what I mean?
Uh hunh.

So we had our program all set. And all we had to do was -- and we couldn't -- the show wasn't together yet. See, they were rushing it. So there wasn't no music even for us to rehearse. So we just had a wonderful -- had a ball on the boat, you see. We all of us had a wonderful trip because we all had our wives and lady friends. And the only one that didn't make it was Teroy, the same trombone player I'm telling you about.

Well, the Christmas before we left. It was Christmas in 1924, we were down at Loew's State. We played Loew's State for Christmas. We doubled at the theater, the Loew's State. And the stage director, the stage manager, had some good muscatel wine. So, we was all celebrating for Christmas. "Merry Christmas", and we'd drink. And Teroy drank too much wine, of the wine. Now, so when it was time for the show he said, "Twenty, fifteen minutes." And we were trying to get Teroy together. Teroy -- cause he was sweet. And Teroy wasn't a rummy. He didn't know how to gauge himself. So now, here he sits up on the stage. You've never seen a band set up like this -- in Loew's State, too -- never seen a band set up like this. Each trumpet was on each side of him. Because we had to lock their legs into his. Because if he had tried to pick up a mute or anything, he would have stumbled over on the stage, you see?
(laugh)
Now, he's sitting there. So we tell him,

"Well, play when you feel like it." As soon as we got -- before we went on, we were pumping black coffee into him. And he sat there on the stage and I guess the people in the audience said, "What a queer setup that is." The trombone between the two trumpets. But then, in the other setup, he would have dropped something and caused the public to know. But do you know, we got away with it. They never realized that he was REALLY as drunk as he was. And we didn't dare to move him until the curtain came down. And then two guys got on each arm of him, the two trumpet players, and we took him on upstairs to the dressing room. Well, that was the funniest thing that ever happened. But the whole time I couldn't play nothing for watching him. Because one mistake, and we'd ruin it.
So, anyway, you got to Europe and you went straight to Berlin. Is that right?

Yep. Well, Berlin was alright. Berlin was the most beautiful city I'd ever seen. The streets were perfect. They were clean. And one thing that we enjoyed was that all the houses in the block were painted -- if they were all blue, they were all blue, if they were all green, it was all green. And this was a new aspect in our life completely, you see.
And we took the best of it. We used to go down to the Lust Gardens, and to the Unter den Linden. And we'd go to Tier Park and --
But tell me, where did you -- did you have to rehearse, then, before you actually went on in Berlin?

I don't know how Arthur Lyons got that show on. For the simple reason that they had -- most of the stagehands were Russian. Germans were there and the Russians and English. Now, it was more of a bedlam. It was more bedlam because the Russians -- and that's when I knew and Arthur asked me -- and he was talking Russian. And then he couldn't speak German, but we had a Jewish fellow with us named Goldberg. Goldberg spoke Yiddish. So Yiddish and German were the same, and he was talking Yiddish, Arthur Lyons was talking Russian, and the Germans were answering back in German and Yiddish and Russian.
And none of you understood any of it.
Yeah. We didn't understand nothing.
Where did they put you up. Were you in a hotel?

We were in a hotel called the PRAGER Platz. And that's where we all rebelled on that, and after that we went about our business. Because they wanted to charge us 50 Marks a night, and stuff like that. Well 50 Marks was $12.50 and that was a whole lot of money in those days, see.
Uh hunh.
But the boys got good money for playing.
And you had to pay for that yourself.
Oh yeah, that's the only thing we had to
I see.

And food. We had to pay for food, but the hauling, the trunks and everything like that. All you had to do was to close your wardrobe trunk like that and the man come and get it and move on to the next place.
But tell me about the -- you know, your arrival in Berlin. Had there been advertising -- were people expecting you?
Oh, yeah.
I mean, this was something new. They hadn't had a black show.

It was something new and it was something like that occasion in Copenhagen that happened. Some of them were waiting to see gorillas and baboons and everything. They didn't know what they were going to see. Well, when these guys come at that time, because they didn't -- they didn't see no bad looking guys, because everybody had (Congolene) on their hair and everybody -- and they couldn't believe that we were Africans. See, some of them said, 'Well they must be from Brazil or some other place. They can't be Africans.' Course, all of the idea they had of American blacks was that they had kinky hair and a big flat nose and big thick lips.
(laugh)
So they didn't know what to think. But, one thing, I think we did something like seventy something performances in Berlin. And everyone packed to the door.
Tell me about the first performance.

Well, the first performance was -- well, Lenidow come and give me a pep talk, you see. He said, "Well Sam, it all depends on you now." We were getting ready to go into the pit. He said, -- and I said, in my brave voice that was shaking and all like that, I said to him, "Well, don't worry, Mr. Lenidow," Dr. Lenidow, we used to call him, "we'll make it. Everything will be alright." (laugh) And I was shaking worse than he was. Because he was trying something, neither one knew that it was going to be a success.
Now, when we started playing. The band just set there and when he give me the signal to start in, I tapped the baton and we started what we used for an overture, "By the Waters of the Minnetonka".
Uh hunh.

And see, now, the people were -- everybody, everything was quiet, see. Because they don't know what we -- whether we're going to jump up and grab the chandeliers or not. They don't know what's going to happen. So we started off. When we finished this number, everything, for about two or three seconds, nothing happened. Everybody set there, (sings). And see,

we said, 'Oh, god, what's happening here.' The American propaganda had been so tough on the Kaiser and that, we didn't know whether they were ready to turn us into sausage or not, you see. So, but, and then when they did start, they started hollering, 'Bis, Bis'. Well, we thought they were saying 'beasts'. They were saying 'bis', encore. But it sounded like to me, they were calling us beasts, b-e-a-s-t.
So, the saxophone, being on this side, they were near the entrance to the pit. They had their horns, one of them was halfway -- they had the door open to the pit, going out.
(laugh)

Getting back in there because they expected things to -- and then suddenly, must have been an American or somebody that had been to America, said, 'Encore'. And I hollered, 'Hey, fellas, come back.' (laugh) (unintelligible), because we didn't know -- because they had done bad propaganda against the German people and we thought that we was taking a chance even being over there. That's the reason a lot of people didn't come in with the show. In 1925, and here with all this propaganda from the first world war.

So, what happened, when we got back in there, then they applauded and they started stomping their feet, see. And hollered, 'Encore, encore.' See we didn't go for 'bis', because we didn't understand it. Encore, encore, bis, bis, encore. Well, then it was bedlam. Then when the curtain come up and we started the

show -- we started off with something like a plantation melody. I think it was a -- "My Old Kentucky Home". And then this mammy comes on and then Old "Strut" Payne comes on and they start singing. And Lyons, I must say, he built a beautiful picture. You know, like on a plantation, how they have lights and all that they have. I must say, they were very clever, between those Russians and all. And with the Germans that understood their business. Well I had never seen anything like that. It was really something out of this world, see. And the people, they got applause for that and then the show was on. And it was on, it was something.

Now, the greatest hit in the show in the first half was the three Eddies. That was Tiny, Shaky, and Chick. Well these three fellows had been named the Three Eddies by Eddie Cantor. And he gave them -- they put on cork, and then they had these white glasses. You know these shorter rim white glasses that you use.*
Uh hunh.

And they had derbies on. And it looks like Eddie Richter dressed in the Follies, you know. Because he had named them the Three Eddies. And they were the fastest thing you had ever seen, for six minutes. For six minutes they was terrific.
But the main thing hasn't started yet. But that second half, we were on stage then. The Three Eddies were up to that
* Plastic fake glasses.

curtain came down for the intermission, were the greatest. But when we hit the stage, they had never seen that at all. What we were going to do. And, well I don't need to tell you any more from that. But when we started playing our showpiece and the wa-wa even guys doing the wow-wow-and growling and halfway dancing and all like that and doing, and the musicians dancing all like that, it was bedlam. It was really bedlam and, you know who held the spot for us, was Adelaide Hall '41 set the stage up for the band, you know. She came on with her old uku-lele and held the curtain. You know, held the curtain while we set up in back. Well when we opened up that, that was something. From then on, we were in the money. And I haven't got out of the money since.
(laugh)

Well, listen Chris, I'm telling you that night was a night never to be forgotten. After the show was over, oh it was pandemonium. Everybody was keyed up and every-body had been relieved. It was a time for kissing each other and hugging and dancing and everything else. Arthur Lyons and the stagehands and the show members, everybody was having a wonderful time.

But, one thing I forgot. As we came into the port -- we went on a British liner, LAMPORT and HOLT line, I think it was. I forgot to tell you, there was a big sign out going into Hamburg, saying 'chocolate', Swiss chocolates, choco-
-late.
Uh hunh.

And that's how the show got its name. Was the Chocolate Kiddies. You see, because there was a little kitty on there -- a couple of kiddies on there, brown skinned, dancing. And Lyons said, "That's the name of the show, 'Chocolate Kiddies'". And that quick, it was 'Chocolate Kiddies". Anyhow, when this was over, so now, they brought me because I was supposed to be the captain of the whole thing because I conducted them through the pit, went through with that alright, and then the band turned out to be the greatest of all the excitements. See because they had seen dancing before over there. There was Dora Dean and others had been over there as individuals, dancing. But, like Lucky Roberts was there with the Pickaninnies. And then Richie Wynn, and all of them, and Greenlee & Drayton, they had been over there dancing, see. But they had never heard these ten or eleven musicians doing what they were doing. So after it was over, Lyons said, "Well we're all going to take a party." I took a couple of the boys with me and Charley Davis and one of the boys and myself. And then Robbins, the music publisher that went over with us, Arthur Lyons, Goldberg, later on was with "Showboat" as a manager. For some reason, he claimed that he could handle colored people. And he handled them by keeping them -- divide and conquer -- keeping them fighting each other. See, that's what he was famous for doing. See he wasn't a very good

person anyhow. Anyhow, so then we went out. Now we went to -- right away the Germans said, "Well we must take you first to a bawdy house." We went to this bawdy house. But here's what I didn't need. I'd been always respected by Lyons and all of them and I had my wife with me, so, as well as I wanted to do something in that bawdy house, I didn't. Because I wanted to keep my respect up. And I was almost slobbering at the mouth, but I still kept my respect. I said, "Oh, no, I wouldn't do it. I brought my wife all the way from America with me. I wouldn't dare to do anything like this, see."
(laugh)

So I was back there the next day with my own boys and we got into what trouble they didn't get that day, so see. Anyhow, so they all had a good time, but Johnny Mitchell went to -- see the other guys wasn't thinking. But, as the leader, I had to keep a certain amount of prestige up. So, but now, the Germans came in like a bunch of flies and all. The next day they grabbed us and they took us to all the places -- now this is where -- first they took us to and the droskys too, we had never seen droskys, too. You know they're something like our horse with the hansom behind.
Uh hunh.
And we went up to the (Krool) Garden, we went to the Kaiser's palace, which was a museum now. Took a

drive down Unter den Linden. And then the others went to Tier Park and then we went into the Tier Gardens, and there was a place there called Krohl Garden, which fascinated us. The Germans had these big bands playing there in these prestige coffee-houses. Sometimes something like 25 men playing in these coffee-houses. Which we don't have today. But in those days it was really a life that we didn't know and Berlin was such a beautiful place that, really, those days there, we really enjoyed.

Now we was all staying at -- we lived at a place called Darmstader Hoff. This all happened in East Berlin, on Friederich-strasse. And as we were standing outside talking, one of the boys, Gene Cedric -- he was tenor saxophone, later on became very popular over here with Fats Waller and some other -- anyhow, he was reading a letter from St. Louis. And it was telling him about -- so the guys all gathered around him and said, 'Gee, you got a letter.' So this old German woman come up too, and she stood right there and was reading over his shoulder. Because the Germans are very inquisitive people. They're a fine race of people and they are well educated, but they're specialists. If a man is a specialist at making cups, he don't know how to make saucers. If he's a doctor, he specializes in one type. If he's the heart man -- they're not general practitioners at nothing. They specialize, and if they specialize at making pianos, he can make the hell out of a piano, but he can't do nothing with a clarinet. Nothing else. He just do whatever he -- they
were specialists in those days, they were not generalists.
Uh hunh.

So now, when this little woman come up and was looking over Gene's shoulder, one fellow said to Gene, "Gene, you've got company." And Gene says, "I see her." And she was there reading his letter, so Gene turned around and said, "Arrrrrrrr", like that, and she stood right there and urinated all over herself.
She got so scared, huh?
Yeah, she was scared. They still believed that we only stayed in America for a little while. That we were brought here until we reached a certain age, and then were taken back to Africa.
(laugh)

They didn't believe we stayed here and was reared, been here since 1620. They didn't believe that. And you didn't know anything. And just like a donkey. They couldn't understand how we learned to blow those horns. We had a trombone player that they swore that he was singing through his horn.
(laugh)

Cause see, Germans play more a la Wagner. (sings a few bars of Wagner) And especially in those days, because it's a very harsh race. They don't have the nice beautiful German, like in Munich and Vienna has. See, Germany is not the

fine arts. The mechanical arts. They excel in things like that. But in the fine arts, like medicine and art and music. That's the reason why the great German composers eventually went to -- like Brahms and all, went to Vienna to live. Because they had the smoothness, the Viennese had the smoothness, while the Germans were -- (hup, hup.) but they were great people. They even had that in the voice,
What about the German musicians. Did they come up to you. There must have been --

Oh, yeah. Yeah, they come up and they couldn't understand it. They couldn't understand what we were doing and why we were doing it. And they didn't know anything about improvising. They were good musicians but they didn't know -- well I'd take a piece, and after the guy's been playing for awhile, I didn't know hardly what he was playing myself.
(laugh)

Especially if they had a solo or something. They'd improvise so much on it that you didn't know what it was. You know, jazz is only the rhythmic -- what I'm trying to say, improvision -- in a rhythmic manner, though. It was syncopated. You see, it's not just improvising, because the white people improvise, but like we say, legato. You write a piece and you have the improvisation on it, but it's not in jazz, you know, in other words, it's not syncopated.
Right.
Well that's one thing the blacks had and
especially the Europeans, they'd never heard that before.
Uh hunh.

You see. So when these fellows would improvise in a rhythmic, syncopated manner, we'd take their own pieces. That's why when you asked me a few minutes ago about "Tannhauser" and all those pieces. We'd first do it like it was. Cause they'd all been trained to -- (sings Tannhauser). And then they turned and come back and, (sings syncopated Tannhauser).
Uh hunh.
Well that's where the Germans -- and some of them said, "Sacrilege". Cause they couldn't see taking the Wagner damn white man, Wagner, and doing him like that, you see.
Right.

See, but that's what it was, see. Because we would play -- and so now, improvising all these things like we would do it. And maybe -- just like many of our pieces we were supposed to have composed were nothing but the white Americans' Baptist hymns and ALL stuff like that. But we turned it around in such a way -- we put it to our, where we -- because we didn't have the instrumentation to do it otherwise. And a lot of times, like when we started the ring shouts and all those things, they had nothing but the bones. Later on they had the banjo. How many people could afford an organ or a piano. My people were way late. It was the generation before me before we had an organ.
And that, we had to pump that. And I was almost coming out of high school before we had the piano.
Uh hunh.

We didn't know anything about those things. And it's just like in sports. Today, very few tennis -- we don't have many tennis players or golf players. Not because we don't have the mentality to do that, but they haven't been brought up in those things, you see.
Right.
That's the way that happened.
You were held over in Berlin, weren't you, at that theater.
Oh, yes. Because at the time it was unknown when we hit Berlin. It was unknown. I mean there was no known quantity of time that we was supposed to have.
Just an open engagement.

They kept coming, and people just kept coming. And we kept setting back dates. Setting back other dates. As long as they could pull us out of Berlin. Because Berlin was the major city and at the same time they were putting the propaganda out, how great we were.
Well, Leonidow was a very big impresario. Didn't he handle Chaliapin and people like that, opera singers.
Yes. This was his first venture into --
with jazz, see.
Uh hunh.

And I guess maybe he could have come over here because he was a very close friend of Hurok's, you know. Then later on they did a lot of work together and we had a second "Chocolate Kitties" with he and Hurok. See both of them were from Russia together. I think that they had been kids in Russia at the same time. So he knew that, but this was his first venture. And so far, it was his greatest.
And you were actually, then, when you opened in Berlin, you were already booked for other cities, or other countries, or what? Was it supposed to be a whole tour?
Not too far. Because he wasn't sure of it.
Uh hunh.

See, there hadn't been any -- an event like this preceeding this. We didn't know what was going to happen. You see he was taking a chance and he was scareder than we were. He was scared to death. But, if it was a success -- the next place, I think, was Sweden.
So he was feeling his way with you.
Yeah.
But you stayed in Berlin for quite awhile, didn't you?
Oh, yeah. I think it was about 70 or 73
or 74 performances.
And during that time -- it was during this time that you recorded for Polydor, wasn't it?
No, who did we record for? No, it wasn't Polydor. // I think I did record later for Polydor, but this wasn't Polydor.
But the first recordings were no --
First wasn't Polydor. Anyhow, we had been there about four or five days and then come the people from the recording company, and said, 'Look, we would like for you to record.'
Okay, so that was Vox that you made those first recordings for in Berlin.

Well this was really a hassle. First we had to decide which of the numbers it was good to record. And another thing we was bothered with at that time was the mikes. We had been so used to having the drum. Now the drummer sat out in the hall and we had to play, we'd just feel what we wanted. And we got some feeling from him, but they didn't record the drum.
Were these microphones or horns at that time?
They were horns.
They were horns, right.
Yeah, there wasn't no mikes at all. It was before the day of the mike.
Uh hunh. So this was before the electric recordings.
Yes. The megaphones, or some kind of horns. The boys played through the horns.
Yeah, horns. So they had to put the drums far away, otherwise they would distort the sound.
That was exactly what it was.
And that made it difficult for you.
Yeah, it was very difficult. And you had to be very true with what you was trying to do as far as you could. Otherwise you had nothing to skate on.
Uh hunh.
Your drum would cover a multitude of sins. But everything had to be true.
But the numbers you recorded, were they all taken from the show?
No.
I notice you did about --
Our specialties, some of them. And then others, like "Alabamy Bound". And we did others, like, "Shanghai Shuffle", and -- "Minnetonka" was our opening...
"By the Waters of the Minnetonka".
And some others we did we had done on the
show, because they had asked for those.
So those would be -- the way they would be on the record would be the exact same arrangement --
Yeah, that we played on the show.
Right.

And so we were doing very well with that. We had made two takes with them and was enjoying ourselves, that's the main thing. And rehearsing. And then riding around and seeing Berlin. There was much to see. The Grunewald, where there was beautiful mansions and all, places, things that we had never seen. Because, you see, Chris, here in America, our home and our paradise and everything was Harlem.
Right. And this was a different world.

Now, we had never seen all these things before. And during the war, I had never seen them, the boys had seen less than I. But during the war, everything was blown down by the Germans. And so the places that were beautiful, we didn't know nothing about -- so now, we're getting a chance of seeing a place like Berlin. And then the people were so much nicer to you. Everybody was very fine and we really enjoyed ourself there. We've got to say that much.
Where did you then go, from Berlin?
We went to Hamburg, the Thalia Theater in Hamburg. And we stayed there about two or three weeks, I think. Because -- we could have stayed longer. Not because the
crowd had died down, but we had to go over to Sweden.
You had commitments. Did the same reception in Hamburg greeted you that --
Same as -- from then on, our receptions were -- up into Russia, they were all the same.
Uh hunh.
Because, we being the first, some things was greater than others. But we were in that thing -- we had no trouble at all.
Was anybody beginning to get homesick? There were some changes in the show, weren't there, in personnel?
Some changes in the show, but not in the band.
The band remained.

The band stayed the same up until Russia. Going into Russia, George Howard decided that he didn't -- he wanted to go home. It wasn't George as much as it was his chorus girlfriend. She wanted to go and George thought, 'Well, I'll go home.' And he regretted it many a day, before he died. He regretted that. But he left on account of that and we replaced him.
But you went -- so you went to Sweden and how long did you stay there? Was it at Stockholm?
Yeah, Stockholm. We played in the, I can't think of the name now. There we played in the -- I know
one thing, it was there that I did a benefit for the Prince Carl of Sweden, for the Red Cross.
Uh hunh.
And we had a great benefit. That was in the Haselbach, it was a great hall there. But the band played, I mean the show was in a place something like the Tivoli would be in Copenhagen.
Um hunh.

Now, but we were a big success. But our greatest success after Berlin was Copenhagen. And that's where we saw the girls before the show, when we came in there, the sophisticated women sitting there with the cigars, you know, the small cigars? And so we used to call them the Great Danes.
Anyhow, this was our greatest success, and that's where pandemonium -- you know we stayed in -- we didn't play but two or three weeks there because they put us out of Copenhagen.
They did?
Because they claimed that we were taking all the money away.
But you were in Copenhagen much later, weren't you?
Oh, yeah.
So we're really ahead of our story.
Yeah, but now, this time, we could have
stayed there four weeks more. But they put us out because --
I mean, did you go to Copenhagen in 1925? After Stockholm?
Yeah, yeah.
I see.
Yeah, that's what I'm talking about, we went to Copenhagen. But the reason why they put us out, not because we were -- we were taking too much of the money out.
Uh hunh.
Everybody was there. That's why I say the greatest success after Berlin was Copenhagen.
Uh hunh.
You see, the Swedish people were all nice and like that, but they didn't have the fire the Danes had. And I'm not saying this because you're from Danish extract, either. (laugh)

I'm saying it because it's the truth. And they made us get out of there, you see? They said, 'You can't take any more money.' And Leonidow almost cried when they put him out. That's where they -- where you saw that article there where they called me an orangutan and all like that. Well they were good people & there, (laugh)
They said in the papers that I translated for you that when it was over and the audience was being
very enthusiastic, you stood center stage, looking very much like an orangutang with a stomach ache. You were taking a bow, right?
That was a fact. Oh, they were a very fine people. And the point of it, they were honest, simply honest. They were honest, eager and simple. And earnest. An earnest honesty, you know what I mean?
Uh hunh.

No put on. It was a great affair. And I only wish I could overlive that again. I'm hoping some day to return to Copenhagen. I just hope I'll have the same success I had then. Because they're very fine people.
So where did you go from Copenhagen.
We came back into Germany. Darmstadt, and Leipzig and Dresden, and places like that.
And all this time, the show was still intact, pretty much.

Yeah. And we didn't -- it broke up, when did that show break up. I mean it didn't break up. But Lottie Gee, and Margaret Simms, and Charley Davis went home from somewhere there. And Adelaide Hall, the Three Eddies. But we added some people who were the stragglers in Europe, and sent and got some people. That's when Mabel Mercer and some people from England joined the show, you know.
Oh, Mabel Mercer did come in with the show?
Yeah, she was with us and she stayed on with us, I think, clean to Russia.
Of course, she was English, anyway.

Yeah. Well it was cheaper. You see, when Arthur Lyons came home, he sold his rights for $40,000. And he came home, and the show lost its standard. Because it was now, these Europeans were -- Goldberg taught them, taught Leonidow and Seroda, was a Polish pianist that had taken over, had been a concert pianist, and he had some money. And Goldberg, a cheap, an American Jewish man. He taught them how to get things cheaper. And by doing that, he lost the standard of a first class production that had opened up. And if he hadn't done that, we would have never been the "Chocolate Kitties" that played practically all over the know civilized world. Because we had first class artists when we left the Club Alabam. But as the first class artists was disgusted after Lyons left, they replaced them with cheaper talent that they found around us. So Lottie Gee had been a prima donna in "Shuffle Along". When she left, we got a woman named Miss Fields, and Miss Fields was a poor imitation of Lottie Gee. You see. And then, but that worked in our favor. Then it worked out so that when the people they come, the only thing they saw with genuine ability, was the band.
I see.
And that didn't hurt the band at all. It made the band still greater.
Made it stand out. Right.
Yeah, you see, so in the end when we went into Russia, it was practically the band. Nobody else was mentioned.
Uh hunh.
They'd become to be subordinate to us, as if they were our satellite.
(laugh)
And when we left New York, we wasn't supposed to be starred. We were there to play for a show.
You were accompaniment.
Yeah. But it turned around, it got switched up and turned around so that the first was last and the last was first, see?
(laugh)
YOU went to Russia. That was still in 1925, wasn't it?
Yeah. No. 1926.
'26. So by that time the show has thinned out, you've got bad replacements, and you have a smaller show, right? When you came into Russia?

Oh yes. Yeah. But a good show, because I mean, it was still good, from the way it was. But the band now was the king. Absolutely king. There wasn't any such thing as are you sure that the band is first? The band was first from
the day we opened up in Berlin. But now, the show was weaker and that made the band look like it was still even better than it was. So, of course, the band kept its personality all to the drum.
And when you -- what was your experience in Russia? Tell me about it. They had never seen really a black band there, had they?

Well, I'll tell you. It was a wonderful experience. Above all, Russia was something that -- you have to go to see it. Because first place, we'll start off with the weather. When we landed in -- when we arrived in Russia, we had made a trip right from Madrid, right in -- stopped in Berlin just for a minute, because we left our wives off in Berlin, and we went on to Russia. Now, on our way into Russia, into Moscow, the train was chased by the wolves, first thing. Now we got into Russia and it was colder than blazes. And when we landed there, but as cold as it was, here's a whole group of college girls, singing Russian songs for us out on the platform. And all we wanted to do was get somewhere and get warm, you see.
Get some of the college girls.
(laugh)
They had wood fires,

You see so, now, we got there. But I'll tell you some American women and some English women need to be going to Russia to find out how to wear a handkerchief on their head -- or, a scarf. They can look beautiful with nothing.

With a scarf. In those days -- of course Russians have everything now -- but in those days they were very poor. And we have seen them, some people laying in the snow, asleep. But that's all finished. And of course, when I come back and was in -- in '52, in Paris, I saw men sleep in the subway, same way. So that was nothing to brag about, but we had a wonderful time, because the time we were in Russia, at Mayday. And that was something that was good to see, because they had the torch burning. And we were up in the window, we lived in a hotel called the Yanka, Yaka Hotel. And they were bright and begging us to come down and join the parade. But we were supposed to be non-partisan, we were artists. But on the whole, there was quite a lot of illiteracy at the time. I know, once we came to -- I was out shopping one day and we had a theater matinee. Well, I realized that the time was gone, so now I can't speak Russian. I can't tell the man where to go, how to get to the theater. I'm late, you see, so I told him to keep driving, you know?
Uh hunh.

'cause There was a great sign language, you see. I told him to keep driving until he come to a statue. Of course we had for our placard, we had for our placard, a big black head, you know what I mean?
Right.
A big, black head like you see in the carnival or something. And that was saying that this black show was there.

and we were a sensation Well, when he got there, he couldn't read it, and nobody else could read it that we passed. So he's there and he can't read what it is, so he don't know where it is. So, I was in a drosky. About that time a little girl came by and she told him where it was. Now, there must have been eight or ten people out there, but they couldn't read it.

Now, another a very wonderful thing. There was a lady, she was a very fine Russian Jewish woman and she spoke English very fluently. And so she said, 'I want to show you something that you don't have in your democracies.' And she took us to the symphony hall. And in this symphony hall, there were 110 musicians. It was a symphony orchestra. And they were all sitting in a circle without a leader. And without a leader they played Tschaikovsky, they played Borodin, and Rimsky-Korsakov. Symphonies.
Uh hunh.

They played these things. And without a leader. And we sat up all night trying to figure how it was done. But the nearest we got to it was that each soloist was the leader. That's what we figured it was, but we can't even prove that. We was guessing at that. But they actually did that for the first time. A hundred and ten men played. All in a circle. They sat in a circle facing each other. And they played -- now that was one of the things that we had never seen before.

Well, tell me about the different places you went to in Europe. The musicians. You said before the musicians came up to you and were curious. They'd never heard improvisation and they didn't know some of the sounds you made with the mutes and so forth.
Yeah, that was the beginning of the --
Were they --
Wait, now.
Were they -- did they try to emulate you. Did they --
Oh, yes.
Ah --

We had a band, after, when we come out of Russia, we went to a place called Fawn Des Westen in Berlin. And again we played and there was a German band on the stand, so that they had an idea that we might do something like this, too. Their improvisation was like cacophony. And they were mixed up. But they tried it; but what happened, this whatcha call, M.C., or what we'd call Master of Ceremonies, I'll never forget what he said. He said, but he said to the Germans, and I don't know what he said, all of it, but we only could understand some places. But it ended up with, 'Deutsches trink Deutsches bier.' Meaning, okay how bad these people, our own sound, applaud for them and give them encouragement. But what I wanted to say, before we left a year later, at the turn of the century, I mean
of the year.
(laugh)
Of the decade. Or what.
We returned to Berlin.
Yeah, this was in -- at the beginning, going into '26.
Uh hunh.

Was another company came over, called the "Black People". And the reason I mention them is because the leader of this company was a pianist, the director, was Claude Hopkins. And along with Claude Hopkins, one of the great singers of the company, was a great artist in the company was two. Maude deForrest and another little girl named Josephine Baker. And Josephine Baker was in -- she sat in our theater at the Palace -- no, the Theater am Zoo, it was. And she listened to our show and all. From that day went on back to Paris, and that's where Josephine Baker became the great Josephine Baker. See, but I wanted to mention that before, because that was a milestone in our travels. When she came there and she got a lot of inspiration from seeing our show. And from then on she went to Paris. And same as like Gertie Saunders was the first scat singer, Josephine Baker was the first stripteaser. And she stripped off everything and put on these bananas and from then on she was on her way.
So all of a sudden you had competition. In Europe, you had another black show.
Oh no, it didn't bother us because Josephine Baker's show didn't last over a couple of months and then Josephine Baker went for herself. was no unity there.
I see.
Because Claude didn't have at that time a band. He just had some pickup men and they worked together.
So in 1926 you made more recordings. This time for Polydor, right? In Berlin.
Oh, yes, for Polydor and then for -- after we come out of England, we made them for Polydor and for a French company.
For Brunswick, I think, you made something.
No.
Pathe.
Pathe, yeah.

Right. But tell me about -- we're still in 1926. I just want to get the chronology of this. And you have been to Russia, you have been to Scandinavia, and you've been -- have you been to Paris at this point?
No. We're getting ready to go to Paris now.
I see.
Because the show closed in '26.
Yeah. And I want to hear about the closing of the show, and why, and what happened to you.

Well, we closed in -- we had a reason for closing. Because, again, the work of Goldberg. Cause we was all tired of it anyhow. We had money and we was all tired of the show. But Goldberg showed -- Leonidow was backed out now. Was -- Sirotq, Sirotq. And Plaskoff was his secretary. Plaskoff was -- both of them were Polish people, you see. And Plaskoff tried to keep the thing together, but Goldberg influenced Sirotq that, 'Look, you're paying these people too much money. And we can get cheaper talent around here. And they'll do the same thing, because they're all the same.' You know what I mean? And that was actually what it was, you see? And he --
Uh hunh.

And he showed him wherein -- but people -- so when we reached Danzig was where the show didn't go any farther. And they closed the show, but Goldberg was forcing the show to close, because that would mean that he would get a better job and have more money, too. But the show would be less. And for his duty of getting these people cheap, he would naturally raise his own salary. Better to put up one man's salary and cut all the other people. Well, the main people wouldn't stand for that, so the show broke right up in Danzig. And we moved on into
Flemming

Friedrichsberg, I think, and waited for Flemming because our trombone player got pneumonia there, see? And, but up in Leningrad we had a wonderful time. We bought some sable coats. I bought a sable coat, and two or three other boys bought sables. And I bought a four carat diamond ring, and things like that. The government hadn't seized yet, you know?
Yeah.
These people had these things and sold them cheap too.
I bought a four-carat diamond ring for $1,000., something like that. Which you can't get one carat for today, you know?
(laugh)
You see, and then I bought my blanket of sables for my wife. She was in Berlin, (unintelligible), because we thought that it wasn't going to be good.
didn't bring her to Russia because I was afraid for her,

But, on the whole, we had a wonderful time. And that was when we went to the Winter Palace in Leningrad. It was Leningrad, then, it was old St. Petersburg. And one thing, I was glad -- a lot of the boys had got in all kinds of fights up there with their family. Those that took their wives. You see, because, at 11 o'clock at night in Petersburg or Leningrad, it's daylight. You can read the newspaper. In the summertime, because that was around the summertime when we got there. And so, we used to, at 11 'o'clock, at 11:30, we were throwing rocks at bullfrogs out there. We left the theater, and we'd go out there. Well, the wives at home say, "Where you been all night?"

"Here it's daybreak and you're just coming home." Well it was only eleven o'clock. They thought we were around having a wonderful time. We did have a wonderful time. The Russian people are like the black people. They have a lot of emotion. They are a really emotional people. And the greatest song that I ever heard -- the greatest singing that I ever heard, outside of black people was the Russian choir on Easter. The Bolsheviks or the Soviets, as now, had cut that out. But nobody had stopped the churches. And we went -- we heard the churches -- there's forty times forty churches in Moscow. And we heard, on Easter, these Russian choirs were something out of this world. Singing. Deep voice and very emotional. Because they're half Asiatic, you know. The Mongols -- when Genghis Khan and his crowd took over, and there's many of them in there. And they were really emotional. And another thing we saw there that I have never seen since, those people in Moscow leaving for Siberia. They walked to Siberia, you know. The captives and all like that. And you could see them. And another thing, those people singing on the Volga. The singing of the Volga -- they have deep voices and emotional voices. I think, it made me think of the Negro spiritual, the Russian folk song.

Let me ask you now, these early years when you were in Europe, were you keeping up with what was going on back home? Were you getting the papers, were you getting records? Did you know who was coming up? And who was doing
No. I was glad to forget it.
Huh?
I was glad to forget it.
(laugh)
No, things weren't like the other day. You know, in America, the black man has come a long way in forty years.
Uh hunh.
You see. And some of the hardships and all that we had, we were happy to say we were out of it. And at one time --
I meant musically. Were you keeping up with the development in music?

Oh, yes. We used to hear over [there] from people coming backward and forward, and getting letters from home. And all like that. What was going on. We saw the rise of Louis Armstrong and Earl Hines, you know what I mean? And heard his first number on scat singing, you know? (sings) And he'd say, instead of saying, (unintelligible). And we knew that the Savoy was going and what Chick Webb was doing a good job and all like that. But, still, they had to catch us. Because when we left there, we were the first.
Uh hunh.
In the East. I don't know what was

happening out West, but we were the first because the man that could have been first, he wasn't. That was because he sacrificed for sensation, he sacrificed teamwork. That was Fletcher Henderson. And, but you can't do that. That's the reason as a good football player, having been the coach of a football team, Notre Dame. Reason they were the greatest. It was because of the teamwork. And when the leader of an organization forgets that teamwork, the individuals don't matter. It's the teamwork. And that's why we were so far ahead of them. And Duke wasn't, there wasn't no Duke then.
Knute Rockne
Uh hunh. Well, let's get back to 1926 now. Did you go to England during '26? When did you go to England?
We only played two dates there. In Birmingham and Holburn Empire in London.
Holburn
Right.

But then we had to leave because, you see, we had previously in contract to go to Nice, at the Hotel Negresco. And from there, the same people that had us in Paris, when we played the Apollo Theater in Paris, it was turned into a dance hall. They sent us to South America, and that's when I opened up South America. '27.
I see, but let's not get that far ahead.

Let's go back to England. And the Holburn Empire in London, for instance. Did you find any difference in the English people? Because at that time there were English jazz people. There were people who were playing some jazz, trying to imitate --
Well, yes, I found a difference, because at those days, Jack Hylton, the greatest of the English bands at the time, hadn't reached his peak.
Un hunh.
He was trying.
Right.
But it wasn't til around the thirties that he reached his peak. And when he did reach his peak, he was a greater band, as a white band, than Paul Whiteman.

But now, in England, you no longer had the language problem. You were able to communicate more, more with people. What I mean is, you were telling me that the Germans did not know about improvisation and were rather astounded at what they heard. Were the English a little more advanced in their knowledge? Of what was going on?
Yes, they were. They were. But England didn't appeal to people so much as it did on the continent, because, outside of the hotels the living wasn't so good.
Uh hunh. No, I'm just talking about music-wise, actually, is what I'm interested in.

Yeah, well that hurt the, your, that hurt you in regards to you music. Because when conditions are not good, you're not happy. So, naturally, well England was another thing -- England was a country that -- well, I don't know how to put it? It's like an older brother. He's not willing to give a younger brother credit for his success. England felt that they were more than America.
It was too close to home.
Yeah. (laugh)
But, what about, how were the audiences, how did they react in England?
Oh, very fine.
As well as the Germans and the Scandinavians.
Oh yeah, very fine. But not with the enthusiasm that the Germans did, or the Danish people. Because England is much colder.
Un hunh.
They are, well they really act like the super race, you know what I mean? And they felt that they were closer to America and this wasn't as great as it might appear to be, you know?
It's a funny thing. It's hard to explain that, but in England people were very nice and they were wonderful in the Holburn Empire in London, but we didn't stay long. If we'd
stayed longer, maybe we'd have played the Hippodrome. But we didn't. I mean the Palladium. But by having a previous engagement, we couldn't stay but those two weeks.
I see. Now, when in 1926, the show was split up and you were now, from then on, you were on your own with the band. Who was booking you and managing you?
I was managing myself.
Uh hunh.
Now, cause Arthur Lyons had come home and there wasn't anyone else. There was nobody else that I thought that much of, you see?
I see.
So I managed myself clean until I came back to America.
Okay, now what happened between 1927, when you were in England, and say, 1929, when you were in Barcelona.
Well, in the meantime, what happened was when we left to go to South America. We went to B.A. [Buenos Aires] in South America and we stayed there I think it was three or six months, I can't remember.
How did that come about?
Well, Lombard -- Mr. L-o-m-b-a-r-t, and company, he had the Apollo in Paris. He turned that into a nightclub. And we played the Apollo. We played in that place.
Well, when we was finished with the Negresco Hotel, we played the Apollo. After the Apollo, he come and said, "Look, I want to send you boys for six months", I think, "into BA." Cause he had a --
B - A ?
B - A. Yeah, Buenos Aires.
Oh.
(laugh)

So he sent us to Buenos Aires, and there we had a place called the Tabarice. The Tabarice was a night-club there. But this nightclub was altogether different from what it was in a civilized country.. Because at that time, BA. wasn't civilized. It wasn't nothing but the gauchos, the gigolos, and the prostitutes, see? Because good people didn't come to the cabarets.
Un hunh.

With good women, there wasn't no such thing as a man bringing his wife or his girlfriend. If they were good people, there wasn't no such thing as that. Everything in the cabaret was a house of flowers lady. And the men were either the gigolos -- and they all did tangos. We were there a month before they'd get up and dance to a foxtrot.
But we felt badly for awhile there, because the floor would be packed on a tango. But when the band come, they'd sit down and they'd applaud, but they wouldn't get up. And we'd do

things like "Tiger Rag" and all like that. So we got almost like we was doing a concert, you know? Because they didn't understand. But as they'd come on, they'd come on more and more. Then after we'd been in BA, or Buenos Aires for three months, then we went to La Plata and another place down there. Rosario. And we stayed there and did theatrical engagements in those places. One month in one place and a month in the other place.
Did you start doing any Latin American type music?

Oh, yeah. We used to do tangos. And the funny thing, we'd do a tango sometime, and we got them down pretty good. And the tango band, which was CANERO, which was the greatest band there they had at the time, CANERO'S band was playing "St. Louis Blues".
(laugh)

And we used to dance on it, but we had a wonderful time. We were playing the tango, and they were playing the "St. Louis Blues". We got to know each other very well, you know. We had a wonderful time there.
Where did you go from to Buenos Aires?
Where from?
From where? From London?
No. We went from Negresco. After we finished in Paris, at the Apollo -- that's the reason why we couldn't stay
in London. We had this engagement for Sandrini -- the agency was Sandrini and Robert.
Uh hunh.
So it was Sandrini and Robert. We went to the Negresco for Satori, and after we finished with Satori, we went to Marseille, went to Gibraltar, and then went on to South America.
I see. That was a long trip.
Yeah. Well, 18 days.
Uh hunh.
21 days coming back, though.
Yeah, now, when you left South America, you didn't come back to the States.
Yeah.
Oh, you did.

Yeah. That was the trouble. We had passage paid to there and to -- from Paris and return. Course we left from Nice, though, our passage was to take us back in to France again. But we didn't do it. We had a boat and all on it and all the guys said, 'How about going home?' So we paid the other half of our fare ourselves, in order to come -- they paid our way half-fare back to the States.
I see. So you came to New York.
Yeah, we come back to New York. And that's where we started for vaudeville.
Now what year did you come back to New -- when did you come back to New York.
Well, that was in the latter part of '27. After we stayed down in BA for six months, we got back into America around in the Fall, I guess. Late Fall, '27. And we left in '28 to come back to Europe.
So you had been gone almost two years.

YEAH. Now, what the thing of it is, when I come back here, now Duke was just beginning to get started for the Cotton Club. But, I had the offer for the Cotton Club. But, at the same day, at this time, I had the offer for the Ufe PALAST Palace in Berlin. So at that time the Cotton Club was nothing.

Now I'd been there from the Club Alabam. I've got all America had to offer from the Club Alabam. See, now, why would I come back to Harlem to work at the Cotton Club. And, the Cotton Club wasn't no network or nothing like that then. So it was just another club in Harlem. Well the boys had been halfway around the world. They said, "Oh, no, we don't want to go back there. Why that's home. That won't do us any good." So the offer we accepted was the Ufe Palace. Ernie Rappe was playing there then, doing the same thing that Paul Ashe and Paul Whiteman was doing in New York. He had them make a presentation. An when we come back there it'd be in a presentation. And that's when had, we brought Slow Kid Thompson, Florence Mills' husband, and Edith Wilson, and Creamer and
Drayton and their trio. And Johnny Hudgins. We had a big presentation there. We stayed there six weeks.
Okay, so now you came back to New York in the Fall of '27.
Right.
How long did you stay in New York?
About a year.
You stayed about a year in New York. Okay, so what --
Yeah. Loew's vaudeville.
You played vaudeville.
That's when I played, I was in Loew's State Theater at least four times, because I played it once from the Club Alabam.
I see.
So altogether, I played Loew's State about five times, altogether. And one engagement we played in Great Lakes, in Buffalo. That's when I inspired the Jimmie Lunceford orchestra.
Why don't we pick up from there the next time.
Yeah. Good.
Okay.
Okay, this is Chris Albertson with Sam Wooding for the Smithsonian Institution, April 27, 1975. This is Interview 4.

Sam, we were talking about your trip to Russia. And, as we left it, you had been in South America. And I just wanted to mention that actually, you were the first person to bring a band -- a jazz band, into Russia. You were also the first American jazz band, or American band, to record outside of the United States, when you made those recordings in Berlin in 1925. And, I believe you were the first band to go into South America.
That's right.
Is that right?
That's right.

So, there are a lot of firsts there. And where we left it, you had just returned to New York from South America, but I understand we left -- we skipped a few things and I think we should go back to, I think, 1925, and you tell us what we skipped. When you went to Spain the first time.

Well, I'll tell you, we had a wonderful time. On our way to Spain. We broke the jump in Switzerland. And, it was a funny thing. The reason why I'm thinking of this Chris, is because we were playing in Zurich. And right out of Zurich is one of those tremendous peaks that Switzerland is known for. I think it was the Matterhorn. Yeah, it was the Matterhorn, see. So, as we -- so, one afternoon a couple of

boys and I said we'll take a ride up to this mountain and then we'd be back for the evening show. Well, before we could get back for the evening show, we never got to the mountain. Because, to us, it looked like it was about 15 or 10 miles away, and we hired a taxicab and we was going to ride up there and ride back. But, evidently, it must have been about 40 miles away, but that's the way it looked to us. So, anyhow, we got back. When we got back, we was glad to get back in and be ready for the show. Because we missed supper and everything, because we'd gone so far. Because we didn't realize. Because being from New York, we didn't know that there would be such a long ways away to look at a mountain peak that looks like it's ten miles away when it's forty miles away.
So, anyhow, everything went very fine in Switzerland. So we moved on to Spain. Now, we be coming up to Spain, and we opened up in Barcelona, you see.
Is this now -- going back -- is this while the show is still with you?
The show is with us.
Right.
The show is with us. It's 1925. The show didn't close until after we came -- in 1926, after we came out of Russia.
I see. Is it -- is this the original
This is the original show. No, this is the original show.
The good one. Right.
So, now we start. Because they really started watering down in Vienna.
Uh hunh.

And that was after we come out of there. So, the funny part of it was, when we got to the -- we've been having a tremendous success everywhere. So we thought that Spain would be a pushover. So we thought. So we go into Barcelona, I don't remember the theater now -- I remember the theater in Madrid was the Infanta Beatriz. But in Barcelona, I don't remember the theater. Anyhow, we opened up. When the band --
Was it the Olympia Theater?
It could have been the Olympia. It could have been the Olympia.
The Olympia or the Casino San Sebastien?
Yeah, well, it wasn't in San Sebastien. That was the casino in San Sebastien. In Barcelona it was the Olympia. Now here's what happened.
When we played, we usually got a standing ovation everywhere. And we'd been spoiled by that. When we finished the opening of the overture. This time, when we finished the overture,

we got a lot of catcalls. "Meow, meow." Like that. So we still don't know what's happening. Now, when the show opens up, we begin to get more catcalls. So we weathered the storm. So when we come off the stage, a fellow that was a fan of us, came around behind the stage and says, "What's happening, what's the matter with you fellows?" "Did they take care of the claque?" It's the first time I heard the word 'claque', you know?
(laugh)

I said, "What claque?" He said, "You know, when you go to play in Spain and Italy, you're going to run on a claque, and if the director or you don't satisfy with a certain amount of money, you in trouble. The show is in trouble." And they could close the show, because they'd keep on -- everybody'd throw some dead cats up on the stage or something like that. So, anyhow, I went to Sirota, and I said, "Listen, have you done anything about the claque?" And he says, "Yes, some of them come to me and said they wanted some money for the show. But I told them I didn't need them, the show was good and people would enjoy it. So let it go." So I said, "You'd better go and find that man and give him some money. Because otherwise the band and the people in the show don't want to go on. Because they know what's happening, and we don't want to go out there and face them." So he sent someone, one of the Spanish fellows around there. He sent him out and he got this man and he satisfied him. We went out then and the show went
down lovely. You see, I mention that because we in America knew nothing about claques.
So that's like blackmail.

Yes, it was a form of blackmail. But we had to do it. Because we couldn't go on. And then we moved on to Madrid. I know it was the Infanta Beatriz there. And we had played the show halfway through when we had to start it all over again. Because Queen Elizabeth and Ferdinand, they came in the theater. And, first place, we didn't know the Spanish National Anthem, so we had to run around and find somebody to play that for us, see?
(laugh)

But anyhow, we started the show all over and we had a wonderful time there in Madrid. But the thing that was bothering us was, we couldn't stay out late because we didn't understand how to get back in the house. Because they have that custom there, applaud, patting your hands and you don't have no key, and if you pat your hands and you don't have no key, anything can happen to you before you get in. You see?

And also, that was our first chance to see a bullfight. And listen to the music of Catalonia. They had the music, in fact, even the instruments were original. This music was the wildest thing. I think it was part Moorish music. It was the

wildest thing you had ever heard. It was like it was written on a different scale than our scale. The diatonic scale. You see, so. And then we had trouble there. But, outside of that, after we finished there we headed straight back. And on our way we stopped in Vienna and -- but we headed straight for Berlin after that. That's where I left the wife off. And then we went into Russia. I thought we should say that because we had quite some experiences down there in Spain. A little different from the regular -- in fact, could almost be considered not European.
Uh hunh.

More Asiatic, or African. See, on account of the Moors that were in there for so many years. And they left their stamp there. Until Le Cid kicked them out of there. But that was way up in Ferdinand and Isabella's time. But the Moors had been there ever since Mohammed's day. Ever since 700.
So that brings -- we have already covered what happened after that.
Yeah.
You went to South America. So let's get back to, I think it was 1927, when you came back to New York.
Uh hunh.
And you went into vaudeville. Now, when the band came back to New York from South America, did you disband, or did you keep the same band.
Well, we kept the same band, with one or two changes. Some of the boys didn't want to travel anymore, you know?
Uh hunh.

So they were replaced. And so now, we got fellows like Jerry Blake, Doc Cheatham. And a queer thing happened to me which I had no business to agree to at that time. And I'm warning all young pianists, don't agree to that anymore. He said, Arthur Lyons said to me, 'Now, the big band leaders now are not playing.' 'They take the baton and stand up.' You know. So, I agreed with him because I didn't want to work no more than I had to work. See, I never did care much for work.
(laugh)

So I agreed with him and I stood up. And from then on, by travelling, I never got any chance to practice. And I began to get rusty on my instrument. After awhile, I just cut out the solos. You see, altogether. And just went on, which was pretty good, as a band conductor standing up.
And then, band conductors got obsolete -- musician band conductors. Because the fad comes in with Cab Calloway, Noble Sisle, and Sunshine Sammy and -- what was this fellow's name --
Baron Lee, and all these fellows. They began to take clowns and stand them in front of the band, you know what I mean?
Uh hunh.

Performing. And those dancers and things like that.

So, outside of Duke, because he was well established, in front of the band. In fact he played less and less, he too. But that's what happened, was because they wanted showmen in front of the band.
Willy Bryant.

Yeah, yeah. Willy Bryant. And Lucky Millinder. They all, Lucky Millinder would jump up on top of the piano and on top of tables and all like that. Well, that wasn't music. But it worked on the people's eyes. People begin to hear with their eyes. Not with their ears, see?
Uh hunh.

And it's like, well today, we have a lot of the hard Rocks. They dress outlandish. You see, because that all makes the picture. Because the people are not really -- have time. And when the singers don't enunciate nothing. You don't understand nothing and it's like we were back in the primitive days, you see.
Uh hunh.
So now I was taken away from the piano. But we started -- Lyons said, 'Well, now we're going to do vaude-'

-ville, which we did. Being a Loew -- he was the Loew agent. So, naturally, the whole year that we were back, we did that. From Loew's, from place to place, place to place, we'd play and play and we'd come back to Loew's State about four times. We'd already played it once out of the Club Alabam. But, here's the point that followed us now was on account of being like that, why we couldn't, we didn't play any more dances, see? We was just playing vaudeville. We had one date that was worth mentioning. We played the Great Lakes Theater in Buffalo and then in that theater we were the inspiring attribute to Jimmy Lunsford's young band at that time. Jimmy had these boys in to the theater every first show. And they sat on the first two rows like he had ordered that, see. They took a lot of our method of playing and all like that, because they felt that we had something. In fact we had a, what do you call, a number there that -- well, more like a glee club. And then, where all the boys came out except the piano and drum and bass. And then we did a -- like a glee club. Well, nobody payed much attention to what we were doing, but it was a big number. Some years later, Jimmy Lunsford come up and get credit for being the band that do with the glee club. And I talked with Jimmy when I had a choir and Jimmy told me in front of all the boys, all the people in the choir, he said, "You know, Sam, you was my inspiration." And I said, "Yes, and you stole my trick, too."

He said, 'Anyhow.' But As thing come on. So we were working in vaudeville at the time and I got this cablegram from Europe to come to the Ufe Palace if I wanted to. And they said the money was good and we had a powow and that was about the same chance I had to go -- the Cotton Club was opening. So we all had a powow, and we decided to take the Ufe Palace, because the Cotton Club was just starting in Harlem and -some of them been born- we had all been born in Harlem and others been living there all their life, and so we said, 'Well, what do we want to go back to Harlem for?' We've been on Broadway, we've been in Berlin, we've been in London, we've been in Paris, and all over the world. Now, we go back to Harlem, for what?' But we couldn't see into the future. We couldn't see that later on it was going to be the greatest club of all of them, see? And so we turned the offer down.
Do you think, now, looking back, that it would have been wise for you to stay? Have stayed?
No, I don't. I still don't. Because I don't think that anyone would have done as well as Duke did.
Uh hunh.

For the simple reason why, I think our music was on too high a plane for it. See Duke came in and his band played what they called 'jungle music'. They were built on the style of Bubba Nisky. And that was the people in that place were Beer Barons, and all like that. They could stand it. When I was down in the Club Alabam, they wouldn't allow us to beat four beats out.
Uh hunh.

Well, when Duke came into the Cotton Louis Metcalf Club, they would allow that. So I loaned Duke Dewey Maycare Louis Metcalf I loaned him Dewey Maycare because they could not play the show at the time. They were a young band and they didn't know what it was all about. Edith Wilson was working with us in vaudeville. And she asked me, what could I do for Duke, could I help him out with anybody. Because they needed a good strong trumpet player. Because Bubba wasn't a good musician as far as reading was concerned. In fact, he had quite a few men in the band that couldn't read at that time. There was four or five of them that wasn't good readers at all. See, and they couldn't cut the show, so she said to me, "Could you loan Duke a man that would help him to put his show over?" I loaned him, so I said, the better man that he should have was Louis Metcalf. He was very good at that time. In fact, he was on a par with any of them at that time. So, I went to the theater manager and I said, "Look." And he said, "alright for the last show, when Miss Wilson goes in to do her doubling at the Cotton Club, could one of the men go out. We can play very well without him." So he said, "Well, I'll see how it comes this show. If this show works out, tomorrow, well I think for my audience, you can, he can get off, excused for the show." And he didn't cut nothing off the salary, either. So, anyhow, everything worked all right, so Louis Met-
-calf went to the Cotton Club and was a lifesaver for Duke Ellington at the time.

But, Chris just asked me, do I think we would have the same success, and I told him I didn't think so. Because if we had gone, or say any other band had gone up there, we'd have played maybe two months, and that would be the end of it. But, because we were just a good band, but an ordinary band. Duke had a sound.

Let me ask you this. When you were in Europe, in different places. Of course, you could go out and hear Spanish music, or you could go out and hear a German beer band, or whatever. But there was no place you could go out and hear jazz.
Oh, no.

So, when you got back to the States, all of a sudden you're back in Harlem and there are all kinds of things going on musically, that are related to your music..Didn't you miss that, when you were in Europe, not being able to drop in here and there and hear other people.

No, I don't want to brag, but I want to say that we were so far ahead of every band, that when we come back, we were just about even. They had been moving on, naturally, but when they moved on, they just got up to us, see?
But wasn't there -- didn't you miss it? Surely, you must have enjoyed hearing -- you felt more at home
in Harlem where you could drop in and hear Duke or whatever, you know?

Well, when we got back to Harlem, I didn't want to leave it. No, I missed it very much and even when I was over there later on with Rap Harrison, I used to say to him, "I certainly would like to get back in Harlem and go to a breakfast dance, or something." I didn't realize that they had stopped having breakfast dances -- but that's what, oh, you missed that. And you missed a place called an after hours club, you know?
Right.
It gives you inspiration. Because without that experience, you ain't going anywhere.
Exactly.

And that's the reason why a lot of kids, that was the reason why Rock and Roll developed. Because the guys looking for something new, they picked up not only the bop, but they picked up the modern jazz.

We're getting -- yeah, I just want to stay on that one thought before we stray far from it. There was much more, in those days, of sitting in, you know of, you'd drop in to a club and you'd play with them, or somebody'd drop into your club and play with you. I would imagine that that inspired a lot of music. People getting together informally and just jamming together. Which is something we don't have any more,
hardly.

No, that's what you miss. You miss that experience. Now when we were in the Nest, way back in the days of the Nest, Henry Bussey, Frank Forani, Johnny Dunn, Tommy Morris, these are fellows all used to come up. Bechet, Sidney Bechet, all of them used to come up and sit with band and play a time. See, when we were doing our arrangements, [we never], but we always had some numbers like "Georgia Brown", "Strutters' Ball", and things like that where we'd say, "Dear Old Southland", okay and things like that, where we'd play just some, four beat, we'd say, "Alright, go into four beats." And we'd play that, and these fellows would all take turns and take the chorus. And I think it was quite a lot of help to many of them. Because they was able to exchange ideas right on the floor and they used to line right up in front of the band, and it would just be myself and the guitar player and the drummer and the bass and the other guys were glad to -- like Garvin Bushell and the other Saxophone player and Bobby and them would be glad to get that -- go off.
Yeah, the break.
And we'd sit down there and play for an hour sometimes. And this would always happen after around two o'clock, you see.
That of course, was also a great experience for the audience.

Oh, of course, it's what they wanted. Otherwise the man would have stopped them. Sometimes they could dance, and sometimes they could just sit and listen to it. If there was anything exceptionally going on, they would just listen to it.
So what were some of the places that you dropped in on, for instance.

Well, there was like Connies Inn, sometimes. And there was Goldgraben's around there. And Edmunds had a place and Connors had a place there on 135th Street, and Edmunds was on 5th Avenue. And there was -- Happy Rhone's was over there where the Cotton Club was eventually put up there. And later on, Jeff Brunt had a place, the Atlantis Club, right next to that. Oh, there was quite a lot of places. And then there was some after hours places. I didn't bother about playing in them, but we used to go to them when we had to convince a young lady that she should be with us. We would go into there setting there and to convince her by pouring some liquor into her and talking to her. We used to do that too, quite often.
What about places that didn't feature music. Where performers would hang out. What places were there?

Well, there was two restaurants. There was a restaurant called Johnny Johnson's and there was the Blue Grass, and then there was Glenn's. Now, these restaurants, we used to go there when we come up from the Club Alabam. And, after

we came back. Where musicians set there and built plans and dreamed. Of course, your breakfast would always consist of an order of hotcakes, two pork chops and three scrambled eggs and coffee and things like that. Of course, some of the boys would drink, but I didn't bother with much of that. But that was the breakfast. That's what was served. Hotcakes and maybe three scrambled eggs and some sausage and potatoes and -- french fried potatoes or home fried potatoes. Well, you see, but when we sit there, that's where you make the brotherhood in a band, and amongst your friends. We set there and we think up ideas, man and a guy say, "Look Sam." Because nobody makes a band alone. A band consists of just as many members as you have in that band. And so, but he has his -- the leader must know what to take and what not to take. But the whole band, no-one can say that he made a band. That is out there from Jim Europe or Duke Ellington right on down the line, you cannot say this man has done it all by himself. Everybody contributes to a band. And everybody's absolutely necessary in a band. It's like a lot of people say. Well, take a football team. Knute Rockne, Rockne and Notre Dame. Yeah, the quarterback is good. But how's he going to get the ball to be good with it if the center, if the two guards are not strong to hold the line until he can throw the ball. And he can throw a pass, but if you don't have an end to catch that pass, and the man's fast enough to run. You don't have Jim Brown or this last boy, O.J. Simpson, to hit the line

and go through. Well, you used to be getting the ball. So, I mean, but everybody -- which is very wrong, even with a baseball team. They'll holler, Tom Seaver. Well, Tom Seaver gets hit, but if there wasn't somebody out there to catch that ball and throw it, when you have a no-hit game, for instance. You have struck out everybody, but the man -- your supporting cast. I think it's very wrong that the newspapers come out and say, 'Tom Seaver did this.' Or it's very wrong to do that.
Yeah, what you're saying --
Give credit to everybody.
Yeah, right. But what about, well let's say, the breakfast dances. What were they like?
The breakfast dances?
Yeah, when did they start? Did they start at midnight, or ---

Well, they'd start around three or four, after the cabarets had closed. And they'd run til about seven or eight o'clock in the morning in those days, see. And then, you see, what made the breakfast dance was the beautiful chorus girls, because we did have some beautiful chorus girls in those days, you see. And when these girls come in -- of course there wouldn't have been any breakfast dance if these girls hadn't showed up. And the beauties of Harlem. And they had, we had beauties. I don't know where they are now, doing some other kind of work. But they were around in those days. And it was

enough to see them -- a guy used to say, "There's a recess in heaven, and all the angels are down here." Well, that made the thing, you see. There wasn't nothing wrong going on. It was just we'd come there and dance and talk and try to build up our future. All kinds of wrong happening in that future, but there it wasn't, there. There it was very straight.

I just wanted to ask you. People like Mr. Lyons, people like that. The white people who were on the business end of it. Your contact, when I say your contact, I don't mean just you, but other musicians and bandleaders -- was it strictly a business contact? Would you ever be invited to Lyons' home, for instance, for dinner? Or would you ever socialize with the white people?
Why do you say I stayed in Europe so long? Because today, you can meet him at the Park Sheraton or same hotel, something like that, but you'll never get to his home.
Uh hunh.

You can count those that would come to his home -- in fact, I don't know of any. So really, it's a bad business association. Because, like, I'm sitting in your home, now. But how many homes could I sit in. Because a lot of transactions -- I told you when I went to Europe. That deal was pulled off in a club or a restaurant at four o'clock in the morning. Well, now picture me in Arthur Lyons home. I don't even know where he lives. We always met outside. Of course,
that line is much better than it has been, but we've all had a -- it's oil and water. East is East and West is West, and never the twain shall meet.
