Right. Now, I've heard this from many musicians. That the only time they were invited to anyone's home was when they were expected to perform.
Yeah. And that's what I hated. If I thought I was invited somewhere so that I could give my musical services, my artistic end of it, I never would go.
Uh hunh.

See, because I didn't like that. And I was very happy -- that's one reason I was very happy to go back to Europe. And I would have no doubt made it my home, but I had relatives back here in the States, and I wanted to see them, and they didn't have enough money to come to see me. So that's what brought me back.
So, in other words, when you came back in 1927, from South America, you hooked up again with Arthur Lyons.
Oh, yes.
Whom you had dissassociated yourself from in Europe, right?
Yeah.
And did he -- he was then responsible for your going back to Europe?
No.
Just for the vaudeville.

For the vaudeville there. And then he turned his business over to -- in '27 or the early part of '28, over to his brother Sam Lyons. And he went to, went out to Hollywood, because everything was moving out that way. And Arthur was really up on the ball. I think he ended up by being the manager for Jack Benny and some big acts out there. Because he was a go-getter. I mean, he -- when I moved him out of that office by him putting us in the Club Alabam, he never looked back. He was somebody that, I wish that I could have had an Arthur Lyons after that.
Uh hunh.

But, in going back to Europe -- I went back for Paul Spadoni, and the man, the errand boy that he sent -- a fellow named Eddie Dussberg -- to meet us in Hamburg, this fellow turned out by using my band as a battle ram. He turned out to have the biggest theater, the Winter Garden theater, in Berlin. Of the vaudeville houses, see. And he turned out to be a great man until Hitler come along and run us both out of there.
Well, let's get back to Europe, when you came back. Who was with you when you went back to Europe in 1927?
Ladnier

I had Tommy Langley, again went back with me. But, Doc Cheatham and Jerry Blake and Freddie Johnson. They were the only new men that I had. The rest of them were the old fellows that had been there before.
So, but we had just as good a band, in fact I think we had better material for a band. As you know from -- you listened to those records. The records we made in about '28 in Barcelona.
'29, I think.
'29. Was a great, was really an advancement over the other band. Over the first band that went over there. And, in fact, I knew better how to arrange. Because I'd had more experience in it.
So, when you came back to the Ufe Palace, you were already known in Berlin. You already had a following.

Oh yes. That's the reason they sent for us. They had this Ernie Rappe there, an American. Because things were down there, you know, in those days it wasn't so good either. Germany needed a shot in the arm. And they began to get it through the organization, that was looking Hitler, began raising his head, this dragon, you know. And you'd see them travelling with their packs on their backs and they'd meet -- the Nazi Party was being organized all the time, see. Which he caught me in time. Cause he caught me right after in '32.
Oh, we'll get to that.
So, how long were you at the Ufe Palace?
It was something like six weeks.
Six weeks.

And then after that, we went to the Triechter in Hamburg, and we stayed there another four weeks. Then we made a tour all the way out to Turkey. And we played all the way along. We were seeing nothing but the casinos. Like the San Sebastien Casino in San Sebastien. Well, it was one of the places where the Spanish king stayed in the summertime. And then we played in Italy, in Milano and Florence and -- we didn't play Rome for some reason, we had to leave. I don't know what happened. And then we went back to Vienna and we played in a place called the Moulin Rouge in Vienna. And it was a funny thing there, we had a chance to go in St. Stephens Church there and go down in the catacombs and see, when John and Paul threw back the Arab squad, the Mohammedan bunch, a lot of the Turks were imprisoned and their skulls are down there like cans of tomatoes. Down in the catacombs. So we had a chance to visit that.
And we was well thought of in Vienna. In fact, we really loved Vienna.
Did you ever play any waltzes?
Huh?
Did you ever play any waltzes?
Oh, no. Oh, we played the famous waltz. "The Blue Danube".
Uh hunh.

We always played that. And the -- cause see, when we had been playing it like we do our work, but it's up fast, you know what I mean. And it has this ring to it. Strauss waltzes, we liked those and I played one or two of them. But not many because they wouldn't want us there for that. They wanted us to do what we call swing. They want jazz. Jazz was well on its way then. Because they even had songs about jazz. Jazz wasn't a music. It was a term that they gave to music.
Right.
There was one song, "Jazz Me". That didn't mean music --
"The Jazz Me Blues".
Yeah, it didn't mean play me music.
Right.

It meant something else. It was sort of a sexual undertone to it. And so jazz, really, I don't know why they stuck that on our music. JAZZ. Because Jazz wasn't really a good word at that time. Like funk wasn't a good word.
Well, a lot of people don't consider it a good word today, you know.
Yeah.
Okay, so you went all over Europe again.
Uh hunh.
And all through the rest of 1927. Do you remember what month you went over in '27?
Uh, let's see.
Was it late in the year?
It was one of the warm months, I don't remember exactly now, but it was one of the warm months, because we didn't wear any overcoats, you see.
I see. So what happened. You went all over, I guess through 1928 and 1929. And I know, in 1929, at one point, you were in Barcelona and you made some records.
That was the second time we'd been in Barcelona.
Right. And you made records in Barcelona that time.
Uh hunh.
And this time I guess you were --
You see, now we were playing a lot of times not just for a week or one concert, but whenever I could get --
Get a whole season, right? A season.
I would take it.
Didn't you play whole seasons in places?
No, we very seldom stayed over a month. Except on place in the Haus GERMANIA, which was in Scharlotten-burg in Berlin. We played three months.
Uh hunh.

Because, in order to take up the time now we were on our own. And we didn't, but some places like Holland and Belgium -- we stayed something like fifteen days in Belgium. But some of the places couldn't afford to pay a band like that. So when we got to a place that could afford to pay, we squeezed it as long as we could.

What about, now, places like Berlin, where you stayed for some length of time. Did people make friends with you who were -- other artists, maybe painters or musicians or composers? Did you get into any kind of a social situation there with people?

Well that was hard -- Chris, that was funny. You know, we were young and we were exposed to something that we wasn't exposed to in America. And that was the association, and cohabiting... (unintelligible). Well Chris, I'll tell you this much. We would meet some artists some times. But not so much. Because you see, we did a lot of solo work. When we was in France, and in Germany, we had our wives with you. And the rest of the time when you could get out, you would try a little -- something a little different. And you would try one of the European ladies, women, you know what I mean? Because it's like anything else. If you have a child and you have reserves. But you put those preserves, you put the jelly up on the top shelf and you say, "Y0u're not to

touch this jelly until Sunday." If you go out to the store or someplace, before you can come back, this boy, or this baby, or this girl, has reached up there and took herself a piece of bread and used some jelly, because she'd be hungry. Why? Not that she needed it so much, but because you had forbidden it. Well, in those days, it wasn't a nice thing to see the two races together. Maybe a black man and a white woman. Well, now when you get to Europe where nobody paid any attention to it as long as they both of them acted their part, well this was a new field.
So there was a novelty in that.
You would go for something. And on the other hand, when you'd, after you'd satisfied yourself with something like that, you'd be glad to get back to your own.

No, what I meant was, that here you were in Europe doing something that was startlingly different in music from what they had been used to. And I thought that possibly people who were in music over there, you know, would be very curious about your music and would cultivate your friendship and want to find out more about jazz music.
Well, they did. But, what I'm telling you, not in great numbers because they -- we didn't have any great numbers. Because maybe they would be interfering with some engagement we had.
I see.

You see. So we would say, 'Oh, here comes the square now. He wants to talk about something.' But, we've got to go around the corner, you know, where we've got to go. So, we'd push him off and as soon as we could get out of his company, we'd get out of it.
Oh. So you discouraged that kind of contact.
Yeah. Because we had other things to do that were more important. Sex.
Right.
(laugh)
Now. Okay, so you stayed, this time you stayed in Europe for many years, didn't you.
Oh yes. I tell you this time, I was thinking about making it my home.
Uh hunh.
Thinking very seriously. I had some money. And this was the time, you know, that we had the crash here.
Right.

Not having had enough education, I had dropped out in the second year of high school. So in those days, I didn't understand what it meant. This crash really meant. And that if a crash came in a principal country, then it would be felt around the world. I didn't understand that. Well,
in Paris I had, oh I guess I might have been worth about $25,000., you know what I mean, in money.
Uh hunh.

So what I did was, I met a Russian that had a formula for making waterproofing. Then a Frenchman that had the prestige, being a Frenchman, he could establish anything in France that he wanted. Well, with the three of us, we went into a business. Now, before we went into this business, I want to show you something. What a lot of times the thoughts of prejudice is in your own mind when other people are not thinking about it. So, but I took one of the fellows' advice, and I went to the embassy and I asked for a lawyer. I was going to check on it. They gave me a lawyer, and if he's living, or if any of his people are living, his name was Hare, H-a-r-e. Anyhow, Mr. Hare was from the southlands, and he brought everything to Paris from the southlands that he could, the brogue --
An American.

Yeah, he was an American. And so he brought the speech and everything. And so he set up there and he said, 'Well now look here, Mr. Wooding, if I were you all I wouldn't fool with that thing, you know. Because things is not so good now, and we shouldn't do that.' [PAUSE IN TAPE]
As I said, he was from the southland, his brogue and his manner of talking. Everything was like that. So he told me, he said, 'Look, we are in the throes of a depression. And

being the principal country, it's felt all around the world." But his actions, his speech. By being, talking, what we used to call people, a southerner, we'd call them 'crackers'. So, on account of his talking -- I didn't believe him. I thought, now this man is telling me this because I'm a black man and he don't want me to go into business with this Russian and this Frenchman. They're white. So, I didn't take his advice. And I regret today. So now, if a guy's talking to me in orangutan language, I don't care if he's white as snow or anything else. If he's telling me something, I'm looking into it.

Anyhow, so I lost -- I went into this business, because we could take a handkerchief and you could waterproof it and for twenty-four hours you could pour a glass of water on this handkerchief and you couldn't feel it on the other side. This was a great formula that this Russian had. Anyhow, we tried to get it with the French Government, or tried to get it with the Roumanian Police, and they didn't have the money to accept it in those days. Anyhow, so I put out something like $18,000. I had about seven or eight thousand left. Now, I did another foolish thing, which we know as colored people. You'd never send good money after bad. So what I did. So when they said, "Well, now, we need some more money." Well, I took this $7,000 or so that I had left to send out to try to save the business. And then I had nothing. Now we're in a devil of a thing. We had nothing and the business can't go on either. Because we had a

big factory, loft like. And we had all these vats there, and these vats there, working these things out. Well, there wasn't nothing to do, now I've lost all my money, you see. Because I still wanted to stay there if I could. Well now, you know how I felt. Now one minute I was what we'd call rich, next minute I'm a beggar.
(laugh)
But I still had the band. I could make money. But I didn't get like -- because in those days $25,000. was a whole lot of money.
Right.

You see, so after that, I didn't -- just went on out and -- but I have always been one thing, Chris. I don't believe in looking back. I didn't sit down and moan, me about Lot's wife. He said, "Son, and you go out in the world, don't look back. If you make a mistake, try not to do that again. But don't worry about it. Don't sit there and grieve over that mistake." So it's just one of those things. You say, well, better luck next time. And we went on out and did some more touring. But I never got together that kind of money again, you know?
Uh hunh.
In fact, I haven't got it together yet. It seemed like I was really in velvet. I was doing really very well. So, went on back and started with the band again. Working
with the band. Course I was still playing with the band at the time.
So, what year was it you went into this business. Was it after the crash in '29?
No, it was, that was, yeah, right after the same year, or the beginning of 1930.
So I went on and I was taking engagements, and I ended up in Valencia in '31.
In Copenhagen.
Yeah. And so, from then, after we finished Valencia, that's we -- where we try giving our first concert. Black concert.
Yeah. You were the first black band to give a concert. And was that the Christmas concert in Copenhagen?
No. This was a concert of our own. We gave it in the concert hall. I mean, the symphony hall. What's that man's name, now? At that time -- I guess he's dead, now.
Mr. Hanson?
Maybe that was the name. Anyhow, ---
Oh, Wilhelm Hanson?
Yeah.
Wilhelm Hanson. He was the big music publisher and promoter on Broadway.
Yeah. Well, we gave it there and it was such a success that we moved on to other places there. And we moved on to Sweden.
That was February 5, 1931. You gave this concert.
Uh hunh.
And it was still called, "Sam Wooding and his Chocolate Kiddies Orchestra". And that was in the, where was it, in the Oddfellow Palais?
Yes.
Yes, which is a big concert hall.

Now you see, from then on we went to Sweden and did the same thing. And made one or two of the lesser cities. And we give, I guess, about ten or eleven of those concerts in all. The last one was in Vienna, I think.
Well, I've seen one of the programs from that concert, I guess it's from the first one, the Danish one.
Yeah.

And I noticed in the program you had, you were doing your versions, you very special versions, of "Tannhauser" and other things from the European classical repertoire. And I've also seen the Danish reviews, and I know that the Danes, the reviewers, were quite startled. They thought for awhile it was sacrilege. But they really loved it. But they had
never heard anything like it. And their descriptions of it are very funny and very enthusiastic. That out of all this chaos, they said, emerged suddenly Tannhauser.
Yes. (laugh)
And apparently, according to those reviews, the audience was just jubilant. And I wonder if, for instance, Tannhauser. Could you demonstrate on the piano how you would do any of these things.

I couldn't right now, because I don't think I would do a good job at it. But I will tell you. You see, we were using modern idioms, but at the same time the solo was sacred to us, you know what I mean?
Uh hunh.

Like, (sings Tannhauser). But at the same time, we would be using, (sings syncopated accompaniment). Things like that, with the saxophone. And it turned out well. Well, we had quite a number of them that we did. Some Rimsky-Korsakov, and one that we had was the "Overture of 1812". And we had it fixed so that you could actually hear the bells of Moscow and we had the drum beating so that now and then it was like the cannons, the Napoleonic cannons were shooting. And we did that up in a great way.
And as far as I know, nobody was doing that in this country.
Oh no. Not, no blacks anyhow.
No.

See, the only one that I know that had given a concert amongst the white musicians was Paul Whiteman. And I was at that concert. That was in 1923 or 1924. And that's when he introduced the "Rhapsody in Blue" with George Gershwin playing it himself. Well, outside of that, nobody else. Because see, we did not play everything in sync. In rhythm. We played it like it was, swing,
Uh hunh.

I had a fellow with me, a young Italian fellow. And like, with the Overture of 1812, some of those, he worked with me, cooperated with me, in making some of the -- like Puccini's opera, and Verdi's, some of these operas we did. Because, like, when we went into the Negresco Hotel, we had to play for supper, you see, and you couldn't play the dance music. Had to play little excerpts from different operas or symphonies, or something like that. So that's how that happened.
What did this Italian do? Did he help you with the arrangements?

Yeah. He did this. He took the -- there was some of the classical numbers, and inserted the correct form in there, and then I'd put our version to it. So that would improve on it. Because we couldn't play against an orchestra of 110 pieces, or 175 pieces, without having some novelty way of approaching it, you see. But in order that the solos and things would be correct, I had him there. He's around here now.
Oh, really? You also did a Christmas concert in Copenhagen. I think it was ( ) or Politiken, one of those Danish newspapers. One of the two big Danish newspapers has an annual benefit concert --
Politiken.
Politiken, yeah. And I saw the reviews of that. And of course there you appeared on the same bill with the Danish Symphony Orchestra, and I think Carl Nilsson was even there.
Yes. I had a couple of writeups also from the symphony orchestra leader in Berlin, too, and the one in Copenhagen. But I lost them. I would have liked to have them, but I lost them.
But that, of course, was an experience that you would not have had in this country.

Absolutely. That's why you think I would love those countries over there. Because they gave us the freedom we wanted, that's all. Now it's altogether different. Things have changed. We've come a long ways in America, America has, as far as the blacks are concerned. Because now, where we have like a Mayor of Detroit, a Mayor of Los Angeles. Why, when I left with this show, that would be inconceivable. But it has happened.
Yes.
You see, so now, we hope that in another
year, we'll get the Chief of Police.
(laugh)
So, so, okay, we're in Copenhagen in the early '30's and you just continued through the thirties, touring and playing just about everywhere.
Yeah.
And did -- before we get to 1939, where -
Oh, I didn't stay there that long.
You didn't stay that long? How long did you stay?
I had a baby -- I don't mean I didn't have the baby, my wife had the baby.
(laugh)
So what had happened, around '32, the Christmas of '31, we started home because I didn't want my child to be born in Europe. See, because there was some doubts as to his citizenship, you know?
Uh hunh.

We was in France at the time, and there was this thing there that unless you declared the child, declared it before it was 18 or something, it would be a citizen of that country. And I didn't want no bother like that, so there wasn't nothing else for me to do. Mother was getting older, so I thought, 'Well, I'd better go home.' And another thing,

Europe had sort of lost the spark. And what made me lose the spark was, when I was in the (HAUS GERMANIA), the year before, for my birthday, which was in June, the fellow gave me three months to return to the following year, next year. To come back there, that was my birthday present, see? And the (HAUS GERMANIA), that was in Scharlottenburg, that was a wonderful place. Where they even -- the roof opened up and the stage came up from the floor, you see? Oh, it was a real, real modern cabaret.
And also, meanwhile, (Duisberg), my manager, Eddie (Duisberg), he had procured six months in London at the Savoy Hotel. That made nine months of the following year was already taken up.
Uh hunh.

See, but what happened was that when they Hitler party began to rear its head and old man von Hindenburg was becoming old and incompetent, see, of handling the government, you see, Hitler was not in power, but he was practically, in the he was making the power. Well, the first thing, they didn't want any American music -- the Nazi Party, they didn't want any American music, and especially the ragtime or jazz played by blacks. They didn't honor blacks at all. So, they refused, they barred the contract, they discredited the contract, and I couldn't use it.
So that was in late '31 or early '32.
'31. And you returned to the United States.

No. Now the six months in the Savoy in London. That was rescinded because Paul Whiteman and Paul Specht and some of the white bands, had refused Jack Hilton's entry into America. Jack Hilton had a much (staged) band that was much better than Paul Whiteman or any of the American stage bands. He had entertainment in his band. See, people living today like Lombardo, they would know.

So, in return, England refused to allow any American band in there. So the contract that I had had was cancelled. Now I got nine months. And with a band like I had and with the money we was making, you couldn't just walk right out to the corner and pick it up. You know?
Uh hunh.
And it was laid off. With the condition of the country and all like that. And with the wife in a pregnant state, there wasn't nothing for me to do but to get on the boat and come on home.
And the rest of the band came with you, huh?
Well most of them. Some of them stayed over there. And of course some of the said, 'Well, I'm not
Was that when Willy Lewis stayed there?
Willy Lewis, yeah.
Because he stayed there throughout the war, even. The Second World War.

Well, he, they got caught over there. Johnny Mitchell was caught in there, too. And they couldn't get out. Johnny Mitchell and, I think that's the reason why Freddie Johnson is dead today. Because they had to -- they were caught and put there to entertain the German officers and everything. They were caught in there, see? They couldn't get out.
So, you came back in late '31.
Yeah.
Right. You came back right into the depression. As, I think, we were about to go into the worst year of the depression.

But by this time here -- but I didn't mind it, because we didn't mind it in Harlem at all because, it's like some of the fellows said, 'We've always been in a depression.' So, it didn't bother us At All. (laugh)
So, what did you do when you came back?

Well, I started organizing a band. After awhile I organized a band and I had in the band such men as Big Catlett Sid Catley. I had Frankie Newton. I had Nicholas Red Nichols. And then the first band, Bushell Butch Elber was with me and Cedric, they came
back with me. And then was, I don't know, not Johnny Mitchell, he stayed over there. I had Bernard on the guitar, and I had --
Bernard Addison.

Yeah. And I had the makings of a better band than I had. Had we been able to go. But in those days, there was no go because if you didn't have a radio network in your place, it wasn't going. A man named Levy, he tried to open a place in Long Island and have us there, but somehow he couldn't get the liquor license or something. Anyhow, Levy was a man that had Eddie Johnson up at a place that later on became the Cotton Club, you know?
Oh, right. So what did you do? Did you get any jobs?
What do you call when you just, I freelanced.
Had you recouped some of the money you had lost on that business arrangement?

No, I played the Arcadia, I played the Arcadia here on Broadway. And we did fairly good for awhile, but first thing you know, we had to get out of that. After we left there -- we stayed there about three months, two months or three, and then we were, then we just moved on. Until we played Pleasure Beach Park. Over here in Connecticut. And that's what was the last straw on the camel's back. We had three men in the

band that were alchoholic. And these three men couldn't play nothing without their -- and they were, two were trumpet players, and the other was a bass player. And so now, these are very essential in the band. So these fellows couldn't play nothing, and a local band made us look like we're amateurs. Well, that was the -- Albert Alvin Nicholss, he came up and he said, "Well, I'm going to Europe." And Sedric He said, "Well, I'm through." "I'm just going to get in a combination." So later on he went with Fats Waller.
Fats Waller.

Yeah. And I said, "I'm through. This is a good chance for me to finish my education." So I go back to Philadelphia and I take a choir, I had a choir. This choir was given credit for being comparable to the Don Cossacks, you see. I have that too.
Was that because you had learned something from your listening experience in Europe?

Yeah, I had. Because I had learned to put the emphasis on the bass. They have great -- the Russians have great bass. And they get together. And they give it body. Oh, we had some terrific music in Moscow.
So you became a choirmaster.
Yeah.
What was the name of the choir?
The Sam Wooding Choir. Southland Singers.
How many pieces?
Oh, about 25.
25 voices. Mixed, mixed --
Men and women.
Men and women, right.
And we could really do a cappella singing, you see, because I studied at Temple under Marjorie Jones and Nancy Campbell, at Temple University. I studied there for that, you know.
So --
At the same time while I was finishing my high school. Cause see, I had to go back to high school.
Right.

Cause, see, I'm only in the second year. And by the time I'd finished that, I had my choir ready. So I wouldn't have got -- gone back to it no more. I would have kept on with the choir, but the Japanese got smart at Pearl Harbor, you know?
Uh hunh.

And all my boys went into defense work, you know? And those that wasn't drafted went into defense work. So there wasn't nothing for me to do but just quit and go back to school. And I went on the the University of Pennsylvania and got my Bachelors and then I got my Masters Degree. But the reason I did that was because my little girl was growing up now, and I wanted to go into one of the campuses and live on the
campus and raise my kid, see. I didn't want them to say that I was a piano plunker.
Uh hunh.
I got my Masters Degree, so I could be considered a professor, you see?
The name you didn't like. The term you didn't like, professor.
Yeah.
So you became a real professor.
Why, that was because the cruisers from the bawdy houses used to say, 'Come on, professor.' And kick out a rag.
So, the choir. When did you start the choir? What year?
'37. But what happened. seems we skipped a lot of years here, what happened between 1932 and '37?

Well, in 1934, I stopped with the band. I come back in 1932, my kid was born in 1932. But I kept fooling around with bands until 1934, til we did this Pleasure Beach Park affair. And then it was no more.
And then, from '34 to '37, were you going a -- going back to high school?
No.
What were you doing?
Well, I didn't start. I went back to Philadelphia. And so I was home, I didn't do nothing for a couple of years or so.
Oh, you stayed with the family.
Yeah. Trying to find out what to do.
Uh hunh.
And then I started, maybe about '36 or '37, well I'll try -- I didn't want any more bands. I didn't intend to ever have another band, you see?
Uh hunh.
So I went to, I said, 'Well, there's some very good voices around Philadelphia.' Mostly blacks, you know.
You were singing spirituals?
Yeah.
Uh hunh.
We had spirituals and art songs. Like "Carry Me Back to Old Virginia", and a lot of, like Stephen Foster's stuff, "Way Down Upon the Swanny River".
And where did this choir perform?
Oh, in the different churches.
In Philadelphia?
We made a tour all over Canada and we went as far west as the Mississippi River. And we went as far

South as Florida. We played in the hotels down there. And up in the Adirondacks. We didn't play in the Catskills, but in the Adirondacks, we played in the Saranac Inn up there in the Adirondacks and places like that. Because, see, we were a cappella. And what we would do is, in the evening with people sitting on the porch, all we had to do was, I had a tuning fork. I'd give them the tune, and we'd start in singing. We didn't need no piano, we could start in anywhere.
So, around 1941, late '41 or '42, Pearl Harbor. You had to disband the choir.
(Went back to school.) Yeah, I had to disband the choir. There wasn't much choir there to disband.
So, you spent the war years in school getting your Masters Degree, Bachelors and Masters. And then you went into teaching, right?

Yeah, I went down to Wilmington. That's where I had Clifford Brown and some other very good students. (Here we go- (unintelligible) And then in '52, when I come back, I was in -- I came back to New York. No, I came back to New York in '47, I think.
Well, tell me about Clifford Brown.

Clifford Brown wasn't the best in my, in the band. But I think my influence set on him moreso than the others. Because Clifford tried harder and he used to come every Saturday to my room became that I stayed in my room in Wilmington, you see. I

still lived with my family in Philadelphia, you see, but I stayed down there because it was too much trouble going back and forward all the time. And he come in and the room I had, had an oil stove, and he'd come and get my oil for me. He and a couple of other -- and a little tenor player, I don't know what become of this little tenor player. But he was about the third man in the band, as far as ability. But now, Clifford, when I used to show him pictures of the band of what we did in Europe. Some I told the truth, and some was lies, but anyhow. I instilled him, and Clifford was the one that really -- and he was such a quiet little guy, that you wouldn't notice that he was taking all of this in as much as he was.

And he was gradually coming along. I showed him how to play, he didn't know how to make an embouchure. Sometimes he'd have it here, sometimes here, and I'd say, "You've got to take it in one place, son, and keep working on it." And I showed him how to play solos; (unintelligible) he passed on part of what I taught him. But I gave him the fundamentals, you know what I mean? So he came on and the next time I saw him, I was in Paris with Rae Harrison, and he walked into the place. Rae worked at a cabaret, she was double in at the Nouveau Elve, at a big cabaret there. See, course I had taught her from the teaching that I had got from Mrs. Jones and Nancy Campbell, I taught her. And she turned out to be -- she had a real high voice.
Was this in '53 or '54 when Clifford was with the Hampton band over there?

Yes. And he came and we hired another cabaret, another fellow and I named Jimmy English. And I had this cabaret, and Ray had quit her job in the Nouveau Elvres, that was next to the Lido in Paris, and she quit the job to come and work with us. Cause we had promised her. It was good money. We promised her, you know?
Uh hunh.
Oh, I don't think she ever got all of it. But we promised her.
(laugh)
We're going to get to that. You were teaching Clifford Brown what years?

I was teaching Clifford Brown in '45 and '46 and going into '47. Then I got sick of it. I got sick of it down there because when you're teaching in those schools, nowadays, you have 40 in a class. But only 5 of them want music. The rest of them want recreation. And they come in the class and socialize and throw rubbers and bottles at you, anything, and have a good time. And so, I wasn't in for that. That was for some young kid that didn't know any different. I've been all around the world. I'm going to be satisfied with teaching -- and then when we had a stupid principal. And when I was giving

them solfeggion and teaching them how to tell what key they were in. And beginning to get Melodia books and teach them how to read the music, he come in there and he said, "Listen, Mr. Wooding, I think you just should just let them sit here and sing and enjoy themselves." This was a school. I said, "Mr. Johnson, this is a school." Said, "I know, but that's what the orders are that I got from the Board of Education." In other words, he was saying some of them going to be cooks anyhow, waitresses and so, so why worry about teaching them music. And they don't need no music to sing on the church choir.
Dont worry About giving THEM...
But Clifford Brown was one of the more serious students.
Well, I had about ten in that band that was good.
Yeah.

I had a girl that was very good bass player. But the principal fired her from school, expelled her from school for some reason. And then she was out of school and she got into trouble and she tried to correct that trouble, an abortion, and the next thing you know, she was dead. She would have been something. Out of the ordinary. They got some good potentialities in the kids in Wilmington.
What about when you -- so in 1947 you quit teaching. And what did you do then?
I come to New York. I didn't have any-
-thing in mind. So I started another choir.
Uh hunh.

And then that's the choir that played with Kenny Spencer and we played the "Ballad of America", you know, that Paul Robeson used to do. Kenneth Spencer did it and then we had the evening in Carnegie Hall. And we had quite a job. That's the one when I walked into Rae. And her mother brought Rae to me at that time, you see.
What was that choir called?
The Sam Wooding Choir.
The Sam Wooding Choir.
Yes. The Sam Wooding Choir. There wasn't no more Southland Singers. It was just the Sam Wooding Choir.
So, now, as we get into the late '40's, bop music is coming up.
Yeah.
And a lot of musicians of your generation could not see bop music, you know. How did you feel about it?

I wasn't even interested in it. I'll tell you why, because as I told you, I didn't have any need to hear any band because I was through with black bands. You see, because the musicians after that Pleasure Beach Park episode, I

said, 'Well, look. I don't want any ulcers. So the best thing I can do is stay away from bands.' So I used to talk French. We'd go sometimes to Montreal and visit and talk some French, you know. And come on back here. And I had a studio. Had a studio over here on LaSalle Street. It was LaSalle Street then. Now LaSalle Street has gone into an apartment house over there. Well, I had a studio over here. And I taught -- that was how Rae Ray's mother brought her to me, was in this studio, you see. And we worked together for one solid year without taking any jobs, any engagements. See, then she started to and took an engagement, and I was more like a manager than an accompanist, you see.
Uh hunh.
But the reason I started accompanying her, I took her to Europe. Because it was easy for me to go to Europe. And the bands over there didn't know how to play for her.
There was one thing that we skipped. Was when you came back from Europe in 19 -- was it late '31 or early '32.
Yeah.
You had told me a long time ago that there was a gentleman over there, a German, who sort of advised you to leave Europe. And he knew more, politically, what was
going to happen.
Well, that was Eddie Duseberg, my manager.
OH, that was your manager.

Yeah. He said, 'Look here, Sam, you're not going to work in Berlin next year.' And I said, 'At the Hauskomminia (unintelligible).' And he said, 'Because the political situation won't allow you.' He had to be careful how he talked, see. 'They won't allow you to do that right now. And so if I was you, I would leave Europe altogether.' Well, he started me to thinking. And then when it showed up that I couldn't go to London for the six months in the Savoy Hotel, well there wasn't nothing to do but -- that closed the deal. With the wife in pregnancy and the child was born in February. That same February, see, and this was around in December. So. And I found the thing was there was nothing to do but just close the book. And start life over.
So, and then you later ran into him, didn't you?
Yes. He come in when we was playing saloon in (PALMA MIRROCA) Tito's, (unintelligible). He come in there and we fell on each other's shoulders and we cried and had a wonderful time, you know.
(laugh)
It was like old times, you know?
And that was long after the war, right?

Yeah. Eddie and I were just like this, We planned together, you know? We fought together. We went out and socialized together. And we had sex together. We had a wonderful time over there, you know. My wife couldn't stand him because she knew we was running around together. My first wife, not the wife I've got now.
Uh hunh.

See, so that's the way that happened. So it was just one of those things. That we had to go back. So we came back here. And when I came back to America, let's see, well, I went back to Philadelphia, because my mother was just living. She died in the next month or something like that. But I was staying with my brother. He's a doctor in Philadelphia, see. And we stayed there. And then I made up my mind what I wanted to do. And I took the choir, see?
Uh hunh.
But now, this choir was unique. Because I gave the choir the same effects that I'd give a band.
Uh hunh.
And actually one man called it sing-music.
YOu never made any records.
Huh?
You never made any records? You never recorded that choir, huh?
No. I couldn't get the -- a friend of mine, Lud Gluskin. He's out there in Hollywood, you know, he had that CBS with Hollywood, Lud Gluskin.
Uh hunh.

Well, Lud Gluskin, he was just a little (E-flat) drummer when -- and a leader, when we was in Berlin, you know? And I -- right now, if I was writing to Lud Gluskin, if he's still in the business, he'd try to do something for me, came here and went in with CBS, you know? But of course, he (unintelligible). I guess he had his relatives or something, put him in. And he went on for years. He was head of the music department out in Hollywood, CBS.
So, I think we've got enough for today. And we leave it at a very nice point. Where Ray enters the picture and you work together and eventually go back to Europe.
Yeah.
So we'll take it up from there next time.
Now, I've introduced her, you know, I've spoken of her.
Right.
And now, we'll do Ray when we come back.
Okay.
And then we'll get to -- don't forget, we've got to get to this band.
Right.

Mt. Morris church hosts 'sweet and sacred' jazz

By James Stinard
HARLEM WEEKLY STAFF
The Mt. Morris Presbyterian Church resounded with music as the Sam Wooding-Rae Harrison Jazz Band poured on the jazz at a memorial benefit concert, Sunday, Oct. 19.

The concert billed as, 'Sweet and Sacred Jazz,' featured Sam Wooding and Rae Harrison along with their eleven man band. Sam Wooding, an energetic 85, wrote most of the jazz selections and conducted the entire program. His vivacious partner and wife, Rae Harrison performed the spiritual and blues songs. For starters, Rae sang, 'Precious Lord,' a gospel hymn written by Tommy Dorsey. Singing slowly, her rich voice resonated throughout the vaulted and glass-domed sanctuary. Rae nursed the words and concluded by repeating the last words of the song, 'I want to cross into heaven,' a total of twenty creative ways.

Introducing the next number, Sam said, 'Our people brought old melodies from Africa, called the blues. This next number, 'Kater Street Blues,' tells about the mean and ugly street I grew up in Philadelphia.'

Even though this is a lively song, one can sense a feeling of melancholy. From the beginning of 'Kater St. Blues,' as well as throughout most of the program, the audience responded by tapping their feet and moving in rhythm to the music, in addition to their enthusiastic applause.
This concert was held to raise funds for a stained-glass window to be dedicated in the memory of the late Rev. Arthur Eugene Adair.

'This program is a fitting tribute to Rev. Adair, who encouraged and promoted all types of music in the church,' said Mrs. Thelma Adair. 'To help the church purchase its pipe organ, Rev. Adair contributed a year of his salary.'
Rev. Adair founded Mt. Morris Presbyterian Church in 1942 and served as its pastor up until his death on Dec. 11, 1979.
Rev. Kumi Dwamena, acting pastor at Mt. Morris, said he felt encouraged by the way the community supported the concert.
