segments.title: Archive copyright notice and interview header
segments.summary: Rutgers IJS copyright notices and the Smithsonian header for Chris Albertson's April-May 1975 interview with Sam Wooding.

segments.title: Born in Philadelphia in 1895; father the Biddles' butler
segments.summary: Wooding gives his birth date and Rodman Street home and describes his father's work as butler and steward for the Biddle family.

segments.title: Father not musical; family plans for the four children
segments.summary: Wooding says his father kept any music to himself, that summers were spent in Atlantic City, and that the children were meant to be dentist, doctor, preacher and nurse.

segments.title: Seeing Williams and Walker, conductor Vaughan and Will Marion Cook
segments.summary: At about six or seven he sees the Williams and Walker show; the pit conductor James Vaughan makes him want to conduct, and he recalls Will Marion Cook's group.

segments.title: Trouble in public school and the Catholic mission school
segments.summary: Distracted by show business, he fights on his first day, is moved by his mother to a Catholic school, and cannot be converted.

segments.title: His mother's organ and the sleeping organ teacher
segments.summary: His mother plays hymns on the organ; he sneaks ragtime on it while his teacher sleeps.

segments.title: Ragtime and why his parents disapproved
segments.summary: He explains that ragtime used four-four time unlike European waltzes and one-steps, and that his parents thought only bums played it.

segments.title: Bethel AME Church and his indifference to religion
segments.summary: The family attends Richard Allen's Bethel AME Church; he is put off by the saloon on the corner and the shouting.

segments.title: Teaching himself ragtime in F-sharp with a friend at age ten
segments.summary: Wooding and a friend play rags in F-sharp and C-sharp on organ and borrowed pianos and hear local players like Jesse Pinkett and Jack the Bear.

segments.title: Father's jitney buses in Atlantic City
segments.summary: His brothers go to Shaw University, and his father buys horse-drawn buses to carry people between the cabarets of Atlantic City's back bay.

segments.title: Watching Eubie Blake at Madison Reed's show
segments.summary: From a beer box at the window he watches Eubie Blake play in Madison Reed's cabaret and takes Blake and Williams and Walker as his inspiration.

segments.title: Writing his first piece at eleven
segments.summary: He writes 'Won't You Be My Little Sweet Household Queen', has it notated by the Biddles' Irish maid, and copyrighted.

segments.title: Miss Jordan's singing classes in public school
segments.summary: Moved to public school, he learns part-singing from a teacher who gives keys with a tuning fork.

segments.title: Playing Philadelphia house rent parties at fourteen
segments.summary: He describes rent parties as a living for the hosts, with pigs feet and potato salad, and the lack of anything but an ordinary piano.

segments.title: How stride piano was copied from bands
segments.summary: Wooding says players like Ralph Rawson and Duke taught him stride, which imitates the bass, alto horn and melody parts of a marching band.

segments.title: Rent party prices, bootleg drink and learning to drink
segments.summary: Albertson asks about the parties; Wooding gives prices, mentions blackberry and gin, and a friend's mother warning them apart.

segments.title: Songs played at rent parties
segments.summary: He names a few songs played for dancing.

segments.title: Rhythm, clapping on the off-beat and the roots of swing
segments.summary: Wooding contrasts European and black rhythm, ring shouts and spirituals, and says they were doing gospel before it was labelled.

segments.title: Blues as secular spirituals; hearing blues in Philadelphia
segments.summary: He says the blues belongs to nobody and was only captured by Handy, and recalls corner guitarists and Baltimore's role in music.

segments.title: Poverty, home-made rhythm and no money for conservatory
segments.summary: He argues poor Southern blacks made music with bones and ran because it was free, and that lack of money kept him from the New England Conservatory.

segments.title: Pay at rent parties and the Early's hangout
segments.summary: A dollar and a quarter was a lot; he describes Early's restaurant and the bakery where credit made them big timers.

segments.title: Skipping class and the cigar lesson from his father
segments.summary: After he and Maceo Mayfield hook school to smoke, his father gives him cigars and he never smokes cigarettes again.

segments.title: His father's family out of slavery
segments.summary: He tells how his grandmother carried his father north from Virginia and how his father educated himself in the Biddles' library.

segments.title: Josephine Berkeley and the cakewalk
segments.summary: Wooding meets the cakewalk dancer Josephine Berkeley, explains what a cakewalk was, and catches her cake at the Greenwaiters' Ball.

segments.title: Dropping out for Atlantic City; Jack the Bear versus Eubie Blake
segments.summary: He leaves school to follow Josephine to Atlantic City and decides Jack the Bear is no match for Eubie Blake.

segments.title: Meeting Charlie Johnson in Atlantic City
segments.summary: Wooding calls Charlie Johnson of Boston a great early help, and says Johnson later partnered with Weloff to open the Paradise.

segments.title: Playing piano 'professor' in Atlantic City bawdy houses
segments.summary: Hired from the corner to play in white and Black brothels, he describes the screens, the acts and the tips in summer and the slump in winter.

segments.title: Lost in Atlantic City, gambling with Charlie Johnson
segments.summary: Out of school and adrift, he gambles with Johnson, whom he calls a great cabaret pianist and bandleader who died poor.

segments.title: The Bucket of Blood job and learning to play for singers
segments.summary: He plays piano at the Bucket of Blood, unable to transpose for singers, and says Atlantic City's cabarets were the real school.

segments.title: Low pay at the Bucket of Blood and almost becoming a pimp
segments.summary: He earned twenty dollars at best, much lost to tabs, and jokes about not making a pimp.

segments.title: Taking food as a hotel waiter and being called a thief
segments.summary: Working as a waiter, he smuggles chicken to hungry musicians until a new steward stops it and a friend accuses him of selling the food.

segments.title: Tips and singers in the cabarets
segments.summary: Albertson asks about tips; Wooding says he was not yet playing for singers, and that singers split tips with the band.

segments.title: Getting his start at the Belmont for Mr. Brown
segments.summary: When Freddy Tunstall walks out, Mr. Brown insists Wooding play upstairs at the Belmont cabaret and he struggles through the keys.

segments.title: Belmont singers: Mabel Richardson, Alice Jackson, Teddy Peters
segments.summary: He names the singers at the Belmont and says Old Man Brown gave him his start.

segments.title: Old Man Brown's advice to read the audience
segments.summary: Wooding recalls the songs sung and Brown's lesson to watch the crowd and play what suits its mood.

segments.title: Right song, right role: Streisand, Williams and Walker, Lionel's saxophone
segments.summary: He argues that wrong songs and wrong casting hold performers back, citing Barbra Streisand, the reversal of Williams and Walker, and a player Vodery switched to saxophone.

segments.title: Willie the Lion Smith in Newark
segments.summary: After leaving Brown he goes to Newark, where he fills in for Willie the Lion Smith who disappears for hours.

segments.title: Kinney's Hall and Janers in Newark
segments.summary: He gives the name and street of Kinney's Hall in Newark and says the war started and his girl left him.

segments.title: Taking Charley Johnson's Newark job; first dope fiend
segments.summary: Charley Johnson recommends Wooding for his Newark job and shows him a drug user nodding off at the piano.

segments.title: Working out his age at the draft
segments.summary: A long exchange in which Albertson and Wooding try to reconcile his 1895 birth, voting at twenty, and being drafted before turning twenty-one.

segments.title: Back to Newark: first wife and return to Atlantic City
segments.summary: He recounts meeting his first wife in Newark and returning to Atlantic City after the season.

segments.title: Opium, cocaine and the sporting life in Newark
segments.summary: He says there was no marijuana then, only hop and cocaine, and describes pimps with opium pipes who tried to break him in.

segments.title: Substituting for Eubie Blake and Madison Reed's key lesson
segments.summary: Back in Atlantic City, he fills in for the sick Eubie Blake and is scolded by Madison Reed for transposing a song from his own key to E-flat.

segments.title: Memorizing songs and busking requests for singers
segments.summary: He explains musicians had to memorize everything and improvise accompaniment for patrons, a skill he says young players now cannot get.

segments.title: Blues in 1918 and the origin of the Bugle Blues
segments.summary: He says many men sang blues in 1918, credits Jim Europe's band with the Bugle Blues not Benny Goodman, and compares Southern and Western blues.

segments.title: The words jazz and funk
segments.summary: Wooding discusses when he first heard the word jazz and how jazz and funk came to mean what they do.

segments.chapter: Charley Johnson and the Army band
segments.title: End of first session and start of second interview
segments.summary: Albertson ends the first interview in Atlantic City around 1918 and begins interview number two on April 24, 1975.

segments.chapter: Charley Johnson and the Army band
segments.title: Atlantic City 1915 and breaking the gambling habit
segments.summary: Wooding recalls going to Atlantic City with an entertainer, Charley Johnson teaching him to gamble, and his quitting after a Sunday morning.

segments.chapter: Charley Johnson and the Army band
segments.title: Charley Johnson and the Paradise
segments.summary: Wooding praises Johnson as the best cabaret organizer who made Weloff's Paradise famous and later came to New York with Smalls.

segments.chapter: Charley Johnson and the Army band
segments.title: What the draft and Army taught him
segments.summary: He says being drafted was the best thing for him because he learned discipline and manhood.

segments.chapter: Charley Johnson and the Army band
segments.title: Army band and Lieutenant Bill Vodery
segments.summary: Wooding says he was a second-class musician in the band led by Bill Vodery, Ziegfeld's arranger.

segments.chapter: Charley Johnson and the Army band
segments.title: Sailing for France and the band's members
segments.summary: He names bandmates, says it took three tries to join the last non-labor-battalion Black band, and that he played baritone horn.

segments.chapter: Charley Johnson and the Army band
segments.title: Bugle Blues copied from the Fifteenth Regiment
segments.summary: The band played Sousa marches and tried to copy Jim Europe's Fifteenth Regiment band's Bugle Blues.

segments.chapter: Charley Johnson and the Army band
segments.title: Army anecdotes: saltpetre, Meuse-Argonne and the German plane
segments.summary: He tells comic stories of the saltpetre prank and shell shock joke and of a German pilot waving at the band.

segments.chapter: Charley Johnson and the Army band
segments.title: Army band repertoire and French audiences
segments.summary: He confirms the Bugle Blues is the Bugle Call Rag, says the band played ragtime and marches, and played for French townspeople.

segments.chapter: Charley Johnson and the Army band
segments.title: Defining jazz as rhythmic improvisation
segments.summary: Wooding says jazz is improvisation plus a rhythmic pattern on any melody, and Black players excel because of rhythm.

segments.chapter: Charley Johnson and the Army band
segments.title: Sousa played straight; Army shaped character not music
segments.summary: The band played Sousa straight, and the Army taught him discipline and appreciation of home.

segments.chapter: Charley Johnson and the Army band
segments.title: Length of service and war's end
segments.summary: He served about fourteen months from early 1918 to 1919 and first heard 'fini la guerre' in the Meuse-Argonne.

segments.chapter: Philadelphia, Detroit and back to Atlantic City
segments.title: Jake Gillum's Madhouse in Philadelphia
segments.summary: He describes his job at the Madhouse, a confusing rough place with prizefighter waiters, which he regained after the war.

segments.chapter: Philadelphia, Detroit and back to Atlantic City
segments.title: Madhouse clientele and the coming of the blues
segments.summary: He says the Madhouse was a black-and-tan crowd, and that blues singers like Ma Rainey and Lucille Hegamin were coming into vogue.

segments.chapter: Philadelphia, Detroit and back to Atlantic City
segments.title: Forming his first band at the Madhouse
segments.summary: Back at the Madhouse he leads a five-piece group of guitar, banjo, bass, drums and piano with Harold Waters and Harry Morris.

segments.chapter: Philadelphia, Detroit and back to Atlantic City
segments.title: Leaving Philadelphia's Madhouse for Atlantic City
segments.summary: Asked about the Original Dixieland Jazz Band, Wooding says he first heard it in Atlantic City, to which he returned in 1920 as it was like Las Vegas.

segments.chapter: Philadelphia, Detroit and back to Atlantic City
segments.title: First jazz band in Atlantic City: Chambers, Dixon, Harrison
segments.summary: He organizes a band playing Margie after hearing ODJB records, with Elmer Chambers, Charley Dixon, Jimmy Harrison and a drummer called Fats.

segments.chapter: Philadelphia, Detroit and back to Atlantic City
segments.title: Lucky Roberts and Eubie Blake's advice about hands
segments.summary: Through Charley Johnson he meets Lucky Roberts, whose big hands and Junkman Rag amazed him, and Eubie Blake tells him not to throw his hands in the air.

segments.chapter: Philadelphia, Detroit and back to Atlantic City
segments.title: James P. Johnson, Willie the Lion Smith and accompanying singers
segments.summary: He recalls James P. Johnson's burning piano at a matinee and compares Roberts, Johnson, Blake and the Lion as pianists.

segments.chapter: Philadelphia, Detroit and back to Atlantic City
segments.title: American musicians, Japanese big bands and jazz as an American product
segments.summary: Wooding complains cabaret owners are too stingy to hire bands, compares Japan's large bands, and says jazz came from the melting pot but Black musicians created most of it.

segments.chapter: Philadelphia, Detroit and back to Atlantic City
segments.title: To Detroit and taking over Bony Allen's cabaret
segments.summary: Jimmy Harrison and Fats talk up Detroit, where Bony Allen, owing the band money, hands over his cabaret.

segments.chapter: Philadelphia, Detroit and back to Atlantic City
segments.title: Running the Detroit cabaret and losing money
segments.summary: The band runs the cabaret on St. Catherine Street with seven entertainers, but cannot play and watch the cash register.

segments.chapter: Philadelphia, Detroit and back to Atlantic City
segments.title: Prohibition liquor, a waitress's warning and leaving Detroit
segments.summary: A man pours whiskey at tables and cheats the band, a waitress tries to warn Wooding, and the partners break up the cabaret and head East.

segments.chapter: Philadelphia, Detroit and back to Atlantic City
segments.title: Detroit's big bands and the Dixieland repertoire
segments.summary: Detroit had twelve-piece bands led by men like Bart Howard, while Wooding's combination played Margie and St. Louis Blues.

segments.chapter: Philadelphia, Detroit and back to Atlantic City
segments.title: Back East with a Dixieland band and the West Indian clarinetist Edwards
segments.summary: Returning in spring 1921 he adds clarinet, saxophone and trumpet, drops Jimmy Harrison who read poorly, and gets endings and introductions for tunes.

segments.chapter: Philadelphia, Detroit and back to Atlantic City
segments.title: Atlantic City's Paradise ownership and Prohibition drinking
segments.summary: He says Charley Johnson worked the Boardwalk while the Paradise changed hands, and that Prohibition increased drinking and bad liquor.

segments.chapter: Philadelphia, Detroit and back to Atlantic City
segments.title: Summer at Ben Allen's place with the two Ethels
segments.summary: He works a season at Kentucky and Arctic Avenue with Ethel Waters, Ethel Williams, Snow Fisher and Izzy Ringgold, and says Waters was an entertainer not a great singer.

segments.chapter: Philadelphia, Detroit and back to Atlantic City
segments.title: Charley Reynolds takes over; hiring the show
segments.summary: Wooding describes Ben Allen and Mike Green as Atlantic City's Black bosses, and how Charley Reynolds hired his band and the entertainers.

segments.chapter: Philadelphia, Detroit and back to Atlantic City
segments.title: Baron Wilkins hires him for New York
segments.summary: Baron Wilkins, the boss of Harlem, offers Wooding a job at his cabaret at about forty dollars a week and the men less.

segments.chapter: Philadelphia, Detroit and back to Atlantic City
segments.title: Frankie Half-Pint Jackson's Palm Sunday joke
segments.summary: Wooding retells how Frankie Jackson preached a risque comic sermon on Jesus, which shocked him.

segments.chapter: Philadelphia, Detroit and back to Atlantic City
segments.title: Other Atlantic City performers: Grace Jackson, Mary Stafford, Mattie Hite
segments.summary: He names Billy Leadman, the dancer Grace Jackson, and singers Mary Stafford, Mattie Hite and Bee Palmer.

segments.chapter: Philadelphia, Detroit and back to Atlantic City
segments.title: Bessie Smith in Atlantic City
segments.summary: Wooding says Atlantic City audiences, who liked joyful or sentimental songs, did not appreciate Bessie Smith's blues.

segments.chapter: Philadelphia, Detroit and back to Atlantic City
segments.title: Crazy Blues, phonographs and wind-up records
segments.summary: He says Perry Bradford deserved the credit for Crazy Blues and that few Black households had wind-up phonographs.

segments.chapter: Philadelphia, Detroit and back to Atlantic City
segments.title: Atlantic City as a playground and the start of the Paradise
segments.summary: He describes rich whites crossing to the Back Bay cabarets after midnight and how Charley Johnson and Ralph Wheelock began the Paradise.

segments.title: Charley Johnson precedes him to New York; the Big Apple
segments.summary: Johnson went to Baron's before Wooding; Wooding does not recall New York being called the Big Apple except for a club.

segments.title: The six-piece band at Baron Wilkins
segments.summary: He lists Elmer Chambers, Charley Dixon, Roland Smith, Walter Edwards and Joey Young, and tells about trombonists Revis Horton and Jimmy Harrison.

segments.title: Baron's cabaret, Bricktop, Al Jolson and a ten-thousand-dollar bill
segments.summary: Wooding recalls Bricktop as hostess at the whites-only Baron's, Leroy's whites-barred place, gangsters and a ten thousand dollar tip.

segments.title: Tuba player Bass Edwards and his cigar
segments.summary: He adds a tuba player who blew cigar smoke through his horn to make the band look on fire.

segments.title: Head arrangements and Sidney Bechet's Dear Old Southland
segments.summary: After Bricktop introduces Sidney Bechet, he plays Dear Old Southland on soprano and makes Wooding's arrangement obsolete.

segments.title: Jazz did not originate only in New Orleans
segments.summary: Wooding argues that jazz arose all over the United States and that Louis Armstrong became great only after coming to New York with Fletcher Henderson.

segments.title: Repertoire and pay at Baron Wilkins
segments.summary: The band played popular songs for entertainers, with salary of forty dollars for him and tips of four to twenty dollars each.

segments.title: Leaving Baron Wilkins to build a band
segments.summary: Declining a doubled salary because the manager Dude Adams wanted two men cut, he leaves after about fourteen months to be a bandleader.

segments.title: Dancing Dodson puts the band on stage at the Regent Theater
segments.summary: His first theater appearance goes badly until Dodson steps in, and the band wins over the audience.

segments.title: A week at the Lafayette with Chappelle and Stinnette
segments.summary: The band plays a week at the Lafayette on a bill with Clarence Williams and Eva Taylor, which makes him feel somebody.

segments.title: Harlem rent parties and Buffet Flats
segments.summary: He says he was above rent parties and describes Buffet Flats with pianolas, liquor in teapots and rooms upstairs, and landlords favouring madams.

segments.title: Baron Wilkins as the political boss of Harlem
segments.summary: Wooding says Baron controlled Harlem for Black people, controlled both parties, and protected Black cabarets with Leroy and Connors from licence denials.

segments.title: The killing of Baron Wilkins by Yellow Charleston
segments.summary: He says Italian gangsters used a deprived addict, Yellow Charleston, to shoot Baron, and Harlem sportsmen hunted him.

segments.title: Music director for Plantation Days; lodging the band in his house
segments.summary: He takes the second company of Plantation Days though he had never been in a pit, and later warns musicians not to house their sidemen.

segments.title: Stranded in Indianapolis
segments.summary: The show's owner and comedian Eddie Green leave with the money and the cast is stranded, his first strand.

segments.title: Maude deForrest, Gus Smith and the TOBA tab shows
segments.summary: Gus Smith organizes tab shows through Indiana and Illinois on the TOBA circuit until the girls are sent home and the group returns to New York.

segments.title: Drummer George Howe points him to the Nest Club
segments.summary: Back in New York, his old drummer tells him that Johnny Carey and Mal Frazier are opening a new club and need a bandleader.

segments.title: Closing interview two and opening interview three
segments.summary: They stop at the Nest and start interview 3 on April 26, 1975.

segments.title: Hired by Johnny Carey and Mal Frazier for the Nest
segments.summary: Wooding recalls how a war buddy sent him to Carey and Frazier, who hired him on a gentleman's agreement with no contract.

segments.title: Building the Nest band and the opening night
segments.summary: He assembles two saxophones, two trumpets and full rhythm, rehearses at home, and at opening the audience applauds instead of dancing.

segments.title: Jungle sound, wa-wa and plunger trumpeters in Harlem
segments.summary: He explains the wow-wow style of Johnny Dunn, Bubber Miley and Tommy Morris, and says Ellington built on it and that funk was not a music term.

segments.title: Down-home music and blues as secular spirituals
segments.summary: He explains 'down home' meant blues, Blue Monday and homesickness, and that blues grew out of ring shouts as secular music.

segments.title: Blues unpopular in Harlem; Dixieland giving way to stomp-era jazz
segments.summary: He says blues singers were not popular, that Prohibition-era bands used racks of effects, and that bands were growing to seven and eight men with arrangements.

segments.title: Vocalists, jive singers and the first scat singers
segments.summary: He says bands did not need a vocalist, and names Gertie Saunders as an early scat singer.

segments.title: Writing the Nest opening and 'Walk, Jenny, Walk' with Henry Creamer
segments.summary: Wooding and lyricist Henry Creamer write the show opening in twenty minutes and turn his song into 'Walk, Jenny, Walk', placed by a song plugger.

segments.title: The Nest Club: clientele, decor and atmosphere
segments.summary: He describes a mixed, high-class crowd of white and Black performers, the bandstand and decor, and bad man Bob Hewlett keeping order.

segments.title: Ethel Waters, Florence Mills and others visiting the Nest
segments.summary: He recalls Ethel Waters and Earl Dancer's quarrel, Florence Mills sitting at a table, and how Mills got her break replacing Gertie Saunders.

segments.title: Agent Arthur Lyons offers him Broadway
segments.summary: Lyons, a struggling agent, listens at the Nest and asks whether Wooding wants to go downtown, which is what the band was working toward.

segments.title: Turned away by a white arranger; learning to write arrangements
segments.summary: A white arranging office changes its tone when it sees they are Black musicians, so Wooding begins writing whole arrangements himself.

segments.title: Lyons's advice never to step backwards; a sound by accident
segments.summary: Lyons tells him Fletcher Henderson is making a mistake going back to a dance hall and offers to put the band in his place.

segments.chapter: Club Alabam and the Europe contract
segments.title: Succeeding Fletcher Henderson at the Club Alabam
segments.summary: After a year at the Nest he takes over the Club Alabam, the first Times Square club, whose audience included Whiteman and Jack Dempsey.

segments.chapter: Club Alabam and the Europe contract
segments.title: Gus Schultz's rule against four-beat music on Saturday
segments.summary: The maitre d' forbids sensuous four-beat playing on Saturday nights, and the club draws rich scions that prepared him for Europe.

segments.chapter: Club Alabam and the Europe contract
segments.title: Refusing to play blues for the Edison Company
segments.summary: The Edison man wants blues, not Wooding's arrangements, and Wooding refuses to be held to it.

segments.chapter: Club Alabam and the Europe contract
segments.title: Substituting for the Marine Band on WEAF radio
segments.summary: Walking in unannounced, his band is put on air to replace the Marine Band and succeeds.

segments.chapter: Club Alabam and the Europe contract
segments.title: The Club Alabam show: Abbie Mitchell, Eddie Rector, Johnny Hudgins
segments.summary: Arthur Lyons puts in a big revue that Wooding learned to conduct and that foreshadowed the Cotton Club shows.

segments.chapter: Club Alabam and the Europe contract
segments.title: Will Marion Cook teaches him to retard for a singer
segments.summary: He asks Will Marion Cook how to slow down with Abbie Mitchell and learns to bend his knees on each retard.

segments.chapter: Club Alabam and the Europe contract
segments.title: J. Rosamund Johnson's advice to listen to the bad bands
segments.summary: The composer Rosamund Johnson, passed over for the Europe job, tells Wooding to listen to the bad bands to learn what not to do.

segments.chapter: Club Alabam and the Europe contract
segments.title: Eddie Rector's drill, Clarence Robinson and Bunny Weldon staging the show
segments.summary: He recalls Rector turning the girls' military drill into jazz and the white producer Bunny Weldon telling dancers to grind.

segments.chapter: Club Alabam and the Europe contract
segments.title: Tin Pan Alley numbers and Abbie Mitchell's daily walk-outs
segments.summary: The show's music was by white Tin Pan Alley writers, and Wooding plays the 'Mississippi Mammy' intro whenever Mitchell threatens not to go on.

segments.chapter: Club Alabam and the Europe contract
segments.title: Arthur Lyons brings in a European impresario
segments.summary: Lyons introduces the Russian impresario Lenidow, who wants a band and a show, and cast members for Europe are found.

segments.chapter: Club Alabam and the Europe contract
segments.title: Winter Garden Sundays and Loew's vaudeville, never the Palace
segments.summary: Wooding played Sunday concerts at the Winter Garden and Loew's vaudeville but never the Palace until accompanying Rae Harrison.

segments.chapter: Club Alabam and the Europe contract
segments.title: Arthur Lyons revealed to be Russian
segments.summary: A fight between Lyons's brother Sam and a Greek busboy exposes in Russian that Lyons was Russian.

segments.title: Signing the Europe contract and the voyage over
segments.summary: The contract was signed at four in the morning in early 1925 and the band, with wives and friends, had a carefree crossing in summer.

segments.title: The drunk trombonist at Loew's State on Christmas 1924
segments.summary: Teroy gets drunk on stage wine, so the band props him between trumpets, gives him coffee, and hides it from the audience.

segments.title: Arriving in Berlin: rehearsal bedlam and hotel costs
segments.summary: He praises Berlin's cleanliness, describes Lyons, Germans and Russians shouting in different languages, and the expensive Prager Platz hotel.

segments.title: German audiences expect Africans
segments.summary: Audiences expected savages and could not believe the band were Americans; they gave seventy sold-out performances.

segments.title: The first Berlin performance and the cry of 'Bis'
segments.summary: Before the opening, Lenidow depends on Wooding; the stunned silence after the overture is followed by 'bis' which they mistake for 'beasts'.

segments.title: The Berlin show: the Three Eddies and the band's showpiece
segments.summary: After the plantation scenes and the Three Eddies, the band's showpiece, introduced by Adelaide Hall, brings the house down and the night ends in celebration.

segments.title: How the show got the name Chocolate Kiddies
segments.summary: A Hamburg chocolate sign gives Lyons the show's title, and the band's playing is the great surprise to audiences who had seen dancers before.

segments.title: After the opening: Berlin night out and sightseeing
segments.summary: Wooding declines a Berlin brothel visit because his wife is along, then tours the Kaiser's palace and coffee-houses with big bands.

segments.title: Germans astonished by Black Americans; the Gene Cedric incident
segments.summary: At the Darmstader Hoff, Gene Cedric scares an inquisitive German woman reading his letter, and Wooding reflects that Germans thought Africans were brought to America temporarily.

segments.title: German musicians, improvisation and syncopating Wagner
segments.summary: German musicians could not follow improvisation, and the band syncopated Tannhauser, which some called sacrilege.

segments.title: Why Black musicians had few instruments and sports
segments.summary: He explains that Black people got organs and pianos late and lacked tennis and golf for the same reasons.

segments.title: Open engagement in Berlin and Lenidow's first jazz venture
segments.summary: The Berlin run was open ended, extended by demand to around seventy performances, for the impresario's first venture into jazz.

segments.title: First recordings in Berlin through acoustic horns
segments.summary: The recording people came after four or five days; the drums were placed in the hall and the band played into horns, recording show numbers.

segments.title: Hamburg and the band staying the same until Russia
segments.summary: After Berlin they play the Thalia Theater in Hamburg; George Howe leaves for home before Russia.

segments.title: Stockholm and a benefit for Prince Carl
segments.summary: In Stockholm he does a Red Cross benefit for Prince Carl of Sweden.

segments.title: Copenhagen success, expulsion and the orangutan review
segments.summary: Copenhagen was the greatest success after Berlin, but authorities put them out for taking all the money, and a newspaper called Wooding an orangutan.

segments.title: The show thins out and the band becomes the star
segments.summary: After Lyons sold his rights, the Goldberg-run production cut costs and replaced stars with cheaper acts, so the band became the show.

segments.title: Arriving in Russia in the cold
segments.summary: The band travels to Moscow, chased by wolves, and is greeted by singing college girls in the freezing cold.

segments.title: May Day in Moscow and a lost drosky ride to the theater
segments.summary: Wooding describes the May Day parade and a drosky ride in which neither driver nor bystanders could read the black head placard.

segments.title: A symphony orchestra playing without a conductor
segments.summary: A Russian woman takes them to hear a 110-piece orchestra playing Tchaikovsky in a circle with no leader.

segments.title: European musicians try to copy the band
segments.summary: At the Fawn des Westen in Berlin a German band attempts improvisation and the master of ceremonies tells the audience to applaud them.

segments.title: Josephine Baker and Claude Hopkins' rival show
segments.summary: Josephine Baker and Maude deForrest come with Claude Hopkins' show and Baker watches Wooding's band before going to Paris.

segments.title: Recordings for Polydor and Pathe; where they had been
segments.summary: Albertson checks the 1926 chronology and recordings for Polydor and a French company, before Paris.

segments.title: Why the show closed in Danzig
segments.summary: Wooding says Goldberg persuaded the Polish backer Sirotq to cut salaries, so the show broke up at Danzig.

segments.title: Leningrad: sables, white nights and Russian choirs
segments.summary: Wooding buys sables and a diamond ring in Leningrad, notes the white nights, and praises the Easter choirs as emotional like spirituals.

segments.title: Glad to forget hardships at home
segments.summary: Asked about keeping up with America, he says he was happy to be out of the hardships of his homeland.

segments.title: Keeping up with Armstrong, Hines and Henderson; teamwork
segments.summary: He says his band was first in the East, and that Fletcher Henderson sacrificed teamwork for sensation.

segments.title: England: Birmingham, the Holborn Empire and Jack Hylton
segments.summary: They played only two dates in England because of a booking at the Negresco in Nice, and he compares Jack Hylton to Paul Whiteman.

segments.title: English audiences and attitudes
segments.summary: English audiences were fine but cooler than German and Danish ones, he says, and acted like an older brother toward America.

segments.title: Managing himself after Lyons left
segments.summary: After Lyons went home, Wooding managed the band himself until returning to America.

segments.chapter: South America and back in New York
segments.title: Buenos Aires: the Tabarin nightclub
segments.summary: Booked through Lombart's Apollo in Paris, the band plays Buenos Aires cabarets full of gauchos and gigolos who sit applauding rather than dance a foxtrot.

segments.chapter: South America and back in New York
segments.title: Tangos and Canaro's St. Louis Blues
segments.summary: The band learned tangos while the leading tango band played St. Louis Blues.

segments.chapter: South America and back in New York
segments.title: The route to South America and the voyage home
segments.summary: They go from Nice via Marseille and Gibraltar to Argentina in eighteen days and return to New York at half fare.

segments.chapter: South America and back in New York
segments.title: Choosing the Ufa Palast in Berlin over the Cotton Club
segments.summary: Back in late 1927, he turns down the Cotton Club for the Ufa Palast presentation in Berlin.

segments.chapter: South America and back in New York
segments.title: A year of vaudeville at Loew's; inspiring Lunceford
segments.summary: He spends about a year in New York playing Loew's vaudeville, including a Great Lakes engagement in Buffalo.

segments.chapter: South America and back in New York
segments.title: Closing interview three; opening interview four; his firsts
segments.summary: Albertson ends the session, opens interview four on April 27, 1975, and notes Wooding was the first to take a jazz band to Russia, record abroad and go to South America.

segments.chapter: South America and back in New York
segments.title: Zurich and an abortive trip to the Matterhorn
segments.summary: On the way to Spain they play Zurich and take a taxi toward the Matterhorn, which proves far farther than it looks.

segments.chapter: South America and back in New York
segments.title: Barcelona: the claque that must be paid
segments.summary: In Barcelona the audience heckles until a fan explains the claque; the producer pays the claque man and the show goes down well.

segments.chapter: South America and back in New York
segments.title: Madrid, the royal visit, bullfights and Moorish-flavoured music
segments.summary: In Madrid they restart the show for the Spanish royals, learn the anthem, and hear Catalonian music he links to the Moors.

segments.chapter: South America and back in New York
segments.title: Same band back from South America; Lyons has him stand up and stop playing
segments.summary: Back in New York with Jerry Blake and Doc Cheatham, he takes Lyons's advice to conduct standing up and loses his piano chops.

segments.chapter: South America and back in New York
segments.title: Showmen replace musicians as bandleaders
segments.summary: He says leaders like Cab Calloway, Noble Sissle, Baron Lee and Lucky Millinder were showmen, so people heard with their eyes.

segments.chapter: South America and back in New York
segments.title: A year of Loew's vaudeville and inspiring Jimmie Lunceford
segments.summary: Lyons books the band for Loew's vaudeville, and in Buffalo the young Lunceford band studies their glee-club number.

segments.chapter: South America and back in New York
segments.title: Turning down the Cotton Club for the Ufa Palast
segments.summary: The band votes for Berlin's Ufa Palast rather than go back to Harlem, a decision Wooding still thinks was right because Duke Ellington's jungle sound suited the club.

segments.chapter: South America and back in New York
segments.title: Lending Louis Metcalf to Duke Ellington
segments.summary: When Edith Wilson asks, Wooding lends trumpeter Louis Metcalf to cover Ellington's show at the Cotton Club, and says Duke had a sound while his band was merely good.

segments.chapter: South America and back in New York
segments.title: Missing Harlem's after-hours clubs while abroad
segments.summary: Wooding says his band was so far ahead that returning put them even with Harlem bands, but he missed breakfast dances and after-hours clubs.

segments.chapter: South America and back in New York
segments.title: Jam sessions at the Nest with Bechet, Dunn and Bussey
segments.summary: Albertson asks about sitting in; Wooding recalls musicians coming up after two in the morning to take choruses on four-beat numbers.

segments.chapter: South America and back in New York
segments.title: Harlem clubs he dropped in on
segments.summary: He names Connie's Inn, Goldgraben's, Edmunds, Connors, Happy Rhone's and the Atlantis Club and after-hours spots.

segments.chapter: South America and back in New York
segments.title: Musicians' restaurants and why a band is everyone's work
segments.summary: Over breakfast at Johnny Johnson's and Glenn's, bands made plans, and he argues every member contributes, comparing it to Notre Dame and baseball teams.

segments.chapter: South America and back in New York
segments.title: Harlem breakfast dances
segments.summary: He describes breakfast dances running from three or four until morning, made by Harlem's beautiful chorus girls.

segments.chapter: South America and back in New York
segments.title: Business contact with whites, never at home
segments.summary: Wooding says he met whites like Lyons only in restaurants and clubs, never homes, and refused invitations that expected him to perform.

segments.chapter: Second European tour and the crash
segments.title: Arthur Lyons leaves for Hollywood; Spadoni sends him back to Europe
segments.summary: Lyons hands his business to his brother and goes to Hollywood, and Wooding returns to Europe under Spadoni through Eddie Duisberg.

segments.chapter: Second European tour and the crash
segments.title: The second European band with Doc Cheatham and Jerry Blake
segments.summary: He lists the new men, Langley, Cheatham, Blake and Freddie Johnson, and says the 1929 Barcelona records show better arranging.

segments.chapter: Second European tour and the crash
segments.title: Ufa Palast, the rise of Hitler and a tour to Vienna
segments.summary: After six weeks at the Ufa Palast and Hamburg, the band tours Spain, Italy and Vienna; he saw Nazi organizing already.

segments.chapter: Second European tour and the crash
segments.title: Playing waltzes and what 'jazz' meant
segments.summary: The band played Blue Danube but audiences wanted jazz, a word Wooding says had sexual undertones.

segments.chapter: Second European tour and the crash
segments.title: Touring Europe on short engagements and the second Barcelona visit
segments.summary: Wooding took whole seasons when places could pay, but mostly stayed under a month, with three months at Haus Germania in Berlin.

segments.chapter: Second European tour and the crash
segments.title: Friendships and sex in Europe
segments.summary: He says they seldom befriended European artists and musicians and instead enjoyed freedom to mix with white women in Europe.

segments.chapter: Second European tour and the crash
segments.title: Staying in Europe, the crash and the lawyer Hare's warning
segments.summary: Planning to settle in Europe with about $25,000, he joins a Russian and a Frenchman in a business despite the American lawyer's warning.

segments.chapter: Second European tour and the crash
segments.title: Losing his savings in a waterproofing venture
segments.summary: He puts about $25,000 into a waterproof handkerchief formula, loses it all, and resolves not to look back.

segments.chapter: Second European tour and the crash
segments.title: First concert by a Black band in Copenhagen
segments.summary: The Chocolate Kiddies Orchestra gives its own concert in February 1931 at the Odd Fellow Palais and then about ten others.

segments.chapter: Second European tour and the crash
segments.title: Jazz treatments of Tannhauser and the 1812 Overture
segments.summary: He describes the band's modern versions of Wagner and Rimsky-Korsakov and a bells-and-cannon 1812 Overture.

segments.chapter: Second European tour and the crash
segments.title: Paul Whiteman's concert, and the Italian helper on classical numbers
segments.summary: Wooding recalls Whiteman's Rhapsody in Blue concert and the young Italian who helped adapt classical excerpts.

segments.chapter: Second European tour and the crash
segments.title: Politiken Christmas concert and how far Black Americans have come
segments.summary: He recalls sharing a bill with the Danish Symphony and says Europe gave freedom, while America now has Black mayors.

segments.chapter: Second European tour and the crash
segments.title: Going home so his child would be born American
segments.summary: With his wife pregnant and citizenship in doubt, he decides to go home at Christmas 1931.

segments.chapter: Second European tour and the crash
segments.title: Nazi pressure voids his Haus Germania contract
segments.summary: He explains that his Berlin birthday-gift contract was barred because the rising Nazi Party did not want American or Black music.

segments.chapter: Second European tour and the crash
segments.title: London Savoy contract cancelled
segments.summary: The Savoy booking collapsed after American bands barred Jack Hylton, so he returned home.

segments.chapter: Second European tour and the crash
segments.title: Willy Lewis and Johnny Mitchell stranded in Europe
segments.summary: Some band members, like Willy Lewis and Johnny Mitchell, stayed and were caught in Germany during the war.

segments.title: Back into the Depression and organizing a new band
segments.summary: Wooding returns during the Depression, which Harlem hardly noticed, and forms a band with Sid Catlett, Frankie Newton, Albert Nicholas and Bernard Addison.

segments.title: Freelancing, the Arcadia and the Pleasure Beach Park collapse
segments.summary: The band plays Broadway's Arcadia then Pleasure Beach Park, where three alcoholic players ruin it and key men leave.

segments.title: Starting the Sam Wooding Choir in Philadelphia
segments.summary: Giving up bands, he forms a 25-voice a cappella choir, the Southland Singers, shaped by Russian bass singing and his Temple studies.

segments.title: Finishing high school and earning degrees at Pennsylvania
segments.summary: After Pearl Harbor his choir members go into defense work, so he returns to school, earning bachelor's and master's degrees at the University of Pennsylvania.

segments.title: The quiet years after the band ended
segments.summary: Wooding explains his child was born in 1932, he stopped bands in 1934 and stayed home in Philadelphia for a couple of years.

segments.title: The choir tours spirituals and art songs
segments.summary: The choir sang spirituals and Stephen Foster songs in churches and hotels from Canada to Florida and the Adirondacks until the war ended it.

segments.title: Teaching Clifford Brown in Wilmington and meeting him in Paris
segments.summary: He remembers Clifford Brown as a quiet, hard-working student he taught embouchure, and who later found him in Paris with Rae Harrison.

segments.title: Why he quit teaching in Wilmington
segments.summary: Wooding quit after classes of forty with few serious students and a principal telling him not to bother teaching music reading.

segments.title: His best Wilmington students and a bassist's death
segments.summary: He had ten good players in the band, including a girl bassist expelled from school who died after an abortion.

segments.chapter: New York choir and Rae Harrison
segments.title: The New York choir, Kenneth Spencer and meeting Rae Harrison
segments.summary: Moving to New York in 1947 he starts a new Sam Wooding Choir that performs the Ballad for Americans with Kenneth Spencer at Carnegie Hall.

segments.chapter: New York choir and Rae Harrison
segments.title: Indifference to bop; teaching Rae Harrison in his studio
segments.summary: He avoided bands after the Pleasure Beach affair, taught Rae Harrison in his studio and took her to Europe as manager and accompanist.

segments.chapter: New York choir and Rae Harrison
segments.title: Manager Eddie Duisberg warns him to leave Europe
segments.summary: Duisberg told him the political situation would bar him from Berlin, and they later reunited in Majorca.

segments.chapter: New York choir and Rae Harrison
segments.title: Back in Philadelphia, the choir with band effects, and Lud Gluskin
segments.summary: He returns to Philadelphia, builds a choir with band-like effects, never records, and mentions his friend Lud Gluskin at CBS.

segments.chapter: New York choir and Rae Harrison
segments.title: End of interview four
segments.summary: Albertson ends the session, planning to cover Rae Harrison and the band next time.

segments.title: Sam Wooding biography and achievements sheet
segments.summary: An appended biography listing Wooding's firsts, publications mentioning him and concert venues.

segments.title: News article on the Sam Wooding-Rae Harrison memorial concert
segments.summary: A newspaper clipping describing their Mt. Morris Presbyterian Church benefit concert of sweet and sacred jazz.

segments.title: Typist's queries and name-check notes
segments.summary: Handwritten and typed notes listing page numbers and questions about names and spellings for the transcript.
